source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE guidance

options.rationale: Her Wells score is high (greater than 4, 'PE likely'); D-dimer should not be used as a rule-out and CTPA is the first-line imaging. Empirical anticoagulation (LMWH or DOAC) is recommended while awaiting imaging if it is delayed beyond a few hours and bleeding risk is acceptable (eTG; THANZ; BTS).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE guidance

options.rationale: V/Q is correct when CTPA is contraindicated (severe contrast allergy, severe renal impairment, pregnancy where V/Q may be preferred). With normal renal function and no allergy, CTPA is first-line. V/Q would be the correct first choice only with contrast contraindication or in pregnancy with normal CXR (eTG; THANZ).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE guidance

options.rationale: Delaying imaging in a high-probability patient is unsafe; PE mortality is concentrated in the first 24 hours. D-dimer is not a screening test independent of pretest probability. Repeat D-dimer is essentially never correct in suspected acute PE (eTG; THANZ).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE guidance

options.rationale: Lower-limb US is useful when chest imaging is contraindicated (e.g., pregnancy with negative initial workup) or to add evidence in equivocal cases. It is not first-line when PE is the principal clinical concern with high pretest probability; a positive US confirms VTE but a negative US does not exclude PE (eTG; THANZ).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE guidance

explanation.summary: Risk stratification of acute PE uses haemodynamic status, sPESI, RV dysfunction (echo or CT), and cardiac biomarkers. Low-risk PE (sPESI 0, no RV strain, normal biomarkers) can be managed as an outpatient with DOAC monotherapy. Intermediate and high-risk PE require admission, and high-risk (shock) PE may need thrombolysis.
key_points: sPESI: age greater than 80, malignancy, chronic cardiopulmonary disease, HR greater than or equal to 110, SBP less than 100, SpO2 less than 90 percent
sPESI 0 = low risk, suitable for outpatient management
DOAC monotherapy first-line: apixaban or rivaroxaban (no bridging)
Apixaban 10 mg BD x 7 days then 5 mg BD
Rivaroxaban 15 mg BD x 21 days then 20 mg daily
Minimum 3 months anticoagulation; consider extended therapy if unprovoked
explanation.pearls: A long-haul flight makes the PE provoked, which typically caps anticoagulation duration at 3 months once the risk factor has resolved.

sources.label: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE guidance

options.rationale: sPESI score of 0 (no malignancy, no chronic cardiopulmonary disease, age less than 80, HR less than 110, SBP greater than or equal to 100, SpO2 greater than or equal to 90 percent) indicates low-risk PE suitable for outpatient management with a DOAC; apixaban regimen is 10 mg BD for 7 days then 5 mg BD for at least 3 months (eTG; THANZ).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE guidance

options.rationale: Warfarin is no longer first-line for unprovoked PE without contraindications to DOACs; DOAC monotherapy avoids parenteral bridging and INR monitoring. Warfarin remains correct for antiphospholipid syndrome (triple positive), severe renal impairment, mechanical valves, or where DOACs are unavailable/contraindicated (THANZ; eTG).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE guidance

options.rationale: Thrombolysis is reserved for high-risk (massive) PE with haemodynamic instability (sustained hypotension, shock) or selected intermediate-high-risk with deterioration. He is haemodynamically stable with no RV strain. Thrombolysis would only be correct with SBP <90 sustained, cardiac arrest, or progressive RV failure on therapeutic anticoagulation (eTG; THANZ).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE guidance

options.rationale: IVC filters are reserved for absolute contraindications to anticoagulation or recurrent PE despite therapeutic anticoagulation. Recent long-haul flight is a transient provoking factor that justifies anticoagulation for 3 months but is not a contraindication. IVC filter would be correct only with active major bleeding precluding anticoagulation (eTG; THANZ).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE guidance

options.rationale: Aspirin alone is inadequate for acute PE treatment; therapeutic anticoagulation for at least 3 months is mandatory. Aspirin has a role in extended secondary prevention AFTER initial 6-12 months of therapeutic anticoagulation in low-recurrence-risk patients (ASPIRE/WARFASA trials), not as initial treatment (eTG; THANZ).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE guidance

explanation.summary: Australian severity scoring for CAP uses SMART-COP (intensive-support prediction) alongside CURB-65 (mortality prediction). SMART-COP greater than or equal to 5 indicates high risk of needing inotropic or respiratory support, warranting HDU/ICU. Severe CAP empirical therapy in Australia is IV ceftriaxone plus IV azithromycin (or doxycycline) to cover Streptococcus pneumoniae plus atypicals.
key_points: SMART-COP: S BP less than 90 (2), M ultilobar (1), A lbumin less than 35 (1), R R greater than or equal to 25 (greater than or equal to 50 yo) (1), T achycardia greater than or equal to 125 (1), C onfusion (1), O xygen low (2), P H less than 7.35 (2)
SMART-COP greater than or equal to 5 = high risk of intensive support
CURB-65: Confusion, Urea greater than 7, RR greater than or equal to 30, BP less than 90 sys or less than or equal to 60 dia, age greater than or equal to 65
Severe CAP: IV ceftriaxone + IV azithromycin (or doxycycline)
Step down to oral after 48 hours of clinical improvement
explanation.pearls: SMART-COP outperforms CURB-65 for predicting ICU need in younger patients - use both.

options.rationale: His SMART-COP is high (multilobar + RR + oxygenation + albumin + SBP scores >=5), indicating high risk of needing intensive respiratory or vasopressor support. Oral therapy and general ward miss this. CURB-65 can underestimate severity in younger patients. Oral amoxicillin + doxycycline is correct for low-severity CAP (SMART-COP 0-2, CURB-65 0-1) (eTG Respiratory).

SMART-COP greater than or equal to 5 indicates a high risk of needing intensive respiratory or vasopressor support and warrants HDU/ICU-level care. Empirical therapy for severe CAP in Australia is IV ceftriaxone plus IV azithromycin (Therapeutic Guidelines Respiratory).

Even if CURB-65 is reassuring at 1, his hypotension, hypoxia, multilobar disease, and biochemical derangements meet inpatient criteria. SMART-COP is more sensitive for need for intensive support in younger patients. Outpatient moxifloxacin would be correct only for low-severity CAP without inpatient indications (eTG Respiratory).

Benzylpenicillin monotherapy does not cover Mycoplasma, Legionella, or atypicals and is inadequate for severe CAP requiring ICU-level support. Benzylpenicillin can be used in confirmed pneumococcal pneumonia without atypical concern, but not as empirical therapy for severe CAP (eTG Respiratory).

Broad-spectrum antipseudomonal + MRSA cover is reserved for risk factors: structural lung disease (bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis), recent hospitalisation, recent broad-spectrum antibiotics, MRSA colonisation, or aspiration with structural disease. He has none of these. This combination would only be correct with documented risk factors or culture-directed therapy (eTG Respiratory).

explanation.summary: Aspiration pneumonia empirical therapy in Australian guidelines is amoxicillin-clavulanate (IV or oral depending on severity), which covers typical respiratory pathogens plus oral anaerobes. Routine addition of metronidazole is no longer recommended. Severity escalates to broader cover only with structural lung disease, recent hospitalisation, or prior MDRO. Address modifiable risk factors: dysphagia management, oral care, head-of-bed elevation, medication review for sedatives.
key_points: Empirical: amoxicillin-clavulanate (IV 1.2 g 8-hourly, oral 875+125 mg BD)
Routine metronidazole addition no longer recommended
Broaden if recent hospitalisation, structural lung disease, MDRO risk
Address dysphagia, oral hygiene, sedative review
Aspiration pneumonitis (chemical) does not need antibiotics unless secondary infection
explanation.pearls: Distinguish aspiration pneumonitis (acute chemical injury, no antibiotics) from aspiration pneumonia (clinical infection, antibiotics) - the time course matters.

options.rationale: Amoxicillin-clavulanate is the standard empirical choice for community-onset aspiration pneumonia without risk factors, but her recent hospitalisation and broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure within 90 days place her in the higher-risk category requiring broader empirical cover (eTG Respiratory).

Recent hospitalisation plus recent broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure are eTG-listed risk factors for Gram-negatives including Pseudomonas in aspiration pneumonia; broader empirical cover with piperacillin-tazobactam is recommended pending cultures, with de-escalation once organism known (eTG Respiratory; Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic).
Amoxicillin alone lacks beta-lactamase coverage for oral anaerobes and Gram-negatives, and oral therapy is inappropriate in this severity with hypoxia and confusion (eTG Respiratory).

Ceftriaxone-metronidazole does not cover Pseudomonas and is less appropriate given her recent ceftriaxone exposure; routine metronidazole is no longer recommended by eTG even when amoxicillin-clavulanate is used (Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic).

Vancomycin plus ciprofloxacin lacks adequate anaerobic cover and empirical vancomycin is not indicated without MRSA risk factors; recent fluoroquinolone exposure also makes empirical ciprofloxacin a poor choice (eTG Respiratory).

explanation.summary: Cardioversion of AF requires either 3 weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation pre-procedure, or TOE-guided cardioversion to exclude left atrial appendage thrombus if duration is greater than 48 hours or uncertain. Even with less than 48 hour duration, peri-cardioversion anticoagulation is recommended and must continue for at least 4 weeks post-cardioversion (atrial stunning); longer-term continuation is governed by CHA2DS2-VA score.
key_points: AF greater than 48 hours or uncertain: 3 weeks anticoagulation OR TOE-guided cardioversion
Minimum 4 weeks anticoagulation post-cardioversion (atrial stunning)
Long-term continuation by CHA2DS2-VA
TOE is alternative when early cardioversion preferred
Aspirin is inadequate peri-cardioversion
explanation.pearls: The 48-hour window is widely misquoted - if duration is uncertain, treat as greater than 48 hours and either anticoagulate for 3 weeks or get a TOE.

options.rationale: The 48-hour window applies only when AF onset is genuinely certain; his earlier symptomatic episode 4 days ago makes total duration uncertain, mandating either 3 weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation or a TOE before cardioversion (CSANZ/NHFA AF 2018).

When AF onset is uncertain or greater than 48 hours, CSANZ requires either 3 weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation or TOE-guided cardioversion; anticoagulation must continue for at least 4 weeks post-cardioversion due to atrial stunning, independent of CHA2DS2-VA score, which only governs longer-term anticoagulation.
Aspirin provides no useful stroke protection peri-cardioversion; therapeutic anticoagulation with heparin, LMWH, DOAC, or warfarin is required (CSANZ/NHFA AF 2018).

Indefinite deferral of rhythm control loses the symptomatic benefit of restoring sinus rhythm in a first symptomatic episode (EAST-AFNET 4); rate control alone does not exempt from anticoagulation decisions guided by CHA2DS2-VA.

Pill-in-pocket flecainide is reserved for selected patients with structurally normal hearts, established rhythm-control plan, and proven safety under monitored conditions; it is not appropriate as a first cardioversion attempt in untreated AF with uncertain duration (CSANZ/NHFA AF 2018).

explanation.summary: Acute breathlessness in the elderly with multiple plausible aetiologies is best disambiguated by integrating bedside POCUS (B-lines, pleural effusion, RV size), biomarkers (NT-proBNP very high favours HF; troponin minor elevation often demand), CXR pattern (upper lobe diversion, Kerley B), and pretest probability for PE (already on therapeutic DOAC reduces probability). Treat the dominant diagnosis first; reassess at 4 to 6 hours and escalate imaging if response is inadequate.
key_points: NT-proBNP greater than 4000 ng/L strongly favours HF as the dominant problem
D-dimer is non-specific in HF, AF, recent infection - do not over-interpret
POCUS B-lines plus elevated JVP plus upper lobe diversion = cardiogenic congestion
Therapeutic DOAC compliance significantly reduces PE probability
Demand troponin in AF with RVR and HF is common and stable
explanation.pearls: Reach for the diuretic first, the CTPA second - reassess at 6 hours and pivot if her congestion improves but hypoxia persists.

sources.label: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE guidance

options.rationale: Clinical, biochemical, and POCUS evidence (elevated JVP, NT-proBNP greater than 4000, B-lines, upper lobe diversion, congestion) points to ADHF as the primary problem; the elevated D-dimer is non-specific in HF and AF on apixaban makes PE unlikely. Initial management is decongestion with IV diuretic and nitrate, with CTPA reserved for inadequate response or evolving features of PE (Heart Foundation/CSANZ HF; eTG; THANZ).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE guidance

options.rationale: She is therapeutically anticoagulated on apixaban (PE on apixaban is rare and would usually present with focal pleuritic pain/hypoxia), has no haemodynamic instability, and her picture is dominated by congestive features (raised JVP, B-lines, BNP >4000). D-dimer is non-specifically elevated in HF and AF and is not a rule-in test. This would be correct if presentation were dominated by pleuritic chest pain, focal hypoxia, or RV strain on POCUS (THANZ; eTG).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE guidance

options.rationale: She is afebrile with no productive cough or focal consolidation; CXR pattern (upper lobe diversion, B-lines) and BNP favour congestion not infection. Antibiotics in cardiogenic pulmonary oedema are antibiotic stewardship failures. Severe CAP empirical therapy would be correct with fever, focal consolidation, raised inflammatory markers, and absent congestion (eTG Respiratory).

The minor troponin elevation is stable and likely demand-related from rapid AF and decompensated HF; there is no ECG evidence of STEMI and no NSTEMI dynamic rise/fall pattern. Type 2 MI from demand ischaemia is managed by treating the underlying decompensation. PPCI is correct only with STEMI (or equivalent) ECG (Heart Foundation/CSANZ ACS).

Shotgun therapy without diagnostic clarity exposes her to harm: broad antibiotics in non-infection, additional anticoagulation on therapeutic apixaban risks bleeding. Uncertainty is better resolved by bedside disambiguation than by combination empiricism. Combination therapy is correct only when truly undifferentiated and bridging is essential (e.g., undifferentiated shock with sepsis and PE both plausible) (Heart Foundation/CSANZ HF; eTG).

explanation.summary: When primary PCI cannot deliver first medical contact to balloon under 120 minutes, fibrinolysis (tenecteplase) plus aspirin, clopidogrel and enoxaparin is the pharmaco-invasive standard, with transfer for angiography 3 to 24 hours later.
key_points: Reperfusion choice is decided by FMC-to-balloon time, not geography per se
Clopidogrel pairs with lysis; ticagrelor/prasugrel pair with primary PCI
RV infarction is preload-dependent: avoid nitrates and diuretics
Pharmaco-invasive angiography 3-24 h after lysis is mandatory, not optional
explanation.context: Inferior STEMI is most often a right coronary artery occlusion. RV involvement raises mortality and requires fluid loading rather than vasodilatation. The 120-minute FMC-to-balloon cut-off reflects evidence that delays beyond that erode the survival advantage of PCI over lysis.

sources.label: Heart Foundation/CSANZ 2016 Australian ACS Clinical Guideline

options.rationale: Inferior STEMI with right ventricular involvement and first medical contact to balloon of 150 minutes exceeds the 120-minute primary PCI window. Heart Foundation/CSANZ pharmaco-invasive pathway is weight-banded tenecteplase plus aspirin, clopidogrel and enoxaparin, followed by transfer for angiography 3 to 24 hours later regardless of clinical course.
source_refs: Heart Foundation/CSANZ 2016 Australian ACS Clinical Guideline

options.rationale: Primary PCI is preferred only when first medical contact to balloon is achievable within 120 minutes. At 150 minutes, delaying reperfusion costs myocardium. This would be correct if the PCI centre were within 60 minutes by road (Heart Foundation/CSANZ).
source_refs: Heart Foundation/CSANZ 2016 Australian ACS Clinical Guideline

options.rationale: Ticagrelor is not used with fibrinolysis because of excess bleeding without ischaemic benefit. Clopidogrel is the preferred P2Y12 inhibitor with lysis. Ticagrelor is appropriate when primary PCI is the reperfusion strategy (Heart Foundation/CSANZ).
source_refs: Heart Foundation/CSANZ 2016 Australian ACS Clinical Guideline

options.rationale: Diagnosis is established on the ECG; troponin is not required to act in STEMI. Nitrates can precipitate profound hypotension in right ventricular infarction, where preload-dependence is critical. This option would be inappropriate even outside the RV setting (eTG).

Conservative management is never appropriate for ST elevation infarction with available reperfusion. Spontaneous reperfusion occurs in a minority and cannot be relied upon. This pathway would be correct only when both lysis and PCI are contraindicated, which is not the case here (Heart Foundation/CSANZ).
source_refs: Heart Foundation/CSANZ 2016 Australian ACS Clinical Guideline

explanation.summary: NSTEMI is risk-stratified into four invasive timing tiers: immediate under 2 hours for instability; early under 24 hours for high-risk; delayed under 72 hours for intermediate; selective for low-risk. GRACE over 140, dynamic ECG and troponin rise all push to the 24-hour pathway.
key_points: GRACE >140 plus dynamic ECG = early invasive (<24 h)
Immediate angiography only for instability or refractory ischaemia
Dynamic troponin rise meeting MI criteria is a high-risk feature
CKD is not a barrier; mitigate contrast nephropathy risk
explanation.context: NSTEMI lacks the time-is-muscle imperative of STEMI but still benefits from prompt revascularisation in high-risk subsets. The GRACE score weights age, vitals, ECG and biomarkers to predict in-hospital mortality and is the dominant trigger for the 24-hour pathway in Australian practice.

sources.label: Heart Foundation/CSANZ 2016 Australian ACS Clinical Guideline

options.rationale: The under-2-hour pathway is reserved for refractory ischaemia, haemodynamic or electrical instability, or mechanical complications. None are present here (Heart Foundation/CSANZ).
source_refs: Heart Foundation/CSANZ 2016 Australian ACS Clinical Guideline

options.rationale: High-risk NSTEMI (GRACE over 140, dynamic ECG change, troponin rise meeting myocardial infarction criteria) warrants invasive angiography within 24 hours per Heart Foundation/CSANZ. She meets all three criteria.
source_refs: Heart Foundation/CSANZ 2016 Australian ACS Clinical Guideline

options.rationale: The 72-hour window is for intermediate-risk patients (GRACE 109-140) without dynamic changes. Her GRACE of 162 with dynamic ST changes places her in the early-invasive group (Heart Foundation/CSANZ).
source_refs: Heart Foundation/CSANZ 2016 Australian ACS Clinical Guideline

options.rationale: Selective/ischaemia-guided strategy is reserved for low-risk presentations (GRACE under 109, no dynamic changes, negative troponin). High-risk biomarker and ECG features override frailty or CKD downgrading (Heart Foundation/CSANZ).
source_refs: Heart Foundation/CSANZ 2016 Australian ACS Clinical Guideline

options.rationale: Stage 3a CKD is not a contraindication; high-risk NSTEMI patients with CKD have greater absolute benefit from early invasive care with contrast minimisation. KHA-CARI supports angiography with periprocedural hydration (KHA-CARI; Heart Foundation/CSANZ).
source_refs: Heart Foundation/CSANZ 2016 Australian ACS Clinical Guideline

explanation.summary: Stable narrow complex regular tachycardia is managed in a stepwise way: vagal manoeuvres (modified Valsalva first), then adenosine 6 then 12 mg, then a rate-controlling agent. Electrical cardioversion is reserved for instability.
key_points: Modified Valsalva (REVERT): supine + 15-second strain + 15-second leg raise
Adenosine 6 mg then 12 mg if needed via large antecubital cannula with flush
Synchronised DC cardioversion if unstable (start 50-100 J biphasic)
Document a 12-lead during and after termination for diagnostic clues
explanation.context: Most regular narrow complex tachycardias are AV-nodal re-entrant or AV re-entrant tachycardia. Both depend on the AV node for re-entry and respond to vagal tone enhancement. A rhythm strip during termination often reveals the mechanism.

sources.label: REVERT trial - Appelboam et al., Lancet 2015

options.rationale: Electrical cardioversion is reserved for haemodynamic instability (hypotension, ischaemia, altered consciousness, pulmonary oedema). She is stable, so vagal manoeuvres and adenosine come first (eTG).

Stable narrow complex regular tachycardia: vagal manoeuvres are first-line. The modified (REVERT trial) Valsalva with supine repositioning and leg raise terminates approximately 43% of episodes versus 17% for standard Valsalva. Adenosine follows if unsuccessful.
source_refs: REVERT trial - Appelboam et al., Lancet 2015

options.rationale: Adenosine is correct after failed vagal manoeuvres in stable SVT. Vagal manoeuvres should not be skipped: they are free, painless and frequently effective. Adenosine causes a brief but intensely unpleasant flushing/chest-pain sensation (eTG).

Beta-blockade can terminate SVT but acts slowly and risks hypotension. It is appropriate as a longer-term rate control agent or for atrial tachycardias, not as the first acute step for stable AV-nodal-dependent SVT (eTG).

Amiodarone has no role in stable narrow complex SVT first-line and carries hypotension, bradycardia and long elimination half-life concerns. It is reserved for refractory broad complex or atrial arrhythmias (eTG).

explanation.summary: Stable monomorphic VT in a patient with prior infarction is managed with intravenous amiodarone; instability mandates synchronised DC cardioversion. Polymorphic VT/torsades is managed with magnesium and correction of the QT trigger.
key_points: Brugada/Vereckei criteria: concordance, AV dissociation, capture/fusion beats = VT
Stable monomorphic VT: amiodarone 300 mg IV over 20-60 min, then 900 mg/24 h
Unstable VT: synchronised DC cardioversion 100-200 J biphasic
Polymorphic VT/torsades: magnesium 2 g, stop QT-prolonging drugs, overdrive pace
explanation.context: When a broad complex tachycardia presents in someone with structural heart disease, the pre-test probability of VT exceeds 95%. Treating it as SVT with aberrancy can be lethal. Default to VT until proven otherwise.

options.rationale: Adenosine in broad complex tachycardia of ventricular origin is ineffective and may accelerate the rhythm if a pre-excited atrial fibrillation is the true diagnosis. With prior infarct and clear VT criteria, adenosine is the wrong drug (eTG).

Stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia in structural heart disease is treated with intravenous amiodarone 300 mg loading over 20 to 60 minutes, then 900 mg over 24 hours. Lidocaine is an alternative, particularly in ischaemic VT, but amiodarone is first-line in Australian practice.

Verapamil in VT can precipitate haemodynamic collapse through negative inotropy and AV block. It is contraindicated in broad complex tachycardia unless fascicular VT is confirmed by an electrophysiologist (eTG).

Beta-blockade in acute monomorphic VT risks hypotension in a patient with impaired ejection fraction and is not a recognised termination agent. It has a role in suppression after termination or for electrical storm (eTG).
Magnesium is first-line for polymorphic VT/torsades de pointes, not monomorphic VT. The northwest axis with concordance and capture beats describes monomorphic VT (eTG).

explanation.summary: ANZCOR adverse features (shock, syncope, ischaemia, heart failure) in any tachyarrhythmia mandate synchronised DC cardioversion. Initial biphasic energies: 70-120 J for narrow regular, 120-150 J for narrow irregular, 100 J for broad regular, escalating to 150 then 200 J.
key_points: Adverse features = synchronised DC cardioversion first, not drugs
Synchronised mode prevents R-on-T induction of VF
Sedate the conscious patient briefly (midazolam ± ketamine/propofol)
Pad placement: anterolateral standard, anteroposterior alternative
explanation.context: The synchronised mode delays delivery to coincide with the R wave. Without sync, a shock landing in the vulnerable T-wave period can precipitate VF. Most modern defibrillators revert to unsynchronised mode after each shock and must be re-armed.

options.rationale: 50 J is reasonable for narrow complex regular tachycardia (atrial flutter) but suboptimal first energy for broad complex VT in an unstable adult (ANZCOR 11.9).

ANZCOR recommends 100 J biphasic synchronised as the initial energy for adult broad complex tachycardia with a pulse, escalating to 150 J then 200 J if unsuccessful. Stacked shocks every 1 to 2 minutes with brief CPR if pulseless arrest develops.
Unsynchronised shock in a perfusing rhythm risks induction of ventricular fibrillation if the shock falls on the T wave. Synchronised mode is mandatory while a pulse is present (ANZCOR 11.9).
Monophasic defibrillators are largely obsolete in Australian practice. If only monophasic available, 200 J synchronised is the starting energy (ANZCOR 11.9).

Pharmacological loading delays definitive treatment in an unstable patient. Electricity is the answer when adverse features are present; antiarrhythmic loading follows successful cardioversion to prevent recurrence (ANZCOR 11.9).

explanation.summary: Torsades de pointes management: magnesium 2 g IV, correct potassium to high-normal (4.5-5.0 mmol/L), withdraw QT-prolonging drugs, and consider overdrive pacing or isoprenaline to shorten QT by accelerating heart rate. Defibrillate (unsynchronised) if pulseless.
key_points: Magnesium first, regardless of baseline level
Aim K 4.5-5.0 mmol/L, Mg over 1.0 mmol/L
Withdraw culprit drugs: many psychiatric, antiemetic, antiarrhythmic, macrolide agents
Overdrive pacing at 90-110 bpm shortens QT if drug measures fail
explanation.context: Torsades arises from early after-depolarisations on a prolonged action potential. Bradycardia exposes the long QT and is often the trigger. The classic cocktail in psychiatric inpatients (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor plus atypical antipsychotic plus hypokalaemia) is high-risk.

options.rationale: Polymorphic VT with a long QT (torsades de pointes) is treated first with intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g irrespective of serum magnesium. Magnesium stabilises the membrane and abolishes early after-depolarisations.
Amiodarone prolongs QT and is contraindicated in torsades. It is appropriate for monomorphic VT (eTG).
Sotalol is a class III antiarrhythmic that further prolongs QT and would worsen torsades (eTG).
Adenosine has no role in polymorphic VT and may transiently prolong QT in susceptible patients (eTG).

Sustained polymorphic VT often cannot be synchronised because of the changing QRS morphology; if persistent or unstable, unsynchronised shock is used (defibrillation). Magnesium is the first pharmacological step in self-terminating runs (ANZCOR 11.9).

explanation.summary: The acute pulmonary oedema triad is loop diuretic, nitrate vasodilator, and non-invasive ventilation. Hold beta-blockers, avoid morphine, withhold fluids, treat the precipitant.
key_points: CPAP/BiPAP reduces preload, afterload and work of breathing
Nitrate is the most effective afterload reducer in hypertensive flash APO
Loop diuretic dose: at least the patient's usual daily oral dose given IV
Identify precipitants: ACS, arrhythmia, non-adherence, infection, anaemia
explanation.context: Decompensation in chronic heart failure is precipitated by an identifiable trigger in over 90% of admissions. Non-adherence to diuretics, dietary salt load, new arrhythmia or silent ACS dominate the differential. The first 90 minutes set the trajectory.

options.rationale: Acute pulmonary oedema with adequate blood pressure is managed with loop diuretic, vasodilator (nitrate) for preload/afterload reduction, and non-invasive ventilation (continuous positive airway pressure or bilevel) which reduces preload, afterload and work of breathing and lowers intubation rate.

Routine morphine is no longer recommended in acute pulmonary oedema because of associations with increased mortality and intubation. Intubation is reserved for non-invasive ventilation failure or impending arrest (NHFA/CSANZ).
Vasopressors are reserved for cardiogenic shock with hypotension. With BP 168/96 she has hypertensive flash pulmonary oedema requiring vasodilatation (NHFA/CSANZ).
Fluid loading worsens pulmonary oedema and is contraindicated. This option pairs an active harm with a correct adjunct (eTG).
Beta-blockade is held or reduced in acute decompensated heart failure with congestion. Initiation in the acute setting risks worsening cardiac output (NHFA/CSANZ).

explanation.summary: Cardiogenic shock without a mechanical complication is managed with noradrenaline to restore mean arterial pressure, dobutamine or milrinone for inotropy, treatment of the cause (urgent revascularisation), and consideration of mechanical circulatory support (intra-aortic balloon pump or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation).
key_points: Noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor (SOAP II, OptimaCC)
Add inotrope (dobutamine/milrinone) once MAP restored
Exclude mechanical complications: VSD, papillary rupture, free wall, tamponade
Early mechanical support discussion with cardiothoracic ICU
explanation.context: Cardiogenic shock complicates approximately 5-10% of STEMI presentations and remains the dominant cause of in-hospital death after acute infarction. Early revascularisation (SHOCK trial) plus protocolised vasoactive support and mechanical support pathways have improved outcomes.

options.rationale: SOAP II and OptimaCC trials show noradrenaline as the preferred first-line vasopressor in cardiogenic shock compared with dopamine and adrenaline, with lower arrhythmia and refractory shock rates. NHFA endorses noradrenaline to restore perfusion pressure while inotropic support is considered.
Dopamine increases arrhythmia and 28-day mortality in the cardiogenic shock subgroup of SOAP II. It is no longer first-line in Australian practice (NHFA).
OptimaCC was stopped early because adrenaline caused more refractory shock and lactic acidosis than noradrenaline. It is reserved for refractory cases or post-arrest physiology (OptimaCC).
Dobutamine is an inodilator and can drop systemic vascular resistance further, worsening hypotension. It is added to a vasopressor (noradrenaline) once mean arterial pressure is restored (NHFA).
Vasopressin is an adjunct when noradrenaline requirements rise or for catecholamine sparing. It is not first-line in cardiogenic shock (NHFA).

explanation.summary: HFrEF foundational therapy comprises four pillars: renin-angiotensin blockade (preferably ARNI), beta-blocker, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, and SGLT2 inhibitor. All four should be initiated and uptitrated before discharge after stabilisation.
key_points: Quadruple therapy initiated simultaneously when stable, not sequenced over months
STRONG-HF: in-hospital rapid uptitration halves 180-day rehospitalisation
SGLT2 inhibitor benefit independent of diabetes status (DAPA-HF, EMPEROR)
Monitor K, creatinine and BP after each titration
explanation.context: The transformation in HFrEF outcomes over the past decade reflects the cumulative effect of four therapies each cutting mortality by approximately 15-25%. Initiating all four at low doses before discharge captures the benefit faster than sequenced outpatient titration.

options.rationale: NHFA/CSANZ recommends all four pillars of HFrEF therapy (ACE inhibitor or ARNI, beta-blocker, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor) initiated during the index admission once euvolaemic and haemodynamically stable. Each provides additive mortality benefit. STRONG-HF demonstrated rapid uptitration during admission halved 180-day rehospitalisation.
Digoxin and ivabradine are second-line for symptomatic relief or rate control after the four pillars are optimised. Neither carries the survival benefit of the foundational therapies (NHFA).
Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are neutral at best in HFrEF; non-dihydropyridines are harmful. Hydralazine-nitrate is reserved for ACE/ARB-intolerant or African ancestry adjunct (NHFA).

Delayed initiation of MRA and SGLT2 inhibitor was the historic pattern and is now superseded by simultaneous quadruple therapy. STRONG-HF showed in-hospital uptitration is safer and more effective (STRONG-HF).

Substitution offers no incremental benefit. If switching, sacubitril-valsartan (ARNI) replaces ACE inhibitor with mortality benefit (PARADIGM-HF), but adding the other pillars is the higher-yield step (NHFA).

explanation.summary: Right ventricular infarction physiology: a stiff, ischaemic right ventricle cannot generate forward flow without high filling pressures. Treatment is fluid loading, avoidance of preload-reducing drugs, and reperfusion.
key_points: V4R ST elevation = right ventricular infarct in inferior STEMI
Avoid nitrates, diuretics and morphine
Fluid bolus 250-500 mL crystalloid, repeat to clinical response
AV block usually resolves with reperfusion
explanation.context: Up to 40% of inferior STEMIs have RV involvement. Recognising the clear lungs with hypotension pattern prevents the reflex error of giving nitrates or diuretics for what looks superficially like heart failure but is the opposite physiology.

sources.label: Heart Foundation/CSANZ 2016 Australian ACS Clinical Guideline

options.rationale: Right ventricular infarction produces preload-dependent low output. Intravenous fluid loading restores right ventricular filling pressures and improves left ventricular preload through ventricular interdependence, typically increasing blood pressure rapidly.
source_refs: Heart Foundation/CSANZ 2016 Australian ACS Clinical Guideline

options.rationale: Nitrates drop preload and can precipitate profound hypotension in right ventricular infarction. They are contraindicated when V4R confirms RV involvement (eTG).
Diuresis worsens the preload-dependent low output state of RV infarction. The lungs are clear; there is no pulmonary congestion to relieve (eTG).
Vasopressor support is reserved for fluid-refractory shock in RV infarction. Fluid loading is the appropriate first manoeuvre (eTG).
AV block in inferior STEMI is usually transient and responds to reperfusion. Pacing is reserved for symptomatic bradycardia unresponsive to atropine and fluid (eTG).

explanation.summary: In decompensated HFrEF, intravenous loop diuretic at a dose at least equal to the total daily oral dose, divided two to three times daily or as infusion. Monitor weight, urine output, electrolytes and renal function daily; escalate or add sequential blockade if response inadequate.
key_points: IV dose at least equal to total daily oral dose (DOSE-AHF)
Switch to IV during congestion: oral absorption is unreliable
Monitor urine output, daily weight, K, creatinine
Sequential blockade (thiazide/metolazone) added for diuretic resistance
explanation.context: Gut wall oedema and splanchnic congestion reduce oral loop diuretic absorption in acute decompensation. The IV route bypasses this. Inadequate initial diuresis predicts prolonged admission and rehospitalisation.

options.rationale: A bolus below her total daily oral dose risks under-diuresis. DOSE-AHF showed equivalent efficacy of 1x versus 2.5x usual oral dose IV, but doses below the usual oral dose are inadequate (DOSE-AHF).

DOSE-AHF supports intravenous loop diuretic at a dose at least equal to the patient's total daily oral dose, typically divided twice or three times daily, or as continuous infusion. Her oral dose is 80 mg twice daily so 80 mg IV twice daily is a reasonable starting dose with response titration.
Gut oedema reduces oral bioavailability in decompensated congestion; intravenous administration is preferred during acute decompensation (NHFA).
Thiazide diuretics are weak monotherapy in heart failure congestion. Sequential nephron blockade with a thiazide is added to a loop in diuretic resistance, not initiated alone (NHFA).
Stopping the mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist removes a survival therapy. Metolazone is a sequential nephron blocker added to a loop in resistance, not first-line (NHFA).

explanation.summary: Mechanical complications of MI (papillary muscle rupture, ventricular septal defect, free wall rupture) typically present 2 to 7 days post-infarct with sudden haemodynamic deterioration. Each is a surgical emergency; medical therapy bridges to theatre.
key_points: Day 2-7 post-MI sudden deterioration = think mechanical complication
Posteromedial papillary muscle has single-vessel (PDA) supply - vulnerable in inferior MI
Echo distinguishes papillary rupture, VSD, free wall rupture, tamponade
Surgery is definitive; medical/mechanical support bridges
explanation.context: The posteromedial papillary muscle receives blood from a single source (the posterior descending artery), whereas the anterolateral papillary muscle has dual supply. This explains why posteromedial rupture is more common after inferior MI. Time-critical surgical referral, not further medical optimisation, defines outcome.

sources.label: Heart Foundation/CSANZ 2016 Australian ACS Clinical Guideline

options.rationale: Acute papillary muscle rupture causing severe mitral regurgitation is a surgical emergency with mortality exceeding 50% medically; emergency mitral valve repair or replacement is the only definitive treatment. Inferior STEMI predisposes via single-supply RCA territory to the posteromedial papillary muscle.
source_refs: Heart Foundation/CSANZ 2016 Australian ACS Clinical Guideline

options.rationale: Papillary muscle rupture is a mechanical, not ischaemic, complication; the artery has already been revascularised. Cath lab is not the answer (Heart Foundation/CSANZ).
source_refs: Heart Foundation/CSANZ 2016 Australian ACS Clinical Guideline

options.rationale: Medical therapy alone in acute papillary muscle rupture is associated with greater than 50% mortality at 24 hours. Diuretics palliate but do not address the structural defect (ESC/EACTS).
Beta-blockade in cardiogenic shock with new severe regurgitation worsens output. The mechanical complication requires surgery, not pharmacological optimisation (ESC/EACTS).
Mechanical support is a bridge to surgery in this setting, not definitive therapy. It reduces afterload while transfer and theatre are arranged but does not repair the valve (ESC/EACTS).

explanation.summary: Stable atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response is managed first with rate control (beta-blocker or non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker). Rhythm control may be added when symptoms persist or in selected groups (younger, first episode, heart failure). Stroke prevention is decided by CHA2DS2-VASc and uses oral anticoagulation, not aspirin.
key_points: Beta-blocker or non-dihydropyridine CCB first-line rate control
Digoxin reserved for HFrEF or where rate cannot be achieved
Cardioversion within 48 h onset without TOE if anticoagulation is started
Aspirin is not stroke prevention in AF
explanation.context: Atrial fibrillation affects approximately 2% of Australian adults rising to over 10% above age 75. The decision tree separates rate vs rhythm control, anticoagulation, and reversible precipitant search (sepsis, hyperthyroidism, ischaemia, alcohol).

options.rationale: Stable atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response and onset under 48 hours: rate control with a beta-blocker is first-line per NHFA/CSANZ atrial fibrillation guidelines. Rhythm control with cardioversion is an alternative but does not improve mortality and requires anticoagulation pre and post.
Electrical cardioversion is reasonable in onset under 48 hours but is not the default first step in a stable patient. Rate control is simpler and avoids procedural risks (NHFA/CSANZ).
Amiodarone is reserved for rate or rhythm control when beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers are contraindicated or ineffective, given its long-term toxicity profile (eTG).
Digoxin is second-line for rate control in patients with heart failure or beta-blocker intolerance, and has slow onset and weak effect during sympathetic activation (eTG).
Aspirin has no role in stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation (NHFA, ESC). At CHA2DS2-VASc 1 in men, oral anticoagulation is considered (not mandated); aspirin is not a substitute.

explanation.summary: Triple therapy after percutaneous coronary intervention in anticoagulated patients is now limited to a brief peri-procedural window; dual therapy (clopidogrel plus oral anticoagulant) for up to 12 months, then anticoagulant monotherapy, is the Australian-endorsed pathway (AUGUSTUS).
key_points: Drop aspirin after the index admission week; continue clopidogrel + apixaban
12 months total of dual therapy, then anticoagulant alone
Apixaban 2.5 mg BD only if two of: age >=80, weight <=60 kg, creatinine >=133 µmol/L
Avoid ticagrelor + anticoagulant combinations
explanation.context: The triple therapy era assumed additive ischaemic benefit but caused unacceptable bleeding. Four large randomised controlled trials (PIONEER-AF, RE-DUAL PCI, AUGUSTUS, ENTRUST-AF) converged on the dual-therapy approach now adopted in NHFA/CSANZ guidance.

options.rationale: Triple therapy (DAPT plus anticoagulant) beyond a brief peri-procedural window markedly increases bleeding without ischaemic benefit. AUGUSTUS, PIONEER-AF and ENTRUST-AF showed dual therapy (single antiplatelet plus oral anticoagulant) is preferred (NHFA).

AUGUSTUS demonstrated that omitting aspirin (after a short peri-procedural week or so) and continuing clopidogrel plus apixaban reduces bleeding without increasing ischaemic events. After 12 months, single oral anticoagulant alone is continued. Apixaban dosing 5 mg BD is correct (she meets no two of age >=80, weight <=60, creatinine >=133 µmol/L).
Ticagrelor in combination with anticoagulation is not recommended due to excess bleeding (NHFA). Warfarin offers no advantage over direct oral anticoagulants in this setting (AUGUSTUS).

Stent thrombosis risk after percutaneous coronary intervention is unacceptably high without any antiplatelet for the first 6 to 12 months. A single antiplatelet (clopidogrel) is required with the anticoagulant during this window (NHFA).
After stent insertion, the antiplatelet of choice in dual therapy is clopidogrel, not aspirin. Continuing aspirin instead of clopidogrel is the historic regimen now superseded (AUGUSTUS).

explanation.summary: Refractory cardiogenic shock with rising lactate despite optimal vasoactive support in a young patient without prohibitive comorbidity is an indication for veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation as a bridge to recovery, transplant or durable mechanical support.
key_points: IABP-SHOCK II: intra-aortic balloon pump does not improve mortality
VA-ECMO provides full cardiopulmonary support (4-6 L/min)
Refer early: outcomes degrade once multi-organ failure established
Australian centres operate 24/7 transfer pathways
explanation.context: VA-ECMO drains venous blood, oxygenates it externally and returns it to the arterial system, fully bypassing the heart and lungs. It is a bridge, not destination therapy. Patient selection (age, comorbidity, neurological status, prospects for recovery or transplant) is critical.

options.rationale: Escalating catecholamine doses worsens myocardial oxygen demand, arrhythmia and lactic acidosis without addressing pump failure. OptimaCC and registry data argue against catecholamine stacking in refractory shock (OptimaCC).

Refractory cardiogenic shock in a young patient without prohibitive comorbidity, with rising lactate and end-organ hypoperfusion despite optimal pharmacological support, is the indication for veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation as a bridge to recovery or definitive therapy. Australian extracorporeal life support centres (eg Royal Prince Alfred, St Vincent's Sydney) accept referrals 24/7.

IABP-SHOCK II showed no mortality benefit for intra-aortic balloon pump in cardiogenic shock after MI. It remains an option only as a temporary bridge when ECMO is unavailable, with limited haemodynamic support (~0.5 L/min) (IABP-SHOCK II).

Milrinone is a phosphodiesterase III inhibitor inodilator; in hypotensive cardiogenic shock it worsens systemic vascular resistance and is not the appropriate escalation. It has a role in pulmonary hypertension complicating right heart failure (NHFA).
PCI was completed 8 hours earlier; repeat angiography is indicated only if a new vessel concern arises. The problem is pump failure, not unaddressed ischaemia (NHFA).

explanation.summary: Acute pulmonary oedema with hypotension and severe aortic stenosis demands cautious preload management: diuresis is required for congestion but vasodilatation is hazardous across the fixed obstruction. Non-invasive ventilation reduces work of breathing. Urgent valve intervention is the definitive treatment.
key_points: Severe AS = preload-dependent; avoid nitrates and aggressive vasodilation
Diuresis is required despite hypotension - congestion will worsen it further
NIV reduces afterload and work of breathing without dropping preload acutely
Definitive treatment is SAVR or TAVI
explanation.context: Severe aortic stenosis is the most common indication for surgical or transcatheter valve replacement in Australia. Decompensated heart failure in this group has high in-hospital mortality without intervention. Acute pharmacological vasodilation, particularly nitrates, is a recognised cause of catastrophic hypotension.

options.rationale: Nitrates in severe aortic stenosis can precipitate profound hypotension because cardiac output is preload-dependent across a fixed obstruction. Vasodilatation is hazardous (eTG).

In hypotensive pulmonary oedema with severe aortic stenosis, the priority is gentle pulmonary decongestion (loop diuretic) and ventilatory support to reduce work of breathing without dropping preload. Avoid vasodilators and beta-blockers acutely; consider urgent cardiology and cardiothoracic input for valve intervention.
Fluid loading worsens pulmonary oedema; morphine increases mortality in acute heart failure. Both interventions are contraindicated (NHFA).
Beta-blockade in acute decompensated heart failure with severe aortic stenosis and hypotension can precipitate haemodynamic collapse. It is held during acute decompensation (NHFA).

Vasopressors are reserved for shock with low systemic vascular resistance or as a bridge in severe aortic stenosis with critical hypoperfusion. The first step is decongestion plus non-invasive ventilation; vasopressors are an escalation if needed (eTG).

explanation.summary: Type 2 myocardial infarction arises from oxygen supply-demand mismatch (sepsis, anaemia, hypoxia, hypotension, tachyarrhythmia) without atherothrombosis. Management targets the precipitant, not antiplatelet/antithrombotic therapy.
key_points: Type 1: plaque rupture, thrombosis; treat with ACS pathway
Type 2: supply-demand mismatch; treat the precipitant
Troponin rise alone does not equal type 1 MI
Routine angiography in type 2 lacks evidence of benefit
explanation.context: The Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction distinguishes five types. Type 2 is increasingly recognised in unwell inpatients and is associated with poor short-term mortality driven by the underlying condition rather than the cardiac event itself.

sources.label: Heart Foundation/CSANZ 2016 Australian ACS Clinical Guideline
Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction 2018

options.rationale: This is type 2 myocardial infarction (supply-demand mismatch from sepsis, hypoxia and tachycardia), not type 1 atherothrombotic infarction. Management targets the precipitant. Antiplatelet/anticoagulant therapy in type 2 MI has no proven benefit and carries bleeding harm (Fourth Universal Definition of MI; Heart Foundation/CSANZ).
source_refs: Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction 2018
Heart Foundation/CSANZ 2016 Australian ACS Clinical Guideline

options.rationale: The invasive NSTE-ACS pathway applies to type 1 myocardial infarction. Applying it to type 2 risks bleeding without benefit (Fourth Universal Definition).
source_refs: Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction 2018

options.rationale: Aspirin in type 2 myocardial infarction has weak evidence and may add bleeding risk in unwell elderly inpatients. Treating the precipitant is the priority (Fourth Universal Definition).
source_refs: Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction 2018

options.rationale: Thrombolysis is reserved for ST-elevation infarction when primary PCI is not timely available. It has no role in type 2 myocardial infarction (Heart Foundation/CSANZ).
source_refs: Heart Foundation/CSANZ 2016 Australian ACS Clinical Guideline

options.rationale: Routine angiography after type 2 myocardial infarction is not indicated unless ongoing symptoms or features suggest underlying coronary disease that would change management. Risk-stratify outpatient with non-invasive imaging if clinically warranted (Fourth Universal Definition).
source_refs: Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction 2018

explanation.summary: Heart failure 30-day readmission is reduced by multidisciplinary discharge bundles: early nurse review (7 to 14 days), structured education, medication uptitration to target doses, and clear self-care/red-flag advice.
key_points: Early review (7-14 days) by HF nurse or GP
Cardiology review within 6 weeks
Telephone/telehealth substitution acceptable for rural patients
Discharge bundle includes weight diary and reasons-to-call card
explanation.context: Hospital readmission within 30 days affects 20-25% of Australian heart failure discharges and is the single largest cost in chronic heart failure care. Multidisciplinary post-discharge programs (such as the Heart Foundation's Connecting Hearts) demonstrably reduce this.

options.rationale: NHFA recommends early post-discharge review within 7 to 14 days by a heart failure nurse or general practitioner for clinical assessment, medication uptitration and reinforcement of self-care, with cardiology review within 6 weeks. Early follow-up reduces 30-day readmission.
Three-month review misses the window when uptitration and decompensation events occur most frequently. Heart failure readmission peaks in the first 30 days (NHFA).
Symptom-triggered follow-up defers titration and self-management education, both of which are key drivers of readmission reduction (NHFA).
Unstructured discharge is associated with 30-day readmission rates over 20%. Multidisciplinary follow-up is standard (NHFA).

Transplantation assessment is reserved for advanced HFrEF (NYHA III-IV despite optimal therapy, recurrent admissions, dependence on inotropic support) in selected younger patients. Her course does not yet warrant referral (NHFA).

explanation.summary: Unstable bradycardia from complete heart block requires immediate pacing. Transcutaneous pacing under sedation is the bridge to transvenous pacing and definitive permanent pacemaker. Atropine has limited effect on infranodal block.
key_points: Adverse features (shock, syncope, ischaemia, heart failure) define instability
Atropine max 3 mg total; ineffective in infranodal block
Transcutaneous pacing - sedate, check capture (mechanical and electrical)
Isoprenaline or adrenaline infusion is alternative chemical bridge
explanation.context: Complete heart block with a broad QRS escape suggests block below the AV node (infranodal), often Mobitz II progressing. Such blocks rarely respond to atropine because atropine's effect is on the AV node itself. Pacing - electrical or chemical - is the answer.

options.rationale: Atropine has limited effect in infranodal block (broad QRS escape, complete heart block with high-grade nodal disease). Maximum dose is 3 mg total; further atropine is unlikely to work and delays definitive therapy (ANZCOR 11.9).

Unstable bradycardia (hypotension, syncope) unresponsive to atropine is managed with transcutaneous pacing as a bridge to transvenous pacing and permanent pacemaker. Sedation is essential as transcutaneous pacing is painful. Isoprenaline or adrenaline infusion is an alternative chemical bridge.
Routine listing fails to address the immediate unstable bradycardia. Pacing is required now; permanent device follows after stabilisation (ANZCOR 11.9).
Amiodarone slows AV conduction and could worsen the block. It is contraindicated (eTG).
Fluid does not address an electrical conduction block. It may briefly support filling pressure but is not the corrective intervention (eTG).

explanation.summary: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection is a non-atherosclerotic cause of acute coronary syndrome, predominantly affecting younger women, peripartum patients and those with fibromuscular dysplasia. Conservative management is preferred unless ongoing ischaemia or instability mandates intervention. Routine percutaneous coronary intervention, thrombolysis and dual antiplatelet duration differ from atherothrombotic care.
key_points: Conservative care: most lesions heal in 4-6 weeks
PCI reserved for ongoing ischaemia/instability; high complication rate
Thrombolysis contraindicated (haematoma propagation)
Screen for fibromuscular dysplasia in extracoronary beds
explanation.context: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection accounts for up to 35% of acute coronary syndrome in women under 50 in Australian registries. The mechanism is intramural haematoma in the coronary wall rather than plaque rupture, which is why the standard atherosclerotic ACS toolkit (stenting, lytic therapy, long dual antiplatelet) does not apply.

sources.label: European Society of Cardiology Position Paper on SCAD 2018

options.rationale: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection with preserved flow and no ongoing ischaemia is managed conservatively; most heal spontaneously over 4 to 6 weeks. Percutaneous coronary intervention in spontaneous coronary artery dissection often propagates the dissection. Single antiplatelet (aspirin) and beta-blocker are standard; dual antiplatelet duration is debated and shorter in spontaneous coronary artery dissection than in atherosclerotic ACS.
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology Position Paper on SCAD 2018

options.rationale: PCI in spontaneous coronary artery dissection has high complication rates (dissection propagation, intramural haematoma extension, stent malapposition once healing occurs). Reserved for ongoing ischaemia, haemodynamic instability or left main involvement (AHA).

Coronary artery bypass grafting in spontaneous coronary artery dissection is technically challenging because of the dissected friable wall and limited landing zones. Reserved for left main spontaneous coronary artery dissection or failed conservative management (AHA).
Thrombolysis in spontaneous coronary artery dissection can propagate the intramural haematoma and is contraindicated (AHA).

Spontaneous coronary artery dissection is not atherosclerotic; statins are not indicated unless other indications exist. Dual antiplatelet duration is shorter than in atherothrombotic ACS, often single antiplatelet alone is preferred (European Society of Cardiology).
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology Position Paper on SCAD 2018

explanation.summary: NSW Health DKA pathway: first hour is 1 L 0.9% saline plus fixed-rate insulin infusion 0.1 unit/kg/h. Add 5% glucose alongside saline when BGL falls below 14 mmol/L to allow continued insulin (which clears ketones) without causing hypoglycaemia. Potassium replacement starts in the second bag once K <5.5 mmol/L.
key_points: 0.9% saline 1 L hour 1, then titrate to deficit (typically 6-10 L deficit)
Fixed-rate insulin 0.1 unit/kg/h; do not bolus
Add 10% glucose when BGL <14 to maintain insulin while preventing hypoglycaemia
Continue subcutaneous long-acting insulin during DKA treatment if type 1 diabetic
explanation.context: DKA pathophysiology: absolute insulin deficiency drives lipolysis and hepatic ketogenesis (beta-hydroxybutyrate, acetoacetate), producing an anion gap metabolic acidosis. Hyperglycaemia causes osmotic diuresis with severe sodium, water and potassium losses. Total body potassium is depleted even when serum potassium appears normal or high (extracellular shift from acidosis and insulin deficiency). Insulin reverses ketogenesis (its primary therapeutic effect) and drives potassium intracellularly, hence the need for aggressive replacement once treatment starts.

sources.label: NSW Health Adult DKA management guideline

options.rationale: NSW Health adult DKA pathway: restore circulating volume first with 0.9% saline 1000 mL over the first hour, then commence fixed-rate insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/h. Insulin started simultaneously with adequate volume resuscitation, not before, to avoid worsening hypotension as glucose-driven osmotic shift reverses.
source_refs: NSW Health Adult DKA management guideline

options.rationale: Bolus insulin is not recommended in adult DKA per NSW Health and JBDS-IP pathways. It risks rapid potassium shift and adds nothing over the fixed-rate infusion (NSW Health).
source_refs: NSW Health Adult DKA management guideline

options.rationale: Starting insulin before fluid resuscitation in a shocked patient drives intracellular potassium shift on top of hypovolaemia, worsening haemodynamics and risking arrhythmia. Fluid first or simultaneously (NSW Health).
source_refs: NSW Health Adult DKA management guideline

options.rationale: 0.9% saline is the standard initial fluid in DKA in NSW Health pathways. Hartmann's (compound sodium lactate) is sometimes used in select centres but contains lactate (converted to bicarbonate) and small potassium load; 0.9% saline remains the protocol default (NSW Health).
source_refs: NSW Health Adult DKA management guideline

options.rationale: Bicarbonate is not routinely recommended in DKA even with pH <7.0. Risks include paradoxical CSF acidosis, hypokalaemia, and impaired tissue oxygen delivery. Reserved for severe acidosis (pH <6.9) with haemodynamic instability (NSW Health).
source_refs: NSW Health Adult DKA management guideline

explanation.summary: NSW Health potassium replacement in DKA: K >5.5 add none, K 3.5-5.5 add 40 mmol/L, K <3.5 hold insulin and replace at 20 mmol/h via central line until K >3.5, then resume insulin with continued replacement. Adequate urine output (>0.5 mL/kg/h) is required before potassium is added.
key_points: K >5.5: hold replacement, recheck in 2 h
K 3.5-5.5: 40 mmol/L of fluid
K <3.5: stop insulin, replace at 20 mmol/h via CVC until K >3.5
Urine output >0.5 mL/kg/h required before adding potassium
explanation.context: DKA depletes total body potassium by 5-10 mmol/kg through osmotic diuresis and protein catabolism. Serum potassium at presentation is paradoxically normal or high because acidosis shifts potassium extracellularly (H+/K+ exchange) and insulin deficiency abolishes intracellular uptake. Insulin therapy reverses both, dropping serum potassium rapidly. Without proactive replacement, dangerous hypokalaemia develops within hours. The 40 mmol/L per litre rate matches typical infusion rates of 1 L/h, delivering 40 mmol/h - the upper limit safe via peripheral cannula on cardiac-monitored bed.

sources.label: NSW Health Adult DKA management guideline

options.rationale: Insulin is driving potassium intracellularly. Waiting until potassium drops below 3.5 risks symptomatic hypokalaemia (arrhythmia, weakness, paralytic ileus). Replacement begins when K <5.5 with adequate urine output (NSW Health).
source_refs: NSW Health Adult DKA management guideline

options.rationale: NSW Health DKA pathway: with serum potassium 3.5-5.5 mmol/L and adequate urine output, add 40 mmol KCl per litre. The patient's K is 4.6 (within this range) and urine output is adequate (>0.5 mL/kg/h), making this the standard step. Higher rates (60 mmol/L) require central access and continuous cardiac monitoring.
source_refs: NSW Health Adult DKA management guideline

options.rationale: 20 mmol/L is insufficient to keep up with the ongoing insulin-driven intracellular shift. NSW Health protocol mandates 40 mmol/L in this serum potassium range with adequate urine output (NSW Health).
source_refs: NSW Health Adult DKA management guideline

options.rationale: Stopping insulin is only indicated if K falls below 3.5 mmol/L; without insulin, ketogenesis resumes and acidosis worsens. K of 4.6 is normal-range and falling; replace potassium, do not stop insulin (NSW Health).
source_refs: NSW Health Adult DKA management guideline

options.rationale: Oral potassium is unreliable in a patient with vomiting and gastroparesis from ketoacidosis. Intravenous route gives predictable plasma levels and is the protocol standard (NSW Health).
source_refs: NSW Health Adult DKA management guideline

explanation.summary: HHS and DKA differ in pathophysiology, presentation and treatment. HHS develops over days in older type 2 diabetics with relative (not absolute) insulin deficiency, allowing enough insulin to suppress ketogenesis but not glucose. Treatment priority is slow fluid replacement; insulin is delayed and given at lower rates (0.05 unit/kg/h) to avoid rapid osmolar shifts.
key_points: HHS criteria: BGL >30, osmolality >320, ketones <3, pH >7.3, HCO3 >15
Mortality 10-20% (vs 1-5% DKA); often elderly with comorbidity
Fluid first; insulin only when glucose plateaus on fluid alone (0.05 unit/kg/h)
Cap osmolality reduction at 3-8 mOsm/kg/h to avoid cerebral oedema
explanation.context: HHS occurs when residual insulin (sufficient to suppress ketogenesis but not gluconeogenesis) is overwhelmed by an intercurrent illness. Days of osmotic diuresis produce severe dehydration (typically 100-200 mL/kg deficit) and hyperosmolality. The slow speed of correction matters because rapid water shift into the relatively hyperosmolar brain causes cerebral oedema (a feared paediatric DKA complication that also occurs in HHS adults). Mortality is higher than DKA largely from underlying comorbidities (cardiovascular, renal, infection) and from complications of correction itself when done too quickly.

sources.label: NSW Health Adult Hyperglycaemic Emergencies guideline
Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state

options.rationale: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS) is defined by hyperglycaemia >30 mmol/L, hyperosmolality >320 mOsm/kg, absent significant ketosis (ketones <3 mmol/L) and absent acidosis (pH >7.3, HCO3 >15). Management priority is slow fluid replacement; rapid osmolality correction risks cerebral oedema and central pontine myelinolysis. Insulin is added only when fluid alone is not driving glucose down (typically after 1-2 L).
source_refs: NSW Health Adult Hyperglycaemic Emergencies guideline
Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state

options.rationale: This is not DKA: ketones are low (0.8 vs threshold 3 mmol/L), pH is normal (7.34), HCO3 is normal (22). DKA protocol with rapid fluids and immediate insulin in HHS risks profound hypotension, hypokalaemia and cerebral oedema (NSW Health).
source_refs: NSW Health Adult Hyperglycaemic Emergencies guideline

options.rationale: Glucose 42 mmol/L rules out euglycaemic DKA (which presents with normal or near-normal glucose). The patient is also not on an SGLT2 inhibitor (eTG).
AKI is present but is a consequence of HHS dehydration and is managed by volume restoration. Dialysis is unnecessary and inappropriately rapid for osmolality correction (NSW Health).
source_refs: NSW Health Adult Hyperglycaemic Emergencies guideline

options.rationale: UTI is the precipitant and needs treatment, but the metabolic emergency itself (severe hyperosmolality, dehydration, AKI) drives morbidity. Both must be addressed in parallel; the dominant immediate task is the metabolic correction (NSW Health).
source_refs: NSW Health Adult Hyperglycaemic Emergencies guideline

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is treated empirically: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV/IM immediately, plus 1 L 0.9% saline with 5% glucose, then 200 mg/24 h hydrocortisone by continuous infusion or 50 mg 6-hourly. Fludrocortisone is not needed acutely because high-dose hydrocortisone provides sufficient mineralocorticoid activity.
key_points: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV/IM stat; do not wait for biochemical confirmation
1 L 0.9% saline + 5% glucose corrects volume, sodium, glucose
Hydrocortisone at >50 mg/day provides adequate mineralocorticoid activity
Sick-day rules: double oral hydrocortisone for fever/infection; IM injection at home if vomiting
explanation.context: Cortisol has a permissive effect on vascular tone: alpha-adrenoceptors require cortisol for normal catecholamine responsiveness. Without it, vasopressors fail and hypotension persists despite fluid. Cortisol also opposes insulin action (so deficiency causes hypoglycaemia), and aldosterone deficiency causes sodium loss and potassium retention. The hyperpigmentation of primary adrenal failure reflects ACTH oversecretion: ACTH and melanocyte-stimulating hormone share a common precursor (proopiomelanocortin), so ACTH excess stimulates melanocytes in addition to the failing adrenal.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Crisis position statement

options.rationale: Adrenal crisis is a clinical diagnosis (hypotension, hypoglycaemia, hyperkalaemia, hyponatraemia in a known Addisonian under stress). Immediate management is hydrocortisone 100 mg IV (or IM if no access) plus 1 L 0.9% saline with 5% glucose to correct volume, hypoglycaemia and electrolytes. Treatment is given before biochemical confirmation; cortisol can be sent but should not delay therapy.
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Crisis position statement

options.rationale: Dexamethasone is acceptable when a Short Synacthen test is planned afterwards (it does not interfere with the cortisol assay) but lacks mineralocorticoid activity essential in primary adrenal failure. Hydrocortisone is preferred in established Addison disease (eTG).

Vasopressors are largely ineffective in adrenal crisis without glucocorticoid replacement because the vascular smooth muscle is refractory to catecholamines in absence of cortisol. Hydrocortisone restores vascular reactivity (permissive effect) (eTG).
Oral therapy is unreliable in vomiting patient and inadequate for crisis. Parenteral hydrocortisone is required (eTG).

Hyperkalaemia in adrenal crisis reflects mineralocorticoid deficiency and resolves with hydrocortisone and saline. Insulin-glucose would worsen hypoglycaemia and is not first-line in this context (eTG).

explanation.summary: Sick day rules: double oral hydrocortisone for febrile illness or moderate physical stress; triple for severe illness; intramuscular hydrocortisone 100 mg for vomiting, diarrhoea, collapse or surgery. Patients (and a household member) should carry IM hydrocortisone and a medical alert bracelet.
key_points: Double oral for fever/infection (sick day rule)
IM hydrocortisone 100 mg + ED if vomiting, drowsy, hypotensive
Major surgery: 100 mg IV at induction, then infusion 200 mg/24 h
Primary AI needs fludrocortisone; secondary AI does not
explanation.context: Cortisol secretion normally rises 5-10 fold during physical stress (infection, trauma, surgery), but adrenal-insufficient patients on replacement doses cannot mount this response. Without temporary dose escalation, the gap between physiological demand and replacement supply precipitates crisis. Education is the single most effective preventive measure: patients with adrenal insufficiency who understand sick day rules and carry IM hydrocortisone have substantially fewer crises and hospital admissions.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Crisis Prevention guidance

options.rationale: Endocrine Society of Australia sick day rules: double oral hydrocortisone for febrile illness, surgery or significant physical stress, then taper back over 24-48 hours as recovery progresses. Tripling is reserved for major stress (surgery, trauma). Pre-loaded IM hydrocortisone is for vomiting or unwell-to-the-point-of-collapse, not yet warranted here.
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Crisis Prevention guidance

options.rationale: Failure to escalate during febrile illness is the commonest precipitant of adrenal crisis in known adrenal insufficiency. Pre-emptive doubling is protective (Endocrine Society of Australia).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Crisis Prevention guidance

options.rationale: IM hydrocortisone and emergency presentation are reserved for vomiting, inability to tolerate oral intake, drowsiness, or hypotension. With preserved oral intake and stable haemodynamics, oral doubling is sufficient (Endocrine Society of Australia).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Crisis Prevention guidance

options.rationale: Switching to prednisone (longer half-life, less mineralocorticoid activity) is not required and removes the diurnal physiological pattern of hydrocortisone dosing. Maintain hydrocortisone and double the dose (eTG).

Fludrocortisone is mineralocorticoid replacement for primary adrenal insufficiency only. In secondary (pituitary) failure the adrenal cortex still responds to angiotensin II, so aldosterone secretion is preserved. Fludrocortisone is not added (eTG).

explanation.summary: Thyroid storm management combines blockade of hormone synthesis (thionamide), release (iodide given >=1 hour after thionamide), peripheral conversion (propranolol, hydrocortisone, PTU), and sympathetic effects (propranolol). Active cooling with paracetamol (not aspirin/NSAIDs) and supportive care complete the package.
key_points: PTU preferred over carbimazole (also blocks peripheral T4 to T3)
Iodide always after thionamide by >=1 hour (Jod-Basedow risk)
Hydrocortisone: blocks T4 to T3, treats relative adrenal insufficiency
Propranolol: rate control and blocks peripheral conversion at high doses
explanation.context: Thyroid storm is decompensated thyrotoxicosis with a mortality of 10-30%. The Wolff-Chaikoff effect describes iodide-induced suppression of thyroid hormone synthesis (the therapeutic intent), but in untreated Graves disease the failure to escape from this effect is unreliable, and iodide can paradoxically increase hormone synthesis through the Jod-Basedow effect if thyroid peroxidase is not first blocked by thionamide. This is why sequence matters: PTU or carbimazole first to block synthesis, then iodide to block release of preformed hormone.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia thyroid storm position statement

options.rationale: Thyroid storm pharmacology has a strict sequence: thionamide first (propylthiouracil preferred over carbimazole because PTU also blocks peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion), then iodide at least 1 hour later (premature iodide before thionamide blockade would worsen the storm via the Jod-Basedow effect), plus propranolol (rate control and inhibits peripheral conversion) and hydrocortisone (blocks T4-to-T3 and treats relative adrenal insufficiency).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia thyroid storm position statement

options.rationale: Giving iodide before thionamide allows the thyroid to use the iodide load to synthesise additional thyroid hormone (Jod-Basedow effect), acutely worsening the storm. Thionamide must precede iodide by at least 1 hour (Endocrine Society of Australia).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia thyroid storm position statement

options.rationale: Surgery is contraindicated during active thyroid storm because of haemodynamic instability and uncontrolled hormone release on manipulation. It is the definitive treatment after metabolic stabilisation (typically several weeks) (eTG).
Radioactive iodine causes a transient release of preformed hormone with potential worsening of thyrotoxicosis in the first 1-2 weeks. It is contraindicated during storm (eTG).

PTU is preferred in thyroid storm because it inhibits peripheral T4 to T3 conversion (carbimazole does not). Aspirin and other NSAIDs that displace thyroid hormone from binding proteins should be avoided; paracetamol is the antipyretic of choice (Endocrine Society of Australia).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia thyroid storm position statement

explanation.summary: Myxoedema coma combines profound hypothyroidism with hypothermia, hyponatraemia, hypoventilation, bradycardia and altered consciousness. Treatment: empirical hydrocortisone first (cover possible adrenal insufficiency), then IV levothyroxine loading, passive rewarming, supportive care. Mortality remains 30-50% even with treatment.
key_points: Hydrocortisone BEFORE thyroid hormone (sequence matters)
IV levothyroxine 200-400 mcg load then 50-100 mcg daily IV
Passive rewarming only; active worsens hypotension
Liothyronine (T3) sometimes added; debate over routine use
explanation.context: Myxoedema coma is decompensated severe hypothyroidism, classically in elderly women in winter after a precipitant (infection, cold exposure, drug, medication non-adherence). Sodium-retaining steroids and free water excretion both depend on thyroid hormone; deficiency produces dilutional hyponatraemia. Hypothermia reflects basal metabolic rate collapse. The adrenal-thyroid interaction matters because thyroid hormone accelerates cortisol clearance, so replacing T4 without first covering with hydrocortisone in someone with marginal adrenal reserve can precipitate adrenal crisis hours into treatment.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia myxoedema coma position statement

options.rationale: Myxoedema coma management: give intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg BEFORE thyroid hormone, because untreated coexisting adrenal insufficiency unmasked by thyroid hormone replacement can precipitate adrenal crisis (cortisol metabolism accelerates as thyroid status normalises). Random cortisol of 198 nmol/L in a critically ill patient is inappropriately low (would expect >500 in true stress). Levothyroxine 200-400 mcg IV loading dose follows.
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia myxoedema coma position statement

options.rationale: Giving thyroid hormone before glucocorticoid in a patient with possible coexisting adrenal insufficiency can precipitate adrenal crisis through accelerated cortisol metabolism. Hydrocortisone empirically first is the safer sequence (Endocrine Society of Australia).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia myxoedema coma position statement

options.rationale: Passive rewarming is preferred in myxoedema coma; aggressive external rewarming causes peripheral vasodilatation, worsening hypotension and triggering arrhythmia. Endogenous heat generation as metabolism recovers with thyroid replacement is the optimal mechanism (Endocrine Society of Australia).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia myxoedema coma position statement

options.rationale: Gut absorption is unreliable in myxoedema coma (gastroparesis, mucosal oedema, hypoperfusion). IV route is required to ensure absorption (Endocrine Society of Australia).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia myxoedema coma position statement

options.rationale: The hyponatraemia in myxoedema reflects reduced free water clearance and resolves slowly with thyroid replacement. Hypertonic saline risks rapid correction and central pontine myelinolysis. Reserve for symptomatic seizures from hyponatraemia, not for hyponatraemia attributable to myxoedema (Endocrine Society of Australia).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia myxoedema coma position statement

explanation.summary: Acute severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizure, coma) is an emergency treated with 3% hypertonic saline 150 mL bolus, repeated as needed for symptom resolution. Target sodium rise 4-6 mmol/L in the first hour, then capped at <=8 mmol/L in 24 hours and <=18 mmol/L in 48 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome.
key_points: Hypertonic 3% saline 150 mL bolus over 10-20 min; up to 3 boluses
Target: +4-6 mmol/L in first hour for seizure/coma; symptom abortion is the endpoint
Then cap: <=8 mmol/L per 24 h, <=18 mmol/L per 48 h
If over-correction: re-lower with dextrose 5% and/or desmopressin
explanation.context: Osmotic demyelination syndrome (formerly central pontine myelinolysis) occurs when chronically adapted hypotonic brain tissue is exposed to rapid osmotic change. Brain cells lose intracellular osmolytes (organic osmolytes, electrolytes) over 24-48 hours to match the hypotonic extracellular fluid, preventing cerebral oedema. Rapid correction overwhelms the slow re-accumulation of these osmolytes, drawing water out of cells faster than they can re-adapt. Pontine oligodendrocytes are particularly susceptible to osmotic flux, producing the characteristic 'locked-in' syndrome 2-6 days after over-correction. Risk factors: chronicity, hypokalaemia, malnutrition, alcohol use disorder, liver disease.

sources.label: European Society of Endocrinology Hyponatraemia guidelines (cited by Endocrine Society of Australia)

options.rationale: Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizure, coma) regardless of chronicity is treated with hypertonic 3% saline 150 mL bolus over 10-20 minutes, repeated up to 3 times until symptoms resolve. Target sodium rise is 4-6 mmol/L in the first hour to abort cerebral oedema, then cap at <=8 mmol/L in the first 24 hours overall to avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome.
source_refs: European Society of Endocrinology Hyponatraemia guidelines (cited by Endocrine Society of Australia)

options.rationale: 0.9% saline in a SIADH-pattern patient (urine osm > serum osm, urine Na high, euvolaemic) can paradoxically worsen hyponatraemia because the sodium is excreted with retained water. Symptomatic seizure also requires faster correction than slow saline allows (ESE/eTG).
