Fluid restriction is appropriate for chronic, mildly symptomatic hyponatraemia. Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizure) needs immediate hypertonic saline; restriction acts too slowly (ESE).
source_refs: European Society of Endocrinology Hyponatraemia guidelines (cited by Endocrine Society of Australia)

options.rationale: Tolvaptan (vasopressin V2 antagonist) is contraindicated in acute severe symptomatic hyponatraemia because its onset is too slow and correction can be unpredictable. Reserved for chronic SIADH (ESE).
source_refs: European Society of Endocrinology Hyponatraemia guidelines (cited by Endocrine Society of Australia)

options.rationale: Demeclocycline (tetracycline that induces nephrogenic diabetes insipidus) is a chronic SIADH management option, not acute treatment. Inappropriate for symptomatic hyponatraemia (eTG).

explanation.summary: Hyponatraemia workup proceeds through serum osmolality (true vs pseudo), volume status (hypo/eu/hyper), and urine indices (urine osmolality and sodium). Euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia with high urine osmolality and high urine sodium, after excluding thyroid and adrenal causes, is SIADH. Small cell lung carcinoma is the classical malignant cause.
key_points: Always check serum osm first to exclude pseudo (lipid, protein) and hyperosmolar (glucose) hyponatraemia
SIADH criteria: hypotonic, urine osm >100, urine Na >40, euvolaemic, normal TFT/adrenal/renal
SCLC, head injury, drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine), pneumonia: common SIADH causes
Treat underlying cause; fluid restrict 800-1000 mL/day; tolvaptan/demeclocycline for chronic
explanation.context: ADH is secreted by the posterior pituitary in response to plasma osmolality (rising) and effective circulating volume (falling). In SIADH, ADH secretion is uncoupled from these stimuli, often from ectopic production (SCLC), CNS pathology (head injury, infection), pulmonary disease (pneumonia, lung abscess), or drugs. Persistent ADH action drives free water retention through aquaporin-2 channels in the collecting duct, diluting serum sodium without volume expansion (escape from the volume effect through pressure natriuresis prevents oedema).

sources.label: European Society of Endocrinology Hyponatraemia guidelines

options.rationale: Hypotonic hyponatraemia (serum osm <275) with inappropriately concentrated urine (urine osm >100), urine sodium >40 mmol/L, euvolaemic clinical state, and normal thyroid and adrenal function defines SIADH. Small cell lung carcinoma is the prototypical malignancy producing ectopic antidiuretic hormone (ADH).
source_refs: European Society of Endocrinology Hyponatraemia guidelines

options.rationale: Pseudohyponatraemia gives a falsely low sodium with normal measured serum osmolality. Here serum osmolality is genuinely low (258), so this is true hypotonic hyponatraemia (ESE).
source_refs: European Society of Endocrinology Hyponatraemia guidelines

options.rationale: Hypovolaemic hyponatraemia features clinical hypovolaemia (which he does not have) and low urine sodium (<20 mmol/L) reflecting aldosterone-driven sodium retention. His urine Na is 62 (ESE).
source_refs: European Society of Endocrinology Hyponatraemia guidelines

options.rationale: TSH is normal (1.8), excluding significant hypothyroidism as the cause (ESE).
source_refs: European Society of Endocrinology Hyponatraemia guidelines

options.rationale: Morning cortisol of 380 nmol/L is reassuringly within normal range. Random cortisol >275 in non-stressed patient usually excludes primary adrenal insufficiency (ESE).
source_refs: European Society of Endocrinology Hyponatraemia guidelines

explanation.summary: A haemolysed specimen is the commonest reason for an unexpectedly high potassium in a well patient with a normal ECG. Confirm with a fresh, free flowing sample (or a blood gas potassium for speed) before committing to emergency treatment.
key_points: Haemolysis, fist clenching, a tight tourniquet and delayed processing all raise the measured potassium.
A normal ECG in a well patient argues against a true severe hyperkalaemia.
Treating an unconfirmed result exposes the patient to hypoglycaemia and unnecessary drug cessation.
explanation.context: Potassium sits mostly inside cells at roughly 140 mmol/L against a serum value near 4 mmol/L, so even modest cell lysis in the tube moves the reported number a long way. That gradient is also why true hyperkalaemia matters: it narrows the resting membrane potential gap, slows phase 0 depolarisation and produces the familiar ECG sequence from peaked T waves through PR prolongation and QRS widening to a sine wave. The clinical skill is deciding which of those two stories the number in front of you belongs to, using the patient, the ECG and the specimen quality rather than the number alone.

sources.label: Kidney Health Australia CARI - Hyperkalaemia management

options.rationale: A haemolysed specimen releases intracellular potassium and overstates the true value, and this patient is asymptomatic with a normal ECG, so the result is confirmed before anyone is treated for it. (Source: Kidney Health Australia CARI - Hyperkalaemia management)
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia CARI - Hyperkalaemia management

options.rationale: Calcium gluconate is given when a reliable potassium is high and the ECG shows peaked T waves, a broad QRS or loss of P waves. Here the ECG is normal and the specimen is unreliable. (Source: ANZCOR adult advanced life support)
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia CARI - Hyperkalaemia management

options.rationale: Insulin with dextrose is used for a confirmed potassium above about 6.5 mmol/L, or lower with ECG change, once membrane stabilisation has been considered. Shifting therapy carries a real hypoglycaemia risk and is not given on an unconfirmed number. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Renal Dysfunction)
A potassium binder suits a confirmed potassium that is persistently raised and total body potassium needs lowering over hours to days rather than urgently. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia CARI - Hyperkalaemia management

options.rationale: Perindopril is stopped when a confirmed potassium is rising on renin-angiotensin blockade, particularly with falling renal function. Stopping a prognostically useful drug on a haemolysed sample is premature. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Renal Dysfunction)

explanation.summary: Drug-induced hyperkalaemia in CKD typically reflects compounding of multiple agents acting on renal potassium handling. Key offenders: ACE inhibitors/ARBs (reduce aldosterone), potassium-sparing diuretics (block aldosterone receptor or sodium channels), NSAIDs (reduce renal perfusion), trimethoprim (amiloride-like sodium-channel block), heparin and ciclosporin/tacrolimus (reduce aldosterone).
key_points: ACE/ARB: reduce aldosterone via renin-angiotensin blockade
MRA (spironolactone, eplerenone): block aldosterone receptor
NSAIDs: vasoconstrict afferent arteriole, reduce GFR and aldosterone
Trimethoprim, amiloride: block epithelial sodium channels (amiloride-like)
explanation.context: Trimethoprim deserves particular note because it is widely prescribed for urinary tract infection and frequently overlooked as a cause of hyperkalaemia. Its structural similarity to amiloride blocks the epithelial sodium channel in the distal tubule, reducing the favourable electrochemical gradient that normally drives potassium secretion. In patients already on RAAS-blocking drugs and with reduced GFR, even a short course can precipitate clinically significant hyperkalaemia. The mechanism is dose-dependent and more pronounced with the higher doses used for Pneumocystis treatment than UTI prophylaxis, but UTI treatment doses are sufficient to provoke this when other contributors are present.

options.rationale: Four hyperkalaemia-promoting drugs are present and compounded by CKD. ACE inhibitor (perindopril) reduces aldosterone; potassium-sparing diuretic (spironolactone) blocks aldosterone receptor; NSAID (ibuprofen) reduces renal perfusion and aldosterone; trimethoprim blocks epithelial sodium channels in the distal tubule (amiloride-like effect). Each independently raises potassium; together in CKD they cause clinically significant hyperkalaemia within days.

Neither atorvastatin nor paracetamol meaningfully affects potassium. Atorvastatin has a small risk of rhabdomyolysis-related hyperkalaemia but not at this dose, and paracetamol does not affect potassium handling (AMH).
Calcium channel blockers and statins do not raise potassium (AMH).
Perindopril alone is correct but missing the major contributors of spironolactone, NSAID and trimethoprim, all of which compound the effect (AMH).
Spironolactone is correct but amlodipine does not contribute to hyperkalaemia. Missing the other three contributors (AMH).

explanation.summary: Euglycaemic DKA on SGLT2 inhibitor presents with high ketones and acidosis at near-normal glucose; the SGLT2 inhibitor lowers glucose by promoting glycosuria, masking the typical hyperglycaemia. Triggers include fasting, surgery, low carbohydrate intake, and acute illness. Treat as DKA with insulin and glucose-containing fluids; withhold SGLT2i pre- and post-operatively (TGA advises stopping at least 3 days before elective surgery).
key_points: BGL may be near-normal; ketones high; acidosis present
Withhold SGLT2i at least 3 days before elective surgery (TGA)
Insulin + dextrose infusion (glucose 10% if BGL near-normal at outset)
Reintroduction of SGLT2i only after careful review and risk discussion
explanation.context: SGLT2 inhibitors increase ketogenesis by promoting fatty acid oxidation (glucagon rises, insulin falls relatively in fasting or stressed states) and reduce renal ketone clearance. Their glycosuric effect lowers plasma glucose, suppressing the usual feedback that would prompt insulin dose increase. The result is sufficient insulin deficiency to drive ketogenesis without the warning signal of hyperglycaemia. The clinical pearl is to check ketones in any SGLT2i patient with abdominal pain, vomiting or dyspnoea even when BGL is normal.

sources.label: TGA SGLT2 inhibitor safety alert - euglycaemic DKA

options.rationale: SGLT2 inhibitor-associated euglycaemic DKA presents with anion-gap acidosis and elevated ketones at near-normal glucose. The empagliflozin lowers renal glucose threshold, suppressing the hyperglycaemia signal that would normally prompt earlier diagnosis. Treatment is identical to standard DKA except glucose-containing fluids are needed from the start to permit insulin without hypoglycaemia. Withhold SGLT2i immediately and indefinitely until cause investigated.
source_refs: TGA SGLT2 inhibitor safety alert - euglycaemic DKA

options.rationale: Starvation ketosis produces mild ketonaemia (1-2 mmol/L) without significant acidosis (pH >7.3, HCO3 >18). Ketones of 4.8 and pH 7.16 indicate DKA-level ketogenesis, requiring insulin not just glucose (eTG).

Sepsis can precipitate DKA but the metabolic emergency is the immediate threat. Lactate 2.1 is mildly elevated but the dominant abnormality is ketoacidosis. Sepsis workup runs in parallel with DKA treatment, not instead (eTG).

SGLT2 inhibitor MUST be withheld during DKA; continuing perpetuates the precipitant. Sliding-scale subcutaneous insulin is inadequate for established DKA, which needs intravenous insulin infusion (eTG, TGA).
source_refs: TGA SGLT2 inhibitor safety alert - euglycaemic DKA

options.rationale: Oral therapy is unreliable in acutely unwell, nauseated, acidotic patient. Established DKA requires IV insulin and fluid (eTG).

explanation.summary: DKA-related cerebral oedema is rare (~1% of paediatric DKA) but carries 20-30% mortality. Warning signs: headache, GCS drop, bradycardia, hypertension, incontinence, abnormal posturing. Treatment is immediate osmotic therapy (hypertonic 3% saline 5 mL/kg or mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg), reduced fluid rate, imaging, and PICU. Prevention focuses on avoiding excessive fluid (>4 L/m2/24 h), rapid glucose correction and bicarbonate.
key_points: Suspicion: headache, GCS drop, Cushing reflex (brady + HTN), in adolescent on DKA Rx
Hypertonic 3% saline 5 mL/kg OR mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg over 20 min
Reduce maintenance fluid rate by one-third
Cap glucose fall at ~5 mmol/L/h by adding 10% dextrose when BGL <14
explanation.context: The pathophysiology of DKA cerebral oedema is debated. Historical theory: rapid osmotic shift from extracellular to intracellular brain compartment as glucose and ketones fall. Newer theory: ischaemic-reperfusion injury, with cerebral hypoperfusion during DKA followed by hyperaemia on rehydration causing vasogenic oedema. Whatever the mechanism, the practical implications are the same: avoid rapid osmolar swings (cap glucose fall, avoid bicarbonate, do not over-resuscitate), monitor neurological status closely, and act immediately on warning signs. Adolescents are at higher risk than adults but the syndrome occurs in adults too.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne DKA Clinical Practice Guideline
Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group DKA guideline

options.rationale: Headache, GCS drop, bradycardia and hypertension (Cushing reflex) in a child being treated for DKA are classic features of cerebral oedema, a feared complication with high mortality. Immediate management is osmotic therapy with hypertonic saline (or mannitol), reduction of fluid rate, and urgent imaging plus PICU. Delay risks brainstem herniation.
source_refs: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group DKA guideline
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne DKA Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Bradycardia and hypertension in this context reflect raised intracranial pressure (Cushing reflex), not hypovolaemia. Increasing fluid would worsen cerebral oedema. The volume status is appropriate after 3 L resuscitation (RCH; APEG).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne DKA Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Rapid glucose fall is itself a risk factor for cerebral oedema. The current rate of glucose fall (35 to 14 in 4 h) is already at the limit. Glucose should be added to fluids to slow descent below 14 mmol/L (RCH).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne DKA Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Bicarbonate is associated with increased cerebral oedema risk in paediatric DKA and is contraindicated outside extreme acidosis with haemodynamic compromise. Would worsen the situation (APEG; RCH).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne DKA Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Drowsy adolescent with bradycardia, hypertension and GCS drop is not nauseous from gastritis; this is a neurological emergency. Antihistamine sedation would mask deterioration (RCH).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne DKA Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis has two types: type 1 (iodine-driven hyperthyroidism in pre-existing thyroid disease) treated with thionamides; type 2 (destructive thyroiditis releasing preformed hormone) treated with glucocorticoids. Discrimination uses vascularity on colour Doppler (increased in type 1, decreased in type 2), uptake scan (low in both but lower in type 2), and inflammatory markers (IL-6 raised in type 2).
key_points: Type 1: pre-existing thyroid disease, raised vascularity, treat with thionamide
Type 2: destructive thyroiditis, low vascularity, raised IL-6, treat with prednisolone
Mixed type: both prednisolone and thionamide
Amiodarone half-life 50-100 days; effects persist long after cessation
explanation.context: Amiodarone is 37% iodine by weight and saturates the thyroid with iodine. In susceptible individuals (pre-existing autonomous nodules or Graves), this drives type 1 thyrotoxicosis through the Jod-Basedow effect (excess iodine substrate). In others, amiodarone or its metabolites have a direct cytotoxic effect on thyroid follicular cells, causing destructive thyroiditis (type 2) with leakage of preformed hormone. The distinction matters therapeutically: thionamides block synthesis (type 1 disease) but cannot affect release of stored hormone (type 2), where glucocorticoid suppression of inflammation is required.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis guidance

options.rationale: The picture is amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis type 2: destructive thyroiditis (reduced vascularity, low uptake, raised IL-6, no underlying autoimmunity). Type 2 responds to glucocorticoids which suppress the inflammatory destruction and reduce hormone release. Type 1 (excess iodine-driven synthesis in pre-existing Graves or nodular goitre) responds to thionamides (carbimazole or PTU). Mixed picture sometimes warrants both.
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis guidance

options.rationale: Carbimazole (thionamide) treats type 1 amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis where hormone synthesis is increased. In type 2 (destructive), thionamides are ineffective because hormone release is from stored preformed hormone, not new synthesis (Endocrine Society of Australia).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis guidance

options.rationale: Surgery is reserved for refractory cases or where rapid control is needed for cardiac decompensation. Initial medical therapy is appropriate (Endocrine Society of Australia).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis guidance

options.rationale: Radioactive iodine uptake is very low because of iodine-induced thyroid suppression from amiodarone. RAI is ineffective until iodine pool depletes (months) (Endocrine Society of Australia).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis guidance

options.rationale: Amiodarone has a half-life of ~50-100 days; thyrotoxicosis persists for months after stopping. Treatment must proceed regardless of whether amiodarone is continued (often it cannot be stopped because of underlying arrhythmia). The decision to stop amiodarone is individualised (Endocrine Society of Australia).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis guidance

explanation.summary: Plasma metanephrines are highly sensitive but generate false positives, most often from drugs that block noradrenaline reuptake. A modest isolated elevation is repeated after withdrawing the interfering agent and under correct sampling conditions before imaging is pursued.
key_points: Tricyclic antidepressants, serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors, levodopa and sympathomimetics all interfere.
Sample supine after 30 minutes of rest; an upright sample raises normetanephrine.
Elevations above three times the upper limit are rarely false and warrant imaging directly.
explanation.context: Screening for a catecholamine secreting tumour is deliberately built for sensitivity, because the consequence of missing one is a perioperative or spontaneous hypertensive crisis. The cost of that design is a low positive predictive value in an unselected hypertensive population, where the prevalence is well under 1%. Metanephrines are measured rather than catecholamines because tumours metabolise catecholamines continuously within the tumour cell, so the metabolites are elevated between the paroxysms that the catecholamines themselves only mark. Interpreting a mildly positive result therefore means attending to the interferences and the sampling before committing to imaging.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma guidance

options.rationale: Tricyclic antidepressants block noradrenaline reuptake and are the commonest cause of a falsely raised normetanephrine. A modest isolated elevation is confirmed off the interfering drug, with correct sampling conditions, before imaging is requested. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma guidance)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma guidance

options.rationale: Adrenal imaging follows once biochemistry is convincingly positive, typically more than three times the upper limit or confirmed on repeat, since imaging an unconfirmed result finds incidentalomas rather than answers. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma guidance

options.rationale: Phenoxybenzamine is started once a catecholamine secreting tumour is confirmed and surgery is planned, or where a crisis is occurring. Blocking on an unconfirmed result causes postural hypotension for no benefit. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma guidance

options.rationale: Investigation can stop where metanephrines are unequivocally within range in a patient with a low pretest probability. A result above the reference limit with suggestive symptoms needs resolution. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma guidance)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma guidance

options.rationale: A meta-iodobenzylguanidine scan is used for localising metastatic or extra-adrenal disease after a tumour is confirmed, not as a way of resolving an ambiguous screening result. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma guidance

explanation.summary: Hypercalcaemic crisis treatment is sequential: fluid first (saline), then anti-resorptive (bisphosphonate, denosumab if bisphosphonate-resistant or renal failure), with calcitonin for rapid temporary control. Treatment is etiological where possible. Malignancy-associated humoral hypercalcaemia (PTHrP) is the commonest severe presentation; granulomatous and vitamin D-mediated need steroids.
key_points: Saline first: 3-6 L/24 h to restore volume and calciuresis
Zoledronic acid 4 mg IV: peak effect 4-7 days, duration weeks
Calcitonin 4 IU/kg s/c 12-hourly: rapid (hours) onset but tachyphylaxis in 48 h
Denosumab: bisphosphonate-resistant or severe renal impairment
explanation.context: Mechanism-cause mapping in hypercalcaemia: PTH-mediated (primary hyperparathyroidism, lithium, tertiary hyperPTH) has raised or inappropriately normal PTH; PTHrP-mediated (squamous cell cancers, breast cancer with bone metastases) has suppressed PTH and raised PTHrP; vitamin D-mediated (granulomatous disease, lymphoma) has raised 1,25(OH)2D with normal 25-OH-D, responsive to steroid; local osteolytic (multiple myeloma, breast bone mets) has normal calciotropic hormones with high bone turnover markers. This patient's suppressed PTH with raised PTHrP and metastatic breast cancer fits humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy.

options.rationale: Severe hypercalcaemia (>3.5 mmol/L) with symptoms is a medical emergency. Initial step is volume expansion with 0.9% saline (3-6 L/24 h) to restore renal perfusion and promote calciuresis. Once volume replete, intravenous bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid 4 mg over 15 minutes) inhibits osteoclast-mediated bone resorption; effect onset 2-4 days, peak 4-7 days, duration weeks. Useful adjuncts: calcitonin (rapid onset, tachyphylaxis), denosumab (refractory cases).

Routine furosemide in hypercalcaemia is no longer recommended: it exacerbates volume depletion (worsening calcium reabsorption) without providing additional calciuresis once volume is restored. Reserve for fluid overload during saline therapy (eTG).
Cinacalcet (calcimimetic) is for primary or tertiary hyperparathyroidism and parathyroid carcinoma. PTH-suppressed humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy does not respond (eTG).

Glucocorticoids work for granulomatous (sarcoidosis, TB) or vitamin D-mediated (lymphoma, multiple myeloma in some cases) hypercalcaemia by reducing 1,25(OH)2D production. PTHrP-mediated humoral hypercalcaemia does not respond (eTG).
Oral phosphate is reserved for hypophosphataemic hypercalcaemia (rare) and carries risks of metastatic calcification and renal injury at high serum calcium. Not appropriate first-line (eTG).

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome occurs when carbohydrate delivery after prolonged starvation triggers insulin secretion, driving phosphate, magnesium and potassium intracellularly. The acutely depleted serum levels cause cardiac arrhythmia, respiratory failure (phosphate-dependent ATP synthesis), seizures and rhabdomyolysis. Prevention: identify risk, replace electrolytes, give IV thiamine before feeds, start at 5-10 kcal/kg/day, build over 7-10 days.
key_points: High-risk features (NICE): BMI <16, weight loss >15% in 3-6 months, intake <5 days, low electrolytes
IV thiamine 200-300 mg before feed (prevents Wernicke and wet beriberi)
Start 5-10 kcal/kg/day, advance by 5 kcal/kg/day if electrolytes stable
Monitor phosphate, magnesium, potassium 12-hourly for first 72 h
explanation.context: During starvation, intracellular phosphate stores deplete despite serum levels appearing normal (whole-body deficit masked by extracellular shift). Carbohydrate delivery stimulates insulin, which drives cellular uptake of glucose along with phosphate (for ATP synthesis), magnesium and potassium. The serum phosphate can drop below 0.3 mmol/L within hours, impairing oxygen delivery (2,3-DPG depletion), muscle contractility, and ATP-dependent cellular processes. Thiamine deficiency superimposed on glucose loading precipitates Wernicke encephalopathy (the classical 'glucose without thiamine in alcoholic' pitfall).

sources.label: NICE Nutrition Support guidelines (referenced by AuSPEN)

options.rationale: He is at very high risk of refeeding syndrome (BMI <16, >10% weight loss, negligible intake >10 days, alcohol misuse - any single feature is high risk; he has multiple). Pre-feed electrolyte replacement, intravenous thiamine (Wernicke prophylaxis), and slow caloric introduction (5-10 kcal/kg/day, building over a week) are NICE-endorsed practice. Phosphate, magnesium and potassium must be replaced before and during feeding because insulin-driven intracellular shift on carbohydrate load will drop them dangerously.
source_refs: NICE Nutrition Support guidelines (referenced by AuSPEN)

options.rationale: Full-rate feeds in high-risk refeeding patient precipitate severe hypophosphataemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypokalaemia, thiamine deficiency exacerbation (Wernicke, beriberi), cardiac arrhythmia and respiratory failure. Slow start is essential (NICE; eTG).

Oral thiamine has poor bioavailability in alcohol use disorder; intravenous loading is required to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy. Oral protein supplements deliver a high caloric load too quickly (eTG).
Parenteral nutrition is reserved for non-functional gut; an enteric route is preferred. TPN at standard rates carries the same refeeding risk and additional line-related and metabolic risks (eTG).
Prolonged fasting worsens malnutrition; the right approach is replace electrolytes AND start low-rate feeds in parallel, building gradually. Total deferral is harmful (eTG).

explanation.summary: Hypoglycaemia mechanism determines management. Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia is prolonged because the drug keeps stimulating insulin secretion until cleared (12-24 hours for gliclazide). Octreotide (somatostatin analogue) directly suppresses beta-cell insulin secretion, breaking the cycle. Other causes (exogenous insulin, post-bariatric, adrenal, hepatic) have different mechanisms and different treatments.
key_points: Sulfonylurea: 24-h observation, octreotide 50 mcg s/c 6-hourly if recurrent
Exogenous insulin: glucose, then observe; pump/regime adjust
Reactive post-bariatric: dietary, acarbose if persistent
Counter-regulatory deficit (adrenal/hepatic): replace deficient hormone or support metabolism
explanation.context: Sulfonylureas bind the SUR1 subunit of the ATP-sensitive potassium channel on the pancreatic beta cell, closing it independently of glucose levels. Insulin secretion continues until the drug is cleared. Glucose infusion temporarily raises BGL but stimulates further insulin secretion (because beta cells are pharmacologically primed), creating a vicious cycle of hypoglycaemia-glucose-hypoglycaemia. Octreotide binds somatostatin receptor 2 on the beta cell, suppressing insulin release at the source and breaking the cycle. Half-life considerations: glibenclamide >24 hours (longer observation), glipizide ~6 hours, gliclazide modified release ~24 hours.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness - Sulfonylurea poisoning

options.rationale: Exogenous insulin hypoglycaemia resolves within hours of cessation. Standard glucose correction and continued monitoring suffice; pump reprogramming and education prevent recurrence (eTG).

Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia is characteristically prolonged and recurrent because gliclazide stimulates ongoing insulin secretion until the drug clears (half-life 12-24 hours). Standard glucose boluses are repeatedly overcome by continued insulin release. Octreotide suppresses pancreatic insulin secretion at the beta cell, breaking the cycle. Observation must extend at least 24 hours from the last dose.
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness - Sulfonylurea poisoning

options.rationale: Post-bariatric (dumping) hypoglycaemia is reactive (high glucose-driven insulin overshoot 1-3 h post-meal). Managed by dietary modification (low glycaemic index, small frequent meals), not octreotide for the acute episode (eTG).
Adrenal hypoglycaemia resolves with hydrocortisone replacement, not octreotide. The deficit is glucocorticoid (cortisol is a counter-regulatory hormone) not endogenous insulin excess (eTG).

Hepatic failure hypoglycaemia reflects depleted hepatic glycogen and impaired gluconeogenesis. Treated with continuous glucose infusion (10% dextrose) and addressing underlying liver disease, not octreotide (eTG).

explanation.summary: Postpartum thyroiditis and Graves disease are distinguished by uptake scan (low in thyroiditis, high in Graves), antibodies (anti-TPO in thyroiditis, TRAb in Graves) and clinical features (Graves-specific eye signs/pretibial myxoedema/vascular goitre in Graves). Thyroiditis is self-limiting and managed with beta-blocker; Graves needs definitive treatment (thionamide, radioiodine or surgery).
key_points: Postpartum thyroiditis: low uptake, anti-TPO raised, hyper to hypo to recovery course
Graves: high uptake, TRAb positive, eye signs/pretibial myxoedema possible
Beta-blocker compatible with breastfeeding (propranolol preferred)
Up to 50% of postpartum thyroiditis progress to permanent hypothyroidism over years
explanation.context: Postpartum thyroiditis is autoimmune thyroid disease with a postpartum trigger (likely immune rebound after pregnancy's relative immunosuppression). The destructive phase releases preformed thyroid hormone from damaged follicles, mimicking hyperthyroidism without increased synthesis (hence low radioactive iodine uptake). After the stored hormone is depleted, transient hypothyroidism occurs (4-8 weeks) before most patients recover. The uptake scan distinction matters therapeutically: thionamides work only when synthesis is upregulated (Graves), whereas symptom control with beta-blocker is sufficient for destructive thyroiditis.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia thyroid in pregnancy and postpartum position statement

options.rationale: Postpartum thyroiditis is a destructive thyroiditis: low uptake on iodine scan, raised anti-TPO antibodies, TRAb negative, no Graves features (eye signs, vascular goitre with bruit). Hyperthyroid phase is self-limiting (4-8 weeks), often followed by hypothyroid phase before recovery. Treatment is symptomatic with beta-blocker only; thionamides are ineffective (no new hormone synthesis) and inappropriate.
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia thyroid in pregnancy and postpartum position statement

options.rationale: Carbimazole blocks new hormone synthesis but postpartum thyroiditis releases preformed hormone from a destructive process. Thionamide is ineffective and unnecessary; would also pass into breast milk (Endocrine Society of Australia).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia thyroid in pregnancy and postpartum position statement

options.rationale: Radioactive iodine is contraindicated during breastfeeding (concentrates in milk). Also unnecessary in self-limiting thyroiditis where uptake is already very low (Endocrine Society of Australia).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia thyroid in pregnancy and postpartum position statement

options.rationale: TRAb negative, low uptake, no Graves-specific features (orbitopathy, pretibial myxoedema, vascular goitre with bruit) make Graves unlikely. Surgery is not indicated (Endocrine Society of Australia).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia thyroid in pregnancy and postpartum position statement

options.rationale: Levothyroxine would worsen current hyperthyroidism. It is reserved for the subsequent hypothyroid phase if symptomatic or persistent beyond 6 months (Endocrine Society of Australia).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia thyroid in pregnancy and postpartum position statement

explanation.summary: Polyuria with hypotonic urine and rising sodium after pituitary surgery is central diabetes insipidus. Distinguish from nephrogenic DI (renal ADH resistance) by desmopressin response: central DI corrects, nephrogenic does not. Treat central DI with desmopressin (s/c, IV, intranasal or oral) titrated to urine output and sodium, alongside careful free water replacement (cap correction at 10 mmol/L per 24 h).
key_points: Central DI: ADH deficit; desmopressin corrects
Nephrogenic DI: ADH resistance; treat cause (lithium, hypercalcaemia)
Cap sodium correction at 10 mmol/L per 24 h (cerebral oedema risk)
Post-pituitary triphasic response: DI, then SIADH, then permanent DI
explanation.context: Pituitary surgery may produce a triphasic response: initial DI from immediate stalk injury (days 1-5), transient SIADH from release of stored hormone (days 5-10), and permanent DI in some (after 10 days). The discrimination matrix uses three variables: plasma sodium (hyper in DI, hypo in SIADH), urine osmolality (low in DI, high in SIADH) and ADH response (intact in primary polydipsia, deficient in central DI, present but ineffective in nephrogenic DI). Diabetes insipidus in this acute postoperative setting requires close monitoring because conscious patients can usually keep up with losses if water is available, but obtunded or post-anaesthetic patients lose the thirst-drive safety net and develop dangerous hypernatraemia quickly.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia diabetes insipidus position statement

options.rationale: Post-pituitary surgery polyuria with hypotonic urine (urine osm <300 with plasma osm >295), rising sodium, and consistent timing reflects central diabetes insipidus from disruption of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) production in posterior pituitary or stalk. Desmopressin (synthetic ADH analogue) corrects the deficit; free water replacement addresses established hypernatraemia (cap correction at 10 mmol/L per 24 h to prevent cerebral oedema from rapid water shift).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia diabetes insipidus position statement

options.rationale: SIADH would produce hyponatraemia with concentrated urine (urine osm >100 in setting of low plasma osm). This patient has hypernatraemia with dilute urine, the opposite picture (eTG).
Cerebral salt wasting causes hyponatraemia with hypovolaemia and high urine sodium (>40), typically after SAH or neurosurgery. This patient has hypernatraemia (eTG).
Osmotic diuresis from hyperglycaemia would show high urine osmolality (from glucose) and serum hyperglycaemia. Urine osm here is low (122) suggesting water diuresis, not solute diuresis (eTG).

Primary polydipsia would produce hyponatraemia and dilute urine, with normal ADH response. This patient has hypernatraemia despite high intake, indicating he cannot keep up with renal water losses (eTG).

explanation.summary: In an asymptomatic adult, Australian guidance diagnoses type 2 diabetes by two abnormal tests on separate occasions: fasting venous glucose at least 7.0 mmol/L, HbA1c at least 48 mmol/mol (6.5 percent) on a standardised assay, OGTT 2-hour at least 11.1 mmol/L, or a single random glucose at least 11.1 mmol/L plus classic symptoms (RACGP 2024).
key_points: Fasting glucose >= 7.0 mmol/L is diagnostic when confirmed
HbA1c >= 48 mmol/mol (6.5 percent) on standardised assay is diagnostic when confirmed
Random glucose >= 11.1 mmol/L is diagnostic only with classic symptoms
Two abnormal results required in asymptomatic patients
explanation.pearls: Avoid HbA1c if haemoglobinopathy, recent blood loss, transfusion, pregnancy or rapidly changing glycaemia.

options.rationale: Beta thalassaemia minor alters red cell turnover and can falsely lower or raise HbA1c depending on the assay; Australian Diabetes Society guidance lists haemoglobinopathy as a setting where HbA1c should not be used, requiring confirmation by repeat glycaemic testing (ADS Position; RACGP).

Because his haemoglobinopathy invalidates HbA1c, Australian diagnosis must rely on two abnormal glycaemic tests on separate days (fasting glucose at least 7.0, OGTT 2-hour at least 11.1, or random at least 11.1 with classic symptoms); repeating the fasting glucose is the most direct confirmatory test (RACGP; ADS).
An isolated random glucose below 11.1 does not exclude diabetes; his fasting glucose of 7.3 mmol/L already meets the diabetes threshold and requires confirmatory testing, not discharge (RACGP).
Fructosamine is not validated as a primary diagnostic test for diabetes in Australian guidelines; confirmation uses standard glycaemic tests (fasting glucose or OGTT) (ADS).
Initiating treatment before establishing diagnosis bypasses confirmation; OGTT is an acceptable confirmatory test but treatment must follow the diagnosis (RACGP; ADS).

explanation.summary: In T2DM with established HFrEF, CKD with albuminuria, or atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, an SGLT2 inhibitor is the preferred add-on regardless of HbA1c, because cardiovascular death, heart failure hospitalisation and CKD progression are reduced independently of glucose lowering (ADS-ADEA; Heart Foundation 2022; KDIGO 2022).
key_points: SGLT2i indicated in HFrEF irrespective of diabetes status
SGLT2i slows CKD progression when ACR is elevated and eGFR is above the threshold (typically >=20 mL/min/1.73m^2 for empagliflozin / dapagliflozin)
Counsel on euglycaemic DKA, sick-day rules, genital mycotic infection
GLP1 receptor agonist (semaglutide, dulaglutide) is the preferred add-on if ASCVD predominates and weight loss is needed
explanation.pearls: Hold SGLT2 inhibitor during intercurrent illness, fasting, or pre-operatively to reduce euglycaemic DKA risk.

options.rationale: Sulfonylureas lower HbA1c but carry hypoglycaemia risk, do not improve cardiorenal outcomes, and offer no benefit in HFrEF or CKD progression. Legacy HbA1c-only agents are a poor choice when there are cardiorenal indications. Gliclazide would be reasonable in T2DM without HFrEF/CKD when cost is constraining or as adjunct to glucose lowering (RACGP 2024; ADS-ADEA Position Statement on T2DM).

SGLT2 inhibitors reduce cardiovascular death and heart failure hospitalisation in HFrEF and slow CKD progression with albuminuria; they are first-choice add-on for T2DM with established HFrEF and CKD with eGFR within approved range (ADS-ADEA Algorithm; Heart Foundation HFrEF guideline 2022; KHA-CARI / KDIGO 2022).

Basal insulin lowers HbA1c but provides no cardiovascular outcome benefit and would be premature when oral and injectable non-insulin options remain. Insulin is correct when patient is glucotoxic (HbA1c >10%, ketonaemia, marked symptoms) or after exhausting oral/GLP-1 RA options (ADS-ADEA Algorithm).

DPP4 inhibitors are weight-neutral, well tolerated, but cardiorenally neutral. Saxagliptin specifically increases HF hospitalisation (SAVOR-TIMI 53). Weight neutrality does not outweigh outcome benefit. DPP4 inhibitors are reasonable as third-line in absence of HFrEF/CKD where SGLT2i/GLP-1 RA are contraindicated (ADS-ADEA Algorithm; AMH).

Thiazolidinediones cause fluid retention via PPAR-gamma sodium reabsorption and are contraindicated in HFrEF (NYHA III/IV). Pioglitazone has glucose-lowering and modest cardiovascular benefits in selected patients, but never with established HFrEF (AMH; ADS-ADEA Algorithm).

explanation.summary: Insulin initiation in type 2 diabetes is indicated when HbA1c is above target despite maximally tolerated oral and injectable non-insulin therapy, or in symptomatic hyperglycaemia, or perioperative or pregnancy contexts. The Australian standard is a once-daily long-acting basal analogue (glargine, degludec, or detemir) given at bedtime, starting at 10 units (or 0.1-0.2 units/kg), with patient-led self-titration of 2 units every 3 days targeting fasting capillary glucose 6-8 mmol/L. Existing metformin, SGLT2 inhibitor and GLP-1 RA continue - their cardiorenal and weight benefits are preserved. Sulfonylureas usually stop with insulin start to reduce hypoglycaemia risk. Counsel on hypoglycaemia recognition (sweating, tremor, hunger, confusion, irritability), 15-15-15 rule (15 g fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck in 15 minutes, repeat once), glucagon availability for severe hypoglycaemia, sick-day rules (continue insulin during illness, increase glucose monitoring), and Austroads driving guidance (check BGL before driving, do not drive under 5 mmol/L).
key_points: Start 10 units nocte or 0.1 to 0.2 units/kg/day
Titrate by 2 units every 3 days based on fasting capillary glucose
Continue oral agents and GLP1 RA
Add prandial insulin only if basal target is met but HbA1c is still high
explanation.pearls: When non-insulin therapy fails in type 2 diabetes, start once-daily long-acting basal insulin (glargine 10 units nocte, titrated by 2 units every 3 days to a fasting capillary glucose 6-8 mmol/L). Continue metformin, SGLT2i and GLP-1 RA (RACGP 2024; ADS-ADEA).

options.rationale: Premixed biphasic insulin covers basal and prandial but has the highest hypoglycaemia risk and least flexibility. This would be correct only when adherence to multi-injection regimens is poor and structured meal patterns are reliable; not first-line for isolated fasting hyperglycaemia (RACGP 2024).

Basal-bolus is reserved for failure of basal alone or significant post-prandial excursions; this patient has isolated fasting hyperglycaemia. Starting with maximal complexity is unnecessary when minimal intervention suffices. Basal-bolus is correct after basal optimisation if post-prandial glucose remains uncontrolled (RACGP 2024).

Once-daily long-acting basal insulin is the preferred initiation strategy in T2DM with elevated fasting glucose; start 10 units (or 0.1 to 0.2 units/kg) nocte and titrate to fasting target, continuing metformin, SGLT2i and GLP1 RA (RACGP 2024; ADS-ADEA Algorithm).

NPH has a 4 to 8 hour peak with higher nocturnal hypoglycaemia risk than long-acting analogues; long-acting analogues (glargine, detemir, degludec) are preferred especially in older patients fearful of hypoglycaemia. NPH may be acceptable on cost grounds or in patients without nocturnal hypoglycaemia concern (RACGP 2024).

Prandial-only insulin addresses post-prandial excursions, not fasting hyperglycaemia, and would miss her dominant abnormality. Prandial-only would be correct with isolated post-prandial spikes and normal fasting glucose (RACGP 2024).

explanation.summary: Symptomatic cerebral oedema is uncommon in adults with DKA, but JBDS notes it occurs in younger adults and those who are physically slight, and the Queensland adult protocol flags younger patients as highest risk. Signs are monitored from admission for at least 24 hours: headache, falling GCS, vomiting, bradycardia and rising blood pressure. Treatment is osmotherapy (mannitol or hypertonic saline) without waiting for imaging, a reduced fluid rate, head-up positioning, then CT and ICU review.
key_points: Headache, falling GCS and a Cushing response during DKA treatment are cerebral oedema until proven otherwise.
Give mannitol (Queensland adult protocol: 20% mannitol 100 mL over 20 minutes) or hypertonic saline without waiting for CT.
Reduce the fluid rate, nurse head up and involve ICU early.
Young adults aged 18 to 25 need more cautious fluid replacement.
explanation.pearls: JBDS advises reducing the fixed-rate insulin infusion to 0.05 units/kg/hour once glucose falls below 14 mmol/L, to limit hypoglycaemia while ketones clear.

sources.label: Queensland Health: Management of DKA in adults (16 years and over)
JBDS-IP: Management of DKA in adults (2023)

options.rationale: Aggressive fluid replacement is a risk factor for cerebral oedema, and JBDS asks for more cautious fluid replacement in young adults aged 18 to 25 for this reason. With suspected cerebral oedema the fluid rate is reduced, not increased; faster fluids suit ongoing shock without neurological signs. (Source: JBDS-IP: Management of DKA in adults (2023))
source_refs: JBDS-IP: Management of DKA in adults (2023)

options.rationale: Headache, a falling GCS, vomiting, bradycardia and rising blood pressure 5 hours into treatment are cerebral oedema until proven otherwise. JBDS advises urgent mannitol or hypertonic saline without waiting for imaging, and the Queensland adult protocol gives 20% mannitol 100 mL over 20 minutes with CT, ICU referral and consultant involvement. (Source: JBDS-IP: Management of DKA in adults (2023); Queensland Health: Management of DKA in adults (16 years and over))
source_refs: JBDS-IP: Management of DKA in adults (2023)
Queensland Health: Management of DKA in adults (16 years and over)

options.rationale: Stopping insulin allows ketogenesis to resume and does not treat rising intracranial pressure. JBDS reduces the fixed-rate insulin to 0.05 units/kg/hour once glucose falls below 14 mmol/L and adds 10% glucose, rather than stopping it. (Source: JBDS-IP: Management of DKA in adults (2023))
source_refs: JBDS-IP: Management of DKA in adults (2023)

options.rationale: A glucose of 11 mmol/L is not hypoglycaemia. Once glucose falls below 14 mmol/L, 10% glucose is run alongside the sodium chloride so the insulin infusion can continue; concentrated dextrose suits true hypoglycaemia. (Source: JBDS-IP: Management of DKA in adults (2023); Queensland Health: Management of DKA in adults (16 years and over))
source_refs: JBDS-IP: Management of DKA in adults (2023)
Queensland Health: Management of DKA in adults (16 years and over)

options.rationale: Headache and drowsiness raise meningitis, but bradycardia with rising blood pressure a few hours into DKA treatment makes cerebral oedema far more likely, and JBDS says osmotherapy must not be delayed. Empirical antibiotics suit fever, meningism or a non-DKA explanation that persists after stabilisation. (Source: JBDS-IP: Management of DKA in adults (2023))
source_refs: JBDS-IP: Management of DKA in adults (2023)

explanation.summary: HHS is defined biochemically by severe hyperglycaemia, effective osmolality >320 mosm/kg, minimal ketosis and absence of significant acidosis. Fluid resuscitation (typically 0.9 percent saline at a slower rate than DKA), VTE prophylaxis and identification of the precipitant are priorities; insulin is added at a lower rate (0.05 units/kg/hour) only after fluids restore perfusion (JBDS HHS 2022; eTG).
key_points: HHS biochemistry: glucose >30, osm >320, ketones <3, pH >=7.30, HCO3 >=15
Slower fluid replacement than DKA (older, comorbid, risk of fluid overload)
Mortality up to 20 percent - higher than DKA
Always give thromboprophylaxis (LMWH unless contraindicated)
explanation.pearls: If ketones are >3 mmol/L and there is acidosis, treat as mixed DKA/HHS using DKA pathway.

options.rationale: Severe hyperglycaemia (>30 mmol/L) occurs in both HHS and DKA; glucose level alone does not discriminate. A value shared by both diagnoses cannot separate them. HHS typically has higher glucose (often >40) but overlap with severe DKA is substantial (eTG Endocrinology - HHS).

Diagnostic features of HHS are marked hyperglycaemia (typically >30 mmol/L), effective osmolality >320 mosm/kg, minimal ketosis (capillary ketones <3 mmol/L) and absence of significant acidosis (pH >=7.30, HCO3 >=15) (JBDS HHS 2022; eTG Endocrinology).
AKI is common in both DKA and HHS due to volume depletion and does not differentiate. AKI severity may favour HHS due to more prolonged osmotic diuresis but is not discriminatory (KDIGO; eTG).

Infection precipitates both HHS and DKA; the precipitant cannot discriminate the metabolic phenotype. The discrimination is biochemical (ketosis and acidosis present in DKA, absent or minimal in HHS), not aetiological (eTG Endocrinology).

Drowsiness can occur in both, although depressed consciousness correlates more closely with osmolality (and therefore is more often severe in HHS). However the DEFINING feature remains the biochemistry pattern (ketones, pH, osmolality), not GCS alone. GCS is supportive but not the specific discriminator (JBDS HHS 2022).

explanation.summary: Severe hypoglycaemia in an older patient on a sulfonylurea plus basal insulin should prompt review of recently introduced interacting drugs (trimethoprim, fluoroquinolones, fluconazole) and declining renal function. Sulfonylureas are best avoided in significant CKD and should usually be ceased before reflexively reducing insulin (RACGP 2024; AMH).
key_points: Trimethoprim, fluoroquinolones, fluconazole potentiate sulfonylureas
Sulfonylureas accumulate in CKD - avoid below eGFR ~30 to 45 mL/min/1.73m^2
Always look for missed meals, weight loss, new infections, new drugs
Older adults with HbA1c <53 mmol/mol on sulfonylurea + insulin are over-treated
explanation.pearls: Hypoglycaemia unawareness develops with recurrent lows - target a slightly higher HbA1c in frail older adults (53 to 64 mmol/mol).

options.rationale: Insulin glargine alone is unlikely to cause this severity in a previously stable patient; reflexive dose reduction without identifying precipitants misses the actual cause. When a sulfonylurea-antibiotic interaction is present, insulin should not be assumed to be the culprit. Glargine dose review is appropriate after identifying and addressing the precipitant (RACGP 2024; AMH).

Trimethoprim potentiates sulfonylureas (CYP2C9 inhibition and competitive renal tubular secretion) and gliclazide accumulates with reduced eGFR; together with poor intake and weight loss, this is the most likely precipitant. Sulfonylureas should be reviewed in CKD and with new interacting antibiotics (AMH; eTG Antibiotic).

Metformin does not cause hypoglycaemia in monotherapy and only minimally contributes in combination therapy because it does not stimulate insulin secretion. Metformin contributes to hypoglycaemia only in extreme overdose or via lactic acidosis indirectly (AMH).

Cefalexin is not a recognised cause of hypoglycaemia. Among antibiotics, fluoroquinolones (gatifloxacin most strongly) and trimethoprim are the main offenders potentiating sulfonylureas. Cefalexin causes hypoglycaemia only through reduced oral intake from nausea, not pharmacologically (AMH).

1 mg IM glucagon is the standard adult dose and her glucose responded - this is not the cause of the original event. Glucagon dose review is appropriate only when initial response fails or in glycogen-depleted states (alcohol, prolonged fasting) (ANZCOR; AMH).

explanation.summary: Thyroid storm is a clinical diagnosis (Burch-Wartofsky score) with hyperthermia, tachyarrhythmia, CNS dysfunction, GI symptoms and a precipitant on a background of hyperthyroidism. Management combines beta blockade, antithyroid drug (PTU or carbimazole), iodine (after antithyroid drug), corticosteroid and treatment of the precipitant. Myxoedema coma is the opposite picture and requires IV thyroid hormone and hydrocortisone (eTG; AMH).
key_points: PTU preferred in storm (blocks peripheral T4->T3 conversion)
Iodine (Lugol's or potassium iodide) given >=1 hour AFTER antithyroid drug
Hydrocortisone covers relative adrenal insufficiency and blocks T4->T3
Avoid amiodarone; avoid aspirin (displaces T4 from binding proteins)
explanation.pearls: Myxoedema coma classically: hypothermia, bradycardia, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia, hypoventilation, depressed GCS - mirror image of storm.

options.rationale: Thyroid storm (Burch-Wartofsky >=45) requires beta blockade, an antithyroid drug (PTU preferred for additional T4-to-T3 conversion blockade), iodine started AFTER the antithyroid drug to prevent substrate loading, hydrocortisone (blocks conversion and treats relative adrenal insufficiency) and supportive care including cooling and treatment of the precipitant (eTG Endocrinology; AMH).

Amiodarone is 37% iodine by weight and PROVIDES the iodine substrate that worsens thyroid storm via the Jod-Basedow effect; it is contraindicated in thyrotoxicosis. Beta blockade (propranolol, esmolol) is preferred for rate control in storm. Amiodarone should be avoided in thyroid emergency (AMH).

The clinical picture fits thyroid storm with a clear precipitant (medication non-adherence). Empirical antimicrobials may be reasonable if infection is also suspected but they do not address the thyroid emergency. Antibiotics first would be correct only if sepsis were the dominant working diagnosis with a separately identified source (eTG Endocrinology).

Myxoedema coma presents with hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation, and depressed consciousness - the OPPOSITE picture (hyperthermia, tachyarrhythmia, tremor here). Thyroid hormone is not a reflex treatment for every thyroid emergency. T4 + steroid is correct only in confirmed myxoedema coma (eTG Endocrinology).

Thyroid storm carries 10 to 30% mortality without aggressive inpatient management; discharge is unsafe regardless of antithyroid drug. Sizing the carbimazole dose to the thyrotoxicosis, as would suit ambulatory severe Graves disease, does not address the storm phenotype. Outpatient carbimazole is correct for stable Graves disease, never for storm (eTG Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: Choice between carbimazole, radioactive iodine and thyroidectomy in Graves disease is guided by relapse risk (TRAb titre, goitre size, age, gender), pregnancy plans and orbitopathy status. Active moderate-to-severe orbitopathy is a relative contraindication to RAI; pregnancy within 6 months precludes RAI; large goitre or compressive symptoms favour surgery (ETA 2021; eTG).
key_points: Carbimazole 12 to 18 months: ~50 percent relapse after stopping
RAI: definitive but worsens orbitopathy in ~15 percent unless steroid prophylaxis given; defer pregnancy 6 months
Surgery: rapid cure, preserves option of pregnancy soon, removes antigen in severe orbitopathy
PTU reserved for first trimester pregnancy or thyroid storm
explanation.pearls: Smoking strongly worsens Graves orbitopathy and RAI outcomes - cessation is mandatory.

options.rationale: RAI can WORSEN active Graves orbitopathy (especially moderate-severe disease, smoking history, high TRAb), and pregnancy must be avoided for 6 months post-RAI - conflicting with her conception plans. RAI would be correct in Graves disease without orbitopathy, not pursuing pregnancy within 6 months, and no large goitre (ESA/ETA 2021).

In Graves disease with moderate-to-severe active orbitopathy, large goitre, plans for pregnancy within 12 months, or patient preference, total thyroidectomy is preferred. It removes the antigenic stimulus, does not worsen orbitopathy and allows immediate trial of conception once levothyroxine is stable. Pre-operative preparation and a high-volume surgeon reduce complications (ETA 2021; eTG Endocrinology).

Long-term low-dose carbimazole is an emerging option for selected patients (with mild disease, low TRAb, no relapse history) but is less effective at definitive cure; high TRAb plus relapse history plus active orbitopathy favour definitive treatment, and carbimazole is teratogenic in early pregnancy. Long-term carbimazole is correct only in mild persistent disease where definitive therapy is declined (eTG; AMH).

PTU carries higher risk of severe hepatotoxicity than carbimazole and is reserved for first trimester pregnancy (when carbimazole has higher teratogenicity) or thyroid storm. Indefinite PTU is the wrong long-term agent. PTU is correct in first trimester or storm only (AMH).

IV methylprednisolone treats active moderate-to-severe orbitopathy but does NOT treat the underlying hyperthyroidism; it complements but does not replace definitive thyroid management. Methylprednisolone is correct as adjunctive therapy for orbitopathy (alongside definitive thyroid treatment), not as monotherapy (ETA 2021).

explanation.summary: Subclinical hypothyroidism is defined by an elevated TSH with a normal free T4. Treatment is generally reserved for TSH persistently >=10 mIU/L, or 4 to 10 with attributable symptoms, pregnancy, infertility or large goitre. Otherwise, monitoring is appropriate; positive TPO antibodies confirm Hashimoto and predict progression (ESA; RACGP).
key_points: Confirm with a repeat after 6 to 12 weeks before labelling
Treat if TSH >=10, symptomatic with TSH 4 to 10, pregnant or planning pregnancy
Start levothyroxine 1.6 microgram/kg/day (lower in elderly and IHD)
Recheck TFTs 6 to 8 weeks after dose changes
explanation.pearls: In pregnancy, treat subclinical hypothyroidism if TSH is above the trimester-specific upper limit (typically >4.0 mIU/L).

options.rationale: In women planning pregnancy or in early pregnancy, Australian and international endocrine guidance recommends treating subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH above 2.5 in pregnancy planning, above trimester-specific limits in pregnancy) particularly when TPO antibodies are positive, to reduce miscarriage and pregnancy complications; pre-conception TSH target is below 2.5 mIU/L (ESA position; RACGP Red Book; ATA pregnancy guidelines).
Deferring treatment delays pre-conception optimisation; positive TPO antibodies plus TSH above 2.5 in a woman planning pregnancy is a treatment indication (ESA; ATA).
Statins do not interfere with TSH; atorvastatin should be ceased on confirmation of pregnancy due to fetal risk, but not for thyroid reasons (AMH).
FNA is indicated for suspicious thyroid nodules; she has no nodule (RACGP).
T3 monotherapy is not recommended for primary hypothyroidism; levothyroxine T4 is the standard (AMH; ESA).

explanation.summary: Symptomatic hypocalcaemia (tetany, seizures, laryngospasm, QT prolongation, prolonged ECG changes) is treated with IV 10 percent calcium gluconate bolus and infusion, replacement of magnesium if low, and transition to oral calcium plus active vitamin D (calcitriol or alfacalcidol) once stable. Calcitriol is required in hypoparathyroidism because PTH-dependent 1-alpha-hydroxylation is impaired (eTG; AMH).
key_points: 10 percent calcium gluconate 10 mL = 2.2 mmol elemental Ca (safer peripherally)
Always replete magnesium - low Mg causes refractory hypocalcaemia
Active vitamin D (calcitriol) needed when PTH is low
Continuous ECG monitoring during IV infusion
explanation.pearls: Post-thyroidectomy hypocalcaemia: check Ca at 6, 12 and 24 hours; transient post-op hypoparathyroidism is common, permanent in 1 to 3 percent.

options.rationale: Oral therapy is correct for asymptomatic mild hypocalcaemia or as maintenance after IV correction. Symptomatic acute hypocalcaemia with tetany or QT prolongation requires IV calcium for prompt myocardial protection. Oral calcium + calcitriol is the maintenance pathway after IV stabilisation (eTG Endocrinology).

Symptomatic hypocalcaemia with tetany or QT prolongation requires IV 10 percent calcium gluconate bolus followed by infusion to prevent rebound. Magnesium replacement is required if low because it perpetuates hypocalcaemia. Oral calcium and active vitamin D (calcitriol) are added for maintenance, with active D needed because of low PTH (eTG Endocrinology; AMH). Practically: 10 mL of 10 percent calcium gluconate (2.2 mmol Ca) in 100 mL of 5 percent dextrose over 10 minutes, then infusion such as 100 mL of 10 percent calcium gluconate in 1 L over 6 to 8 hours, with active vitamin D needed because PTH is low.

Calcium chloride contains 3x more elemental calcium per mL but is highly irritant and risks severe extravasation injury via peripheral line; calcium gluconate is preferred for peripheral administration. Calcium chloride is correct only via central venous access or in cardiac arrest (AMH; eTG).

Magnesium 0.74 mmol/L is borderline and replacement is appropriate (low Mg perpetuates hypocalcaemia by impairing PTH release and action), but Mg alone will not correct her acute symptomatic hypocalcaemia in the required timeframe. Mg-alone is correct in pure hypomagnesaemic hypocalcaemia with mild symptoms (eTG Endocrinology).

Cinacalcet is a calcimimetic that LOWERS calcium in hyperparathyroidism; it is contraindicated in hypocalcaemia and would worsen her presentation. Cinacalcet is correct in primary or secondary hyperparathyroidism, never in hypocalcaemia (AMH).

explanation.summary: After SAH or other brain injury, distinguishing SIADH from CSW depends on volume status. Both have low serum osmolality and inappropriately concentrated urine with high urine sodium. CSW shows hypovolaemia (weight loss, postural hypotension, dry mucous membranes, polyuria); SIADH shows euvolaemia. CSW is treated with isotonic saline plus sodium replacement; SIADH with fluid restriction (or tolvaptan if persistent). Limit sodium correction to 8 to 10 mmol/L per 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination (ENLS 2023; Australian Stroke Foundation).
key_points: Volume status is THE distinguishing feature between SIADH and CSW
After SAH, hypotonic fluids are avoided; isotonic or hypertonic preferred
Symptomatic severe hyponatraemia: 3 percent saline 150 mL bolus, target rise 4 to 6 mmol/L
Limit correction to 8 to 10 mmol/L per 24 h (6 to 8 if high risk for ODS)
explanation.pearls: If sodium overcorrects, re-lower with DDAVP and 5 percent dextrose - cerebral pontine myelinolysis is devastating and preventable.

options.rationale: Fluid restriction is correct for SIADH (euvolaemic hyponatraemia); this patient is hypovolaemic with polyuria, weight loss, and postural hypotension after SAH. Restricting fluid would worsen cerebral hypoperfusion and the risk of delayed cerebral ischaemia (DCI). Post-neurosurgical hyponatraemia should not be treated as SIADH without volume assessment (Australian Stroke Foundation; ENLS 2023).

The clinical picture (polyuria, weight loss, postural hypotension, dry mucous membranes after SAH) plus high urine sodium fits cerebral salt wasting (CSW), where treatment is volume and sodium replacement, not restriction. Maintaining euvolaemia and avoiding hyponatraemia reduces delayed cerebral ischaemia in SAH (Australian Stroke Foundation; ENLS 2023).

Tolvaptan (V2 antagonist) treats SIADH by increasing free water clearance; it would worsen hypovolaemic hyponatraemia in CSW and is contraindicated in volume depletion. SIADH-specific therapy should not be used without confirming the volume state. Tolvaptan is correct only in confirmed euvolaemic SIADH (AMH).

Hypertonic saline bolus is correct for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizures, coma) for a target rise of 4 to 6 mmol/L in 1 to 2 hours, but a single bolus without ongoing maintenance volume in CSW under-treats volume depletion and risks overshoot. Hypertonic saline is correct as part of CSW management when sodium fails to rise on isotonic saline, not as sole therapy (ENLS 2023).

Free water in 5% dextrose worsens hyponatraemia and is contraindicated; in any neurocritical patient it also increases intracranial water content. Dextrose is appropriate only for documented hypoglycaemia (ENLS 2023).

explanation.summary: Acute ischaemic stroke reperfusion choices: IV thrombolysis within 4.5 hours of last seen well if no contraindication (BP <185/110, no recent DOAC dose within 48 h unless levels confirmed sub-therapeutic, no recent major surgery/bleeding/stroke). Mechanical thrombectomy within 6 hours for anterior circulation LVO (M1/ICA) with ASPECTS >=6 and disabling deficit; window extends to 24 hours if perfusion imaging shows salvageable penumbra. Thrombectomy is delivered with or without prior thrombolysis (Australian Stroke Foundation).
key_points: DOAC within 48 hours is a relative contraindication to thrombolysis unless levels measured
Thrombectomy window 0 to 6 h with CT/CTA; 6 to 24 h with perfusion imaging (DEFUSE-3, DAWN criteria)
Pre-thrombolysis BP target <185/110 mmHg
DAPT (aspirin + clopidogrel) for 21 days then aspirin alone after minor stroke / high-risk TIA (CHANCE / POINT)
explanation.pearls: Door-to-needle target 60 minutes; door-to-groin target 90 minutes - process matters more than algorithm minutiae.

options.rationale: IV thrombolysis is contraindicated within 48 hours of a DOAC dose unless DOAC levels are confirmed sub-therapeutic (anti-Xa for apixaban). His last apixaban was at 0700, well within 48 hours. Anticoagulant timing must be checked before thrombolysis in any LVO. Thrombolysis is correct only when DOAC is excluded or levels are sub-therapeutic (Australian Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines).

Pre-thrombolysis BP target is <185/110 mmHg; for thrombectomy without thrombolysis higher BP is tolerated (typically <220/120). Aggressive lowering to <140/90 risks penumbral hypoperfusion and infarct extension. Tight BP control is correct only POST-thrombectomy with successful recanalisation (Australian Stroke Foundation; ENLS).

Within 6 hours of last seen well, with a proximal M1 occlusion, NIHSS >=6 and ASPECTS >=6, mechanical thrombectomy is indicated. IV thrombolysis is contraindicated due to recent apixaban; proceed directly to thrombectomy. BP target pre-procedure is <185/110 (Australian Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines).

Antiplatelet alone is not the reperfusion treatment for a proximal LVO; thrombectomy is the standard of care. Antiplatelet within 24 hours of thrombolysis would also be contraindicated. Aspirin-only is correct only for ischaemic stroke without LVO and outside reperfusion windows (Australian Stroke Foundation).

Idarucizumab reverses DABIGATRAN, not apixaban. Andexanet alfa partially reverses factor Xa inhibitors but is expensive, not universally available, and not routinely used to enable thrombolysis (risk of rebound). Direct transfer to thrombectomy avoids the reversal pitfall. Idarucizumab and andexanet alfa target different DOACs (AMH; Australian Stroke Foundation).

explanation.summary: Modern Australian guidance for TIA emphasises urgent same-day specialist assessment regardless of ABCD2 score. Brain and vascular imaging, antiplatelet initiation (DAPT for 21 days after high-risk TIA or minor non-cardioembolic stroke per CHANCE/POINT), risk factor control and rhythm monitoring for occult AF underpin secondary prevention (Australian Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines).
key_points: All suspected TIAs: same-day specialist assessment
Aspirin 300 mg loading, then DAPT 21 days for high-risk TIA / minor stroke
BP, lipid, glucose, smoking cessation, anticoagulation if AF detected
Carotid imaging within 24 to 48 hours for anterior circulation events
explanation.pearls: ABCD2 is still useful as a teaching tool but does not safely triage TIA to deferred care.

options.rationale: Australian Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines mandate urgent same-day assessment for all suspected TIAs regardless of ABCD2 score, with same-day brain and vessel imaging to identify large-vessel stenosis that may warrant urgent intervention, initial antiplatelet load, and cardiac monitoring to detect occult AF. DAPT for 21 days (aspirin plus clopidogrel) is then recommended after high-risk TIA per CHANCE/POINT data, but the initial step is urgent referral with aspirin loading.

Australian guidance has moved away from ABCD2-based triage because lower scores still carry meaningful early stroke risk; all suspected TIAs require same-day specialist assessment (Australian Stroke Foundation).
Two-week deferral risks recurrent stroke; same-day specialist assessment with same-day imaging is the standard (Australian Stroke Foundation).

Empirical anticoagulation without documented AF exposes her to bleeding risk in the immediate post-TIA window before imaging excludes haemorrhage; rhythm monitoring is appropriate but not in place of urgent imaging (Australian Stroke Foundation).
Carotid imaging is critical but must occur within 24 to 48 hours, not weeks; same-day referral with CTA is the standard pathway (Australian Stroke Foundation).

explanation.summary: After a first unprovoked seizure in an adult, MRI brain and EEG outpatient form the standard recurrence-risk workup. Antiepileptic drug initiation is not routine but may be considered if recurrence risk is high (epileptiform EEG, structural lesion). Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022 mandates a minimum 6-month non-driving period for private vehicles after a first seizure (longer with risk factors), and longer abstinence for commercial vehicles (eTG Neurology).
key_points: Workup: MRI brain, EEG, electrolytes, glucose, calcium, magnesium, drug screen
AED start considered if recurrence risk high (e.g. structural lesion, epileptiform EEG, nocturnal seizure)
Private vehicle: minimum 6 months off driving after first seizure
Commercial vehicle: minimum 5 years seizure-free off medication
explanation.pearls: Counselling and documentation of driving restriction is the doctor's legal and professional duty - patients self-report to road authority.

options.rationale: First unprovoked seizure workup includes outpatient MRI brain (preferred over CT for structural lesions) and EEG to assess recurrence risk. Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022 requires a minimum 6-month non-driving period after a first seizure for private licence, longer for commercial. The treating doctor must counsel and document this (Austroads AFTD 2022; eTG Neurology).

Antiepileptic monotherapy after a single unprovoked seizure with no abnormalities is not routinely recommended; the modest reduction in recurrence is offset by drug burden. 1-month suspension is well short of the Austroads minimum (6 months private). Valproate is teratogenic and inappropriate in a woman of reproductive age without explicit pre-conception counselling. Multiple errors (eTG Neurology; Austroads).

There are no features of meningitis (no fever, headache, neck stiffness, altered consciousness); LP is not indicated for an isolated first seizure. LP is correct with fever, headache, or focal neurology suggestive of CNS infection (eTG Antibiotic).

Continuous video-EEG is for diagnostic uncertainty (PNES vs epilepsy) or pre-surgical evaluation, not standard first-seizure workup. Specialised testing should not precede standard workup. Routine outpatient EEG (with sleep deprivation if first study negative) is the standard first investigation (eTG Neurology).

Commercial driving requires longer abstinence under Austroads AFTD: typically 10 years seizure-free off medication, or 5 years on medication with strict conditions. Immediate return is unsafe and legally non-compliant. The treating doctor must specifically document commercial-vs-private status (Austroads AFTD 2022).

explanation.summary: Convulsive status epilepticus is defined as a seizure lasting 5 minutes or more, or recurrent seizures without recovery of consciousness between, and carries a 20-30% mortality. The Australian stepwise approach is first-line benzodiazepine (IM midazolam 10 mg, IV lorazepam 4 mg or IV diazepam 10 mg) repeatable once at 5-10 minutes; second-line IV antiepileptic (levetiracetam 60 mg/kg, sodium valproate 40 mg/kg, or phenytoin 20 mg/kg) - the ESETT trial showed these are roughly equivalent and levetiracetam is preferred for its tolerability; third-line refractory status requires intubation with propofol, midazolam or thiopental infusions and continuous EEG. Imaging, lumbar puncture and toxicology workup all happen in parallel with - never instead of - seizure termination. Common reversible drivers in adults include anticonvulsant non-adherence, alcohol withdrawal, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia and CNS infection.
key_points: Two benzodiazepine doses then escalate, do not repeat indefinitely
Second-line: levetiracetam, phenytoin or valproate (ESETT showed equivalent efficacy)
Refractory (>30 min despite second-line): intubation and continuous anaesthetic infusion
Always check glucose; consider thiamine, eclampsia, hyponatraemia, toxic causes
explanation.pearls: In benzodiazepine-refractory status, IV levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (max 4.5 g) over 10 minutes is non-inferior to phenytoin and sodium valproate (ESETT 2019) and is the default Australian second-line agent for its ease and safety profile.

options.rationale: Two adequate benzodiazepine doses have already been given with no response; further benzodiazepine risks respiratory depression without added benefit. The next step is escalation, not a repeat of first-line. Escalate to second-line antiepileptic (levetiracetam, phenytoin, or valproate) (eTG Neurology; ANZCOR).

After two adequate doses of a benzodiazepine, second-line therapy in convulsive status epilepticus is IV levetiracetam, phenytoin (or fos-phenytoin), or sodium valproate. Levetiracetam at 60 mg/kg over 10 minutes is recommended by ESETT and current Australian eTG and NSW Health guidance (eTG Neurology; ESETT 2019).

Anaesthetic induction is third-line, after a second-line antiepileptic has failed; jumping to anaesthesia skips a step and commits to ICU intubation unnecessarily. Propofol induction is correct in confirmed refractory status epilepticus (failure of second-line agent) (eTG Neurology).

Oral phenytoin via NG tube has unpredictable absorption and is too slow for acute status; IV phenytoin (20 mg/kg, max rate 50 mg/min) is the parenteral option if levetiracetam is not chosen. The oral route is unsuitable in an emergency. NG phenytoin is correct only for outpatient initiation or maintenance, not acute status (eTG Neurology; AMH).

Empirical glucose is reserved for hypoglycaemia; his glucose is 7.4 mmol/L. Thiamine is appropriate if alcohol use disorder is suspected (always BEFORE glucose to prevent Wernicke precipitation) but does not terminate the seizure. Thiamine + glucose is correct in suspected alcohol-related seizure with hypoglycaemia (eTG Neurology).

explanation.summary: Giant cell arteritis is a medical emergency due to risk of permanent visual loss. Diagnosis is clinical (age >=50, new headache, jaw claudication, temporal artery tenderness, raised ESR/CRP) supported by temporal artery biopsy (skip lesions; sensitivity ~75 percent) or vascular ultrasound (halo sign). High-dose corticosteroid is started immediately, with biopsy within 1 to 2 weeks. Tocilizumab is steroid-sparing in established disease (eTG Rheumatology).
key_points: Visual symptoms or jaw claudication: IV methylprednisolone 0.5 to 1 g daily for 3 days then oral prednisolone
Otherwise: oral prednisolone 40 to 60 mg daily
Aspirin 100 mg daily reduces ischaemic complications (controversial; review individual bleeding risk)
Tocilizumab and methotrexate are steroid-sparing options
Bone protection (calcium, vitamin D, bisphosphonate), PCP prophylaxis if high-dose long-duration steroid
explanation.pearls: ESR and CRP are usually both elevated; isolated normal CRP makes GCA very unlikely.

options.rationale: Amaurosis fugax and a new relative afferent pupillary defect with reduced visual acuity indicate ophthalmic involvement of giant cell arteritis, which is a sight-threatening emergency requiring IV pulse methylprednisolone rather than oral prednisolone alone. Biopsy can still be performed within 1 to 2 weeks of steroid initiation. Calcium, vitamin D and PJP and bone protection planning are needed but not immediate (eTG Rheumatology; ARA position).
Oral prednisolone 60 mg is standard for GCA without visual involvement; the presence of amaurosis fugax and RAPD escalates to IV pulse methylprednisolone (eTG; ARA).
CT brain does not diagnose GCA and waiting for biopsy risks permanent blindness within hours to days; steroid must be started on clinical suspicion (eTG).
Tocilizumab is steroid-sparing add-on therapy for established disease; it does not replace acute high-dose corticosteroid in the emergency setting (eTG; ARA).

New severe headache in someone over 50 with raised inflammatory markers, jaw claudication and visual loss is not migraine, and triptans are contraindicated in suspected ischaemic disease (eTG Neurology).

explanation.summary: IM adrenaline is the single most important treatment in anaphylaxis. Adult dose is 0.5 mg of 1:1000 (10 microgram/kg, maximum 0.5 mg) into the anterolateral mid-thigh, repeated every 5 minutes as needed. Place supine with legs elevated unless airway compromise. Give high-flow oxygen and IV fluid (20 mL/kg crystalloid). Corticosteroids and antihistamines are adjuncts only (ASCIA 2024; ANZCOR).
key_points: IM adrenaline first, IV adrenaline infusion if refractory after 2 to 3 doses
Supine with legs elevated, high-flow oxygen, IV crystalloid bolus
Observe for biphasic reaction for at least 4 hours (longer if severe)
Discharge with EpiPen (or two), ASCIA action plan, allergy referral
explanation.pearls: If the patient is on a beta blocker and refractory, glucagon 1 to 5 mg IV may help by bypassing the beta receptor.

options.rationale: After two doses of IM adrenaline without adequate response, ASCIA recommends IV adrenaline infusion (5 to 15 microgram per minute titrated) alongside aggressive fluid resuscitation; persistent stridor and shock require airway preparation including senior anaesthetic and ENT support, with surgical airway equipment ready (ASCIA 2024; ANZCOR).
Refractory anaphylaxis (no response after two IM doses) is the indication for IV adrenaline infusion under monitored conditions; persisting with IM alone delays effective therapy (ASCIA 2024).
Steroids and antihistamines are adjuncts only and do not reverse acute anaphylaxis; promethazine can worsen hypotension; neither addresses refractory disease (ASCIA 2024; AMH).
Glucagon is reserved for refractory anaphylaxis in patients on beta-blocker; she is on no medications, so IV adrenaline infusion is the next step (ASCIA 2024).
Nebulised therapies are adjuncts for persistent bronchospasm or laryngeal oedema after systemic adrenaline; they do not replace IV adrenaline infusion in refractory shock (ASCIA 2024).

explanation.summary: STOPP v2 and Beers Criteria identify benzodiazepines (and Z-drugs) as inappropriate in older adults due to falls, fractures, delirium, and cognitive impairment. Deprescribing requires a slow taper over weeks to months with non-pharmacological insomnia strategies (CBT-I, sleep hygiene).
key_points: Benzodiazepines and Z-drugs both on STOPP and Beers for older adults
Falls risk approximately doubles; hip fracture risk significantly elevated
Taper 10-25% every 1-2 weeks over 8-12 weeks (longer for higher doses)
CBT-I is first-line for chronic insomnia
explanation.pearls: Diazepam-equivalent conversion is sometimes used to standardise tapering; e.g. temazepam 20 mg approx diazepam 10 mg.

options.rationale: Benzodiazepines significantly increase falls and fracture risk in older adults; continuing without deprescribing addresses the wrong target (Beers Criteria; STOPP v2 - benzodiazepines).
