source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Community-acquired pneumonia and empyema

explanation.summary: Recurrent malignant pleural effusion in a patient with months of life expectancy is managed with definitive control: talc pleurodesis if lung re-expands fully, or indwelling pleural catheter if trapped lung or patient preference favours ambulatory drainage. Both are first-line options under TSANZ.
key_points: Talc pleurodesis: 70-80% success when lung re-expands fully
IPC: equivalent symptom outcomes (AMPLE trial), suits trapped lung
Recurrent thoracentesis: only when prognosis <1 month or both refused
VATS pleurodesis: reserved for failure of bedside approach
explanation.context: Malignant effusions form when tumour seeds pleural surfaces, obstructing lymphatic drainage and producing exudate. Mean survival from diagnosis varies by primary (breast 7-15 months, lung 3-6, mesothelioma highly variable). The pleurodesis vs IPC choice hinges on lung re-expansion: trapped lung (from tumour rind or organised effusion) means apposition of pleural surfaces cannot occur, and talc cannot create the adhesion needed; IPC then provides ambulatory drainage without requiring fusion.

sources.label: TSANZ Malignant Pleural Effusion position statement
AMPLE trial - Thomas et al., JAMA 2017

options.rationale: Indwelling pleural catheter (IPC) is one valid option, particularly when lung does not re-expand (trapped lung). With full lung re-expansion and good performance status, talc pleurodesis can offer a definitive solution with similar quality of life. Both are listed in TSANZ; choice is patient-centred.
source_refs: TSANZ Malignant Pleural Effusion position statement

options.rationale: With full lung re-expansion on drainage, talc pleurodesis is highly effective (~70-80% success) and offers a single-procedure definitive option for patients with reasonable life expectancy. Talc induces pleural fibrosis through inflammatory adhesion. AMPLE trial (TSANZ-endorsed) compared IPC and pleurodesis with similar outcomes; selection is preference-based.
source_refs: TSANZ Malignant Pleural Effusion position statement
AMPLE trial - Thomas et al., JAMA 2017

options.rationale: Repeated thoracentesis is appropriate only when life expectancy is short (under 1 month) or both pleurodesis and IPC are unsuitable. With ~12 month prognosis and the burden of three taps in 6 weeks, a definitive intervention is warranted (TSANZ).
source_refs: TSANZ Malignant Pleural Effusion position statement

options.rationale: VATS pleurodesis offers similar outcomes to bedside chemical pleurodesis but requires general anaesthesia and longer recovery. Reserved for situations where bedside approach has failed or diagnostic biopsy is also needed (TSANZ).
source_refs: TSANZ Malignant Pleural Effusion position statement

options.rationale: Systemic therapy may help over weeks but does not address acute symptoms from a tense effusion. Local control is the immediate need; systemic therapy continues in parallel (TSANZ).
source_refs: TSANZ Malignant Pleural Effusion position statement

explanation.summary: Tuberculous pleurisy in Australia is most often seen in migrants from high-prevalence countries (Vietnam, China, India, Philippines, sub-Saharan Africa). The triad of lymphocyte-predominant exudate, elevated ADA (>40 U/L), and high pre-test probability supports empirical 4-drug therapy without waiting for culture, alongside mandatory NSW Health notification.
key_points: ADA >40 U/L in lymphocytic exudate: PPV ~95% in high-prevalence cohorts
AFB smear sensitivity in pleural fluid <10%; culture takes 4-6 weeks
Empirical 4-drug regimen: RIPE for 2 months then RI for 4 months
Notification mandatory under Public Health Act 2010; contact tracing
explanation.context: Tuberculous pleurisy arises from rupture of a subpleural caseous focus into the pleural space, eliciting a delayed hypersensitivity reaction that produces the lymphocytic exudate. ADA is elevated because T-lymphocytes activated against mycobacterial antigens secrete this enzyme in pleural fluid. The combination of high ADA, lymphocytic predominance and clinical context gives sufficient pre-test probability to treat empirically; awaiting culture risks both individual progression (miliary TB, chronic empyema) and community transmission.

sources.label: NSW Health Policy Directive PD2014_050 Tuberculosis Management

options.rationale: Lymphocytic exudate with ADA above 40 U/L in a migrant from a high-TB-prevalence region has a positive predictive value of approximately 95% for tuberculous pleurisy. NSW Health TB Program accepts empirical commencement of standard 4-drug therapy while culture is awaited, with mandatory notification. Pleural biopsy can confirm but is not required before treatment in classical presentations.
source_refs: NSW Health Policy Directive PD2014_050 Tuberculosis Management

options.rationale: Pleural biopsy improves diagnostic yield to 80-90% (cell-block or VATS) but treatment should not wait 6 weeks for culture in a high-probability presentation with public health implications. Empirical treatment is the standard pathway (NSW Health).
source_refs: NSW Health Policy Directive PD2014_050 Tuberculosis Management

options.rationale: The presentation (chronic constitutional symptoms, lymphocytic exudate, high ADA, high-prevalence background) is not consistent with bacterial pneumonia. Treating empirically for CAP delays appropriate therapy and risks TB progression and contact transmission (eTG).

Tuberculous effusions usually resolve with anti-tuberculous therapy alone; pleurodesis is not indicated and may worsen residual fibrosis. Drainage is reserved for very large symptomatic collections after therapy commenced (NSW Health).
source_refs: NSW Health Policy Directive PD2014_050 Tuberculosis Management

options.rationale: Quantiferon detects latent or active TB infection but cannot distinguish between them and adds nothing to a positive Mantoux in this clinical picture. Diagnostic stewardship favours moving to treatment now (NSW Health).
source_refs: NSW Health Policy Directive PD2014_050 Tuberculosis Management

explanation.summary: Systemic thrombolysis is the primary reperfusion treatment for high-risk (haemodynamically unstable) PE, and the decision rests on weighing bleeding risk against a high risk of death. ESC 2019 splits contraindications into absolute (previous haemorrhagic stroke or stroke of unknown origin, ischaemic stroke in the previous 6 months, central nervous system neoplasm, major trauma, surgery or head injury in the previous 3 weeks, bleeding diathesis, active bleeding) and relative (TIA in the previous 6 months, oral anticoagulation, pregnancy or the first post-partum week, non-compressible puncture sites, traumatic resuscitation, refractory hypertension above 180 mmHg systolic, advanced liver disease, infective endocarditis, active peptic ulcer). When lysis is contraindicated, surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed treatment is the alternative where available.
key_points: Absolute: central nervous system neoplasm, previous haemorrhagic stroke, ischaemic stroke within 6 months.
Absolute: major trauma, surgery or head injury within 3 weeks, bleeding diathesis, active bleeding.
Relative: TIA within 6 months, oral anticoagulation, pregnancy or first post-partum week, active peptic ulcer.
Relative: refractory hypertension above 180 mmHg systolic, advanced liver disease, infective endocarditis.
explanation.pearls: The 2016 Australian ACS guideline lists stroke or TIA within 12 months as a contraindication to fibrinolysis for STEMI, a longer window than the 6 months in the ESC PE table.

options.rationale: ESC 2019 lists a transient ischaemic attack in the previous 6 months as a relative contraindication. An ischaemic stroke, rather than a TIA, in the previous 6 months would be absolute. (Source: ESC 2019 Acute Pulmonary Embolism Guidelines)

ESC 2019 lists central nervous system neoplasm as an absolute contraindication to fibrinolysis, alongside previous haemorrhagic stroke, ischaemic stroke in the previous 6 months, major trauma, surgery or head injury in the previous 3 weeks, bleeding diathesis and active bleeding. (Source: ESC 2019 Acute Pulmonary Embolism Guidelines)

Oral anticoagulation is a relative contraindication in ESC 2019, and the Australian ACS guideline also calls warfarin a relative contraindication. It would become absolute only as active bleeding or a bleeding diathesis. (Source: ESC 2019 Acute Pulmonary Embolism Guidelines; HFA/CSANZ Australian ACS Clinical Guideline 2016)

Pregnancy and the first post-partum week are relative contraindications in ESC 2019. Active post-partum bleeding would make lysis absolutely contraindicated. (Source: ESC 2019 Acute Pulmonary Embolism Guidelines)
Active peptic ulcer is a relative contraindication in ESC 2019. Bleeding from the ulcer would be active bleeding, which is absolute. (Source: ESC 2019 Acute Pulmonary Embolism Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Australian LTOT criteria require stable resting hypoxaemia confirmed on two ABGs at least 3 weeks apart while not actively exacerbating: pO2 <=55 mmHg outright, OR pO2 56-59 mmHg with cor pulmonale, polycythaemia or pulmonary hypertension. Use >=15 h/day reduces mortality; >18 h/day is preferred.
key_points: Two ABGs >=3 weeks apart while stable, post-exacerbation recovery, on optimised therapy
pO2 <=55 mmHg = standalone criterion; 56-59 needs polycythaemia/cor pulmonale/PHT
Smoking cessation required for safety (fire risk with oxygen)
>=15 h/day for survival benefit; nocturnal-only insufficient
explanation.context: The NOTT (US) and MRC (UK) trials in the early 1980s established that continuous oxygen for chronically hypoxic COPD doubled 5-year survival versus no oxygen, and that nearly-continuous (>18 h) outperformed nocturnal-only. Mechanism is reversal of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, lowering pulmonary artery pressure, unloading the right ventricle and reducing the polycythaemic drive. Crucially, LTOT does not improve survival in patients with milder hypoxaemia, exercise-only desaturation, or nocturnal-only desaturation.

sources.label: TSANZ Adult Domiciliary Oxygen Therapy guidelines
Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X Concise Guide

options.rationale: She meets Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand eligibility for long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT): stable COPD with pO2 <=55 mmHg, or 56-59 mmHg with polycythaemia, cor pulmonale or pulmonary hypertension. Two ABGs at least 3 weeks apart while clinically stable and off smoking confirm eligibility. LTOT reduces mortality when used for at least 15 hours per day (NOTT, MRC trials).
source_refs: TSANZ Adult Domiciliary Oxygen Therapy guidelines
Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X Concise Guide

options.rationale: She already meets criteria after stable repeat assessment. Delaying LTOT denies proven mortality benefit (TSANZ).
source_refs: TSANZ Adult Domiciliary Oxygen Therapy guidelines

options.rationale: Nocturnal-only oxygen does not improve mortality in COPD with chronic daytime hypoxaemia. LTOT requires >=15 hours/day (and ideally >18 hours/day) for survival benefit (TSANZ).
source_refs: TSANZ Adult Domiciliary Oxygen Therapy guidelines

options.rationale: TSANZ recommends smoking cessation before LTOT primarily for fire safety, but a documented 8-month period of cessation with biochemical confirmation can satisfy this criterion. 12 months is not a uniform requirement (TSANZ).
source_refs: TSANZ Adult Domiciliary Oxygen Therapy guidelines

options.rationale: Polycythaemia in chronic hypoxia is the body's adaptive response; reversing it without correcting hypoxaemia reduces oxygen-carrying capacity. Address the underlying hypoxia with LTOT and the polycythaemia will resolve (TSANZ).
source_refs: TSANZ Adult Domiciliary Oxygen Therapy guidelines

explanation.summary: The triad of oral candidiasis, dysphonia and dermal thinning is highly specific for inhaled corticosteroid effect. Local effects reflect deposition in oropharynx and larynx; systemic effects reflect pulmonary absorption (10-50% of dose). Spacer use, mouth rinsing and lowest effective dose minimise all categories.
key_points: ICS local effects: candidiasis, dysphonia, sore throat (spacer + rinse reduce)
ICS systemic effects: bruising, adrenal suppression, osteoporosis, cataract, growth velocity reduction in children
LABA: tremor, tachycardia, hypokalaemia
LAMA: dry mouth, urinary retention, glaucoma exacerbation
explanation.context: Despite inhaled delivery, ICS reach systemic circulation via pulmonary absorption (which mostly bypasses first-pass metabolism) and via swallowed fraction. Higher-potency molecules (fluticasone propionate) have more systemic effect than newer molecules (ciclesonide, mometasone furoate) that undergo more first-pass deactivation. Dermal thinning with bruising on sun-exposed areas (forearms, dorsum of hands) is one of the earliest visible signs of systemic steroid exposure and should prompt dose review, technique check and consideration of step-down.

sources.label: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia)

options.rationale: Oral candidiasis, dysphonia (from laryngeal muscle myopathy or local steroid deposition) and dermal thinning with bruising are signature inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) effects. Local effects (candidiasis, dysphonia) are reduced by spacer use and post-dose mouth rinsing; systemic effects (bruising, adrenal suppression, osteoporosis with high doses) reflect pulmonary absorption.
source_refs: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia)

options.rationale: LABA effects are predominantly cardiovascular (palpitations, tachycardia, fine tremor, occasional hypokalaemia). Candidiasis, dysphonia and bruising are not LABA effects (eTG).
LAMA effects reflect antimuscarinic activity: dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation, precipitation of glaucoma. Candidiasis, dysphonia and bruising are not LAMA effects (eTG).

Montelukast effects include neuropsychiatric (FDA boxed warning for depression and suicidality), sleep disturbance, and rarely Churg-Strauss syndrome. Candidiasis, dysphonia and bruising are not montelukast effects (eTG).

Theophylline causes nausea, headache, tremor, tachyarrhythmia and seizures at toxic levels. It is rarely used in modern Australian practice. Candidiasis, dysphonia and bruising are not theophylline effects (eTG).

explanation.summary: ARDS management is built on lung-protective ventilation (TV 4-8 mL/kg PBW, P-plateau <=30, driving pressure <=15). Severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 <150) escalates to prone positioning >=16 h/day (PROSEVA), neuromuscular blockade (ACURASYS - debated), and ECMO referral (EOLIA). HFOV and nitric oxide are not first-line.
key_points: Lung-protective: TV 4-8 mL/kg PBW, P-plateau <=30, driving pressure <=15
PROSEVA: prone >=16 h/day reduces mortality in severe ARDS (P/F <150)
ECMO referral: PaO2/FiO2 <80 despite optimisation, or P-plateau >30 to achieve TV 6
PEEP titration: use higher PEEP for moderate-severe ARDS (P/F <200)
explanation.context: ARDS is characterised by diffuse alveolar damage with non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, reduced compliance and severe hypoxaemia. Lung-protective ventilation reduces mortality (ARMA trial 1999) because high tidal volumes cause cyclical alveolar overdistension (volutrauma) and shear stress at the interface of aerated and collapsed lung (atelectrauma). Proning works through gravitational redistribution: supine, the dorsal lung is dependent, atelectatic and poorly aerated while still well-perfused (shunt). Proning reverses dependency, recruits dorsal alveoli, homogenises ventilation-perfusion matching, and reduces shunt fraction. PROSEVA demonstrated a 16% absolute mortality reduction in severe ARDS with this single intervention.

sources.label: ANZICS Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome position statement
PROSEVA trial - Guerin et al., NEJM 2013

options.rationale: Severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 <150) refractory to lung-protective ventilation has a mortality benefit from prone positioning for >=16 hours per day (PROSEVA trial). Prone positioning recruits dorsal atelectasis (the dorsal lung is the dependent region when supine), homogenises ventilation-perfusion matching, and reduces ventilator-induced lung injury.
source_refs: ANZICS Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome position statement
PROSEVA trial - Guerin et al., NEJM 2013

options.rationale: Lung-protective ventilation in ARDS uses tidal volume of 4-8 mL/kg predicted body weight and plateau pressure <=30 cmH2O. Increasing tidal volume worsens ventilator-induced lung injury through volutrauma and atelectrauma (ARDSNet ARMA trial; ANZICS).
source_refs: ANZICS Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome position statement

options.rationale: OSCAR and OSCILLATE trials showed no benefit or harm from HFOV in ARDS. It is no longer recommended (ANZICS).
source_refs: ANZICS Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome position statement

options.rationale: Reducing PEEP would worsen alveolar derecruitment and oxygenation. Plateau pressure 32 is at the upper acceptable limit; the answer is to reduce driving pressure by lowering tidal volume slightly or improving compliance through proning, not by withdrawing PEEP (ANZICS).
source_refs: ANZICS Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome position statement

options.rationale: Inhaled nitric oxide improves oxygenation transiently in ARDS but has no mortality benefit and increases renal injury risk. Reserved as a temporising bridge in life-threatening hypoxaemia awaiting other rescue therapies (ANZICS).
source_refs: ANZICS Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome position statement

explanation.summary: PE workup uses pretest probability (Wells or revised Geneva) to direct testing. PE-unlikely (Wells <=4): D-dimer; if negative, PE excluded. PE-likely (Wells >4): CTPA directly. Age-adjusted D-dimer cut-off (age x 10 mcg/L for over-50s) reduces false positives without missing cases.
key_points: Wells <=4 = unlikely; D-dimer rules out if negative
Wells >4 = likely; proceed directly to CTPA
Age-adjusted D-dimer: age x 10 mcg/L for those over 50
Pregnancy/contrast allergy: V/Q scan or leg US instead of CTPA
explanation.context: D-dimer is a fibrin degradation product elevated whenever cross-linked fibrin is being lysed. It has high sensitivity for VTE (>95%) but poor specificity (rises with age, infection, malignancy, pregnancy, recent surgery). The age-adjusted threshold (instead of fixed 500 mcg/L) corrects for the rise in baseline D-dimer with age, recovering specificity in older patients without sacrificing sensitivity. The PE-unlikely + negative D-dimer pathway has a 3-month VTE rate <1%, comparable to a negative CTPA, while avoiding imaging in 30% of patients.

options.rationale: Two-level Wells PE-unlikely (<=4) is followed by D-dimer testing. A negative age-adjusted D-dimer (age x 10 mcg/L for over-50s; conventional <500 for under-50s) rules out PE without imaging. CTPA is reserved for positive D-dimer or PE-likely Wells (>4).
CTPA in PE-unlikely patients without D-dimer leads to unnecessary contrast exposure, radiation and over-diagnosis of subsegmental PE. D-dimer reduces imaging by 30% in this group (eTG).

V/Q scan is appropriate when CTPA is contraindicated (severe contrast allergy, renal impairment, pregnancy) and the chest x-ray is clear. It is not the next step in a Wells-unlikely workup before D-dimer (TSANZ).

Leg ultrasound looks for deep vein thrombosis but does not exclude PE if negative. It can be a useful adjunct when imaging exposure must be minimised (pregnancy) but is not first-line in PE-unlikely workup (TSANZ).

Empirical anticoagulation in PE-unlikely patients without diagnostic confirmation exposes to bleeding risk without evidence-based indication. It is reserved for PE-likely patients with delays to imaging exceeding 4 hours (eTG).

explanation.summary: Severe GPA with crescentic GN and pulmonary nodules requires induction with high-dose corticosteroid plus either rituximab or cyclophosphamide. KHA-CARI 2022 favours rituximab for PR3-AAV, relapsing disease, and women of reproductive age. Steroid taper follows PEXIVAS reduced-dose schedule. Plasma exchange is reserved for severe alveolar haemorrhage or coexistent anti-GBM, not used alone.
key_points: Severe AAV = creatinine rise, crescentic GN, alveolar haemorrhage, neurological involvement
Induction = high-dose steroid + rituximab or cyclophosphamide
Rituximab preferred for PR3, relapses, fertility preservation
PEXIVAS established reduced-dose steroid taper; PLEX is adjunctive only
Azathioprine/MMF are maintenance, not induction
explanation.pearls: Saddle-nose plus cavitating lung nodules plus crescentic GN is the textbook GPA triad; PR3-ANCA positive in ~80% (KHA-CARI 2022).

sources.label: KHA-CARI Recommendations for the Management of ANCA-Associated Vasculitis 2022

options.rationale: Methotrexate is reserved for induction in non-severe GPA without major organ threat (no creatinine rise, no alveolar haemorrhage). With crescentic GN and pulmonary nodules this is severe disease requiring rituximab or cyclophosphamide (KHA-CARI ANCA-Associated Vasculitis 2022; EULAR/ERA-EDTA endorsed by RACP).
source_refs: KHA-CARI Recommendations for the Management of ANCA-Associated Vasculitis 2022

options.rationale: Severe GPA with crescentic GN and pulmonary involvement requires high-dose glucocorticoid induction plus rituximab or cyclophosphamide. KHA-CARI 2022 favours rituximab as first-line for relapsing disease, PR3 positivity, and women of reproductive age to preserve fertility; the RAVE and RITUXVAS trials established non-inferiority. Steroid taper follows the PEXIVAS reduced-dose schedule.
source_refs: KHA-CARI Recommendations for the Management of ANCA-Associated Vasculitis 2022

options.rationale: Azathioprine is a maintenance agent following induction with rituximab or cyclophosphamide, not an induction agent. Using azathioprine upfront leaves crescentic GN under-treated and risks irreversible loss of renal function (KHA-CARI 2022).
source_refs: KHA-CARI Recommendations for the Management of ANCA-Associated Vasculitis 2022

options.rationale: MMF was inferior to cyclophosphamide for induction in MYCYC and is not recommended for severe GPA with renal or alveolar involvement. It is acceptable only for non-severe disease when rituximab and cyclophosphamide are contraindicated (KHA-CARI 2022).
source_refs: KHA-CARI Recommendations for the Management of ANCA-Associated Vasculitis 2022

options.rationale: PEXIVAS showed plasma exchange does not reduce death or ESKD in AAV and should not be used alone. PLEX may still be considered for diffuse alveolar haemorrhage with hypoxia or coexisting anti-GBM, as an adjunct to standard induction, not in place of it (KHA-CARI 2022).
source_refs: KHA-CARI Recommendations for the Management of ANCA-Associated Vasculitis 2022

explanation.summary: EGPA is distinguished by the triad of late-onset asthma/nasal polyposis, peripheral eosinophilia >=1.0 x10^9/L, and a vasculitic phase with mononeuritis multiplex, palpable purpura, eosinophilic pneumonitis and sometimes cardiac involvement. ANCA is positive in only ~40%. The 2022 ACR/EULAR classification weights asthma + eosinophilia + nasal polyposis most heavily.
key_points: EGPA = asthma + eosinophilia + nasal polyps + vasculitis
ANCA positive in ~40%, mostly MPO/p-ANCA
Cardiac involvement is the leading cause of mortality - obtain echo and troponin
Treatment: high-dose steroid + cyclophosphamide or mepolizumab for severe disease
explanation.pearls: An asthmatic on escalating steroids who develops foot-drop, purpura and eosinophilia is EGPA until proven otherwise (KHA-CARI; eTG Rheumatology).

sources.label: KHA-CARI Recommendations for the Management of ANCA-Associated Vasculitis 2022

options.rationale: MPO-ANCA is found in only ~40% of EGPA and is also the dominant ANCA in MPA. It is not specific for EGPA. ANCA positivity in EGPA correlates with the vasculitic phenotype (glomerulonephritis, neuropathy) rather than identifying the syndrome itself (Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).

ACR/EULAR 2022 classification weights eosinophilia >=1.0 x10^9/L, obstructive airways disease, and nasal polyposis most heavily. This patient meets all three; mononeuritis multiplex and extravascular eosinophil-rich infiltrates add further score. GPA classically has nasal destruction without asthma/eosinophilia; MPA lacks both (KHA-CARI 2022; ACR/EULAR criteria).
source_refs: KHA-CARI Recommendations for the Management of ANCA-Associated Vasculitis 2022

options.rationale: Palpable purpura occurs across all small-vessel vasculitides including IgA vasculitis, cryoglobulinaemia, GPA and MPA. It is not discriminatory. Normal renal function is more typical of EGPA than GPA/MPA but is a supportive negative, not the diagnostic anchor.
Mononeuritis multiplex is seen in EGPA but also in polyarteritis nodosa, GPA, MPA, RA-associated vasculitis and cryoglobulinaemia. It supports vasculitis but does not specify which.

Ground-glass infiltrates are non-specific and seen in GPA, MPA (alveolar haemorrhage), infection and cardiogenic causes. EGPA pulmonary infiltrates are typically transient and migratory, but the appearance alone is insufficient.

explanation.summary: Takayasu arteritis is a large-vessel vasculitis of the aorta and its major branches, typically presenting in women under 40 with limb claudication, asymmetric pulses or BP, bruits and constitutional symptoms. Diagnosis is by cross-sectional imaging (CTA, MRA or PET-CT) showing characteristic long-segment wall thickening and stenoses. Treatment is high-dose corticosteroid with a steroid-sparing agent (methotrexate, azathioprine or biologics).
key_points: Takayasu: young woman, BP/pulse asymmetry, bruits, claudication
Diagnosis = imaging of aorta + major branches (CTA/MRA/PET-CT)
Distinguish from GCA: GCA is >50, cranial, with TAB
Treatment: prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day + methotrexate or biologic; revascularise only when inflammation suppressed
explanation.pearls: Always check BP in both arms in a young woman with constitutional symptoms - a >10 mmHg difference is a red flag for large-vessel vasculitis (eTG).

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology - Large vessel vasculitis

options.rationale: Temporal artery biopsy is the test for giant cell arteritis, which characteristically affects patients over 50 with cranial symptoms. A 28-year-old with upper-limb claudication and asymmetric pulses fits Takayasu (large-vessel vasculitis of the aorta and major branches), where biopsy is not feasible and imaging is the diagnostic modality (eTG Rheumatology).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology - Large vessel vasculitis

options.rationale: Takayasu is diagnosed by imaging the aorta and its primary branches, demonstrating long-segment wall thickening, stenoses or occlusions in characteristic distributions (arch vessels, subclavian, renal, mesenteric). CTA, MRA or PET-CT all qualify; CTA is most accessible and rapidly demonstrates luminal narrowing plus wall thickening. ACR/EULAR 2022 classification requires imaging confirmation in a patient <60 with characteristic vessel involvement.
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology - Large vessel vasculitis

options.rationale: Carotid duplex can detect the macaroni sign of homogeneous wall thickening in proximal carotids, but it cannot evaluate the descending aorta, renal or mesenteric vessels which are commonly involved in Takayasu. As a sole investigation it under-stages disease extent and misses critical lesions (eTG Rheumatology).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology - Large vessel vasculitis

options.rationale: Catheter angiography was the historic gold standard but is now reserved for interventional planning or when non-invasive imaging is non-diagnostic, given radiation, contrast load and arterial access risk in a young woman of reproductive age. CTA/MRA also visualises vessel wall thickening, which catheter angiography cannot (eTG Rheumatology).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology - Large vessel vasculitis

options.rationale: FDG-PET demonstrates vessel-wall inflammation but without anatomical co-registration localisation is imprecise, and luminal stenoses are not characterised. PET-CT is useful for disease activity assessment but a structural study (CTA or MRA) is the appropriate first diagnostic test (eTG Rheumatology).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology - Large vessel vasculitis

explanation.summary: GCA is a clinical-imaging-histological diagnosis. Glucocorticoid must be started immediately on clinical suspicion (IV methylprednisolone 1 g/day for 3 days if visual or neurological involvement, otherwise oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg). Temporal artery biopsy or temporal/axillary artery ultrasound should occur within 2 weeks of treatment start to preserve diagnostic yield. Biopsy length 1 to 2 cm minimises false negatives from skip lesions.
key_points: Steroid first, then biopsy - never the reverse
TAB yield preserved up to ~2 weeks after steroid start
Minimum biopsy length 1 cm (ideally 2 cm)
Temporal artery ultrasound (halo/compression) is an accepted alternative
Tocilizumab is steroid-sparing for relapsing or steroid-toxic GCA
explanation.pearls: The transient monocular blindness here is amaurosis fugax from anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy - the next event may be permanent (eTG).

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology - Large vessel vasculitis

options.rationale: While early biopsy is preferable, the diagnostic yield of TAB does not fall meaningfully in the first 1 to 2 weeks of steroid therapy because skip lesions and giant cells persist. Insisting on <24 h can lead to logistical delay of steroid (the actual sight-saving intervention) without diagnostic gain (eTG Rheumatology).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology - Large vessel vasculitis

options.rationale: BSR and EULAR guidance, adopted in eTG, accept TAB yield as preserved within 14 days of steroid initiation. The biopsy should be at least 1 cm (ideally 2 cm) to overcome skip lesions. Critically, steroid must never be delayed waiting for biopsy when GCA is clinically suspected, because the next ischaemic event may be permanent monocular or bilateral blindness.
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology - Large vessel vasculitis

options.rationale: Diagnostic yield falls substantially beyond 2 weeks of steroid exposure as inflammatory infiltrates resolve. A 4 to 6 week delay would compromise histological confirmation, which is important for long-term steroid commitment and steroid-sparing decisions (eTG Rheumatology).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology - Large vessel vasculitis

options.rationale: Temporal artery ultrasound (halo sign, compression sign) is increasingly used and may obviate biopsy in centres with operator expertise, but where ultrasound is unavailable or equivocal, biopsy remains the standard. The decision is not contingent on a negative ultrasound (eTG; EULAR).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology - Large vessel vasculitis

options.rationale: Clinical response to high-dose steroid is non-specific and occurs in many inflammatory conditions. Without histological confirmation, the patient may be committed to 18 to 24 months of steroid for the wrong diagnosis, with substantial harm. Biopsy provides the anchor for long-term management (eTG).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology - Large vessel vasculitis

explanation.summary: Newly diagnosed RA should receive a conventional synthetic DMARD within 12 weeks of symptom onset - the window of opportunity. Methotrexate is the anchor drug: start 10 to 15 mg weekly with folic acid, escalate to 20 to 25 mg, with a short prednisolone bridge. Treat-to-target with reassessment at 3 months and switch or add if remission/low disease activity not achieved.
key_points: Treat within 12 weeks (window of opportunity)
Methotrexate is first-line; start 10 to 15 mg, escalate to 20 to 25 mg weekly
Folic acid 5 mg on a non-MTX day to reduce mucositis and cytopenias
Steroid bridge for 8 to 12 weeks while MTX takes effect
PBS requires failure of 2 csDMARDs before biologic subsidy
explanation.pearls: Anti-CCP at high titre with early erosive risk predicts aggressive disease - escalate decisively (Australian Rheumatology Association).

options.rationale: Sulfasalazine is a reasonable second-line or methotrexate-intolerant choice but is less effective than methotrexate in seropositive erosive-risk disease. With high anti-CCP titre and high disease activity, methotrexate is the preferred first-line agent (Australian Rheumatology Association/eTG Rheumatology).

Hydroxychloroquine is a weak DMARD reserved for mild disease, SLE overlap or as combination therapy. As monotherapy in seropositive RA with moderate-to-high disease activity it under-treats and accepts ongoing joint damage (eTG Rheumatology).

Methotrexate is the EULAR/ACR/Australian Rheumatology Association first-line DMARD for newly diagnosed RA. Start 10 to 15 mg weekly, escalate by 5 mg every 2 to 4 weeks to a target of 20 to 25 mg as tolerated, with folic acid 5 mg on a non-MTX day. A short tapering prednisolone bridge controls symptoms during the 6 to 12 week onset of MTX action. Window of opportunity treatment within 12 weeks prevents erosions (eTG Rheumatology).

Triple therapy is an option for established RA failing methotrexate monotherapy or where biologics are contraindicated/unavailable. Australian first-line is methotrexate monotherapy with escalation to combination or biologic if target not met by 3 to 6 months. Starting all three simultaneously increases toxicity without proven first-line benefit (eTG Rheumatology).

PBS criteria require failure of at least two conventional synthetic DMARDs (one being methotrexate at >=20 mg/week for 3 months unless intolerant) before TNF-alpha inhibitor subsidy. Upfront biologic also exposes the patient unnecessarily to infection, reactivation TB and infusion-related risks before less expensive effective therapy is trialled.

explanation.summary: Before starting methotrexate, screen for hepatitis B (HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs), hepatitis C and HIV; assess baseline FBC, U&E, LFTs and chest X-ray; screen for TB with IGRA if from high-prevalence country or epidemiological risk; counsel on alcohol (<4 std drinks/week), pregnancy avoidance (3 months washout before conception in both partners), and live vaccines. Isolated anti-HBc positivity flags occult HBV and requires HBV DNA and antiviral prophylaxis planning before immunosuppression.
key_points: MTX pre-checks: FBC, U&E, LFTs, hep B/C/HIV, IGRA, CXR, pregnancy
Isolated anti-HBc = occult HBV - check HBV DNA, plan antiviral cover
Alcohol <4 std drinks/week
Folic acid 5 mg on non-MTX day
Monitor FBC, U&E, LFTs at 2-4 weekly initially then 3-monthly
explanation.pearls: Anti-HBc positive patients in HBV-endemic populations are common in Australian clinics; missing this is a sentinel error (ASHM).

sources.label: ASHM - Hepatitis B reactivation in immunosuppression

options.rationale: Reducing alcohol intake is essential and the eTG/Australian Rheumatology Association advice is no more than 4 standard drinks per week. However, this is a counselling intervention concurrent with starting therapy; it does not itself defer initiation and can be addressed alongside antiviral planning.

Isolated anti-HBc positivity in a patient from a HBV-endemic country indicates past or occult HBV infection. Methotrexate alone has low reactivation risk but when biologics or rituximab follow, reactivation can be fatal. Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine (ASHM) and gastroenterology bodies recommend HBV DNA quantification and consideration of entecavir/tenofovir prophylaxis before immunosuppression escalation. This is the highest-priority pre-treatment action.
source_refs: ASHM - Hepatitis B reactivation in immunosuppression

options.rationale: ALT 1.5x ULN in an obese drinker with metabolic risk likely reflects MAFLD or alcohol-related liver disease. eTG permits methotrexate with baseline transaminases up to 3x ULN provided monitoring is planned. Mere repetition without addressing aetiology or reactivation risk is insufficient.

Vaccination updates are important but inactivated vaccines (flu, pneumococcal, COVID-19, HBV catch-up) can be given before or after methotrexate. Live vaccines (varicella, MMR) should be avoided once methotrexate is started, but a 2 to 4 week delay to vaccinate does not address the HBV reactivation question, which is potentially lethal (eTG; ATAGI).

IGRA has high specificity and a single negative result in an asymptomatic patient with a normal CXR is sufficient before starting methotrexate. Repeat testing is reserved for new exposure or for biologic initiation in high-risk patients. Repeating IGRA delays therapy without informational gain.

explanation.summary: Methotrexate is contraindicated in pregnancy and must be stopped 1 to 3 months before conception in both partners. Bridge to pregnancy-compatible DMARDs - hydroxychloroquine and sulfasalazine - which can also be continued during lactation. Certolizumab pegol is the TNF-inhibitor of choice in pregnancy due to minimal placental transfer. Leflunomide requires colestyramine washout. RA tends to improve in pregnancy and flare postpartum, so plan postnatal escalation.
key_points: MTX: cease 1-3 months pre-conception in both partners
Pregnancy-compatible DMARDs: hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine
Pregnancy-compatible biologic: certolizumab pegol
Avoid: leflunomide (2-year half-life), MMF, cyclophosphamide
Plan postpartum flare review and lactation-compatible medication
explanation.pearls: Always counsel both partners; paternal MTX exposure also requires washout per ARA position statement.

sources.label: Australian Rheumatology Association - Medication in pregnancy

options.rationale: Methotrexate is teratogenic and abortifacient. Australian Rheumatology Association and eTG advise a washout of at least 1 to 3 months before attempting conception (UK BSR uses 3 months; some current guidelines accept 1 month given short half-life). However, ceasing without a replacement DMARD risks flare during conception. Both partners should have a washout discussion (eTG Rheumatology).

Methotrexate must be stopped at least 1 to 3 months before conception. Bridge to pregnancy-compatible DMARDs - hydroxychloroquine and/or sulfasalazine - which can be continued throughout pregnancy and lactation. This maintains disease control, reduces flare risk and avoids the fetal harm of MTX (eTG Rheumatology; ARA Position Statement).
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association - Medication in pregnancy

options.rationale: Methotrexate exposure in early embryogenesis causes neural tube defects, craniofacial abnormalities and limb defects, and is abortifacient. By the time pregnancy is confirmed (5 to 6 weeks), exposure has already occurred during organogenesis. This approach causes the harm it is supposed to avoid (eTG).

Leflunomide is teratogenic with an active metabolite that persists for up to 2 years. Colestyramine washout is required before conception, and it is contraindicated in women planning pregnancy. This is a worse choice than continuing methotrexate (eTG).
Folic acid does not abrogate methotrexate teratogenicity. Methotrexate is contraindicated in pregnancy regardless of folic acid dose. This is a common but dangerous misconception (eTG).

explanation.summary: Psoriatic arthritis presents with peripheral synovitis (especially DIPs), dactylitis (sausage digit), enthesitis, nail changes (pitting, onycholysis) and the radiographic pencil-in-cup with juxta-articular new bone. RF/anti-CCP are typically negative. First-line systemic therapy is methotrexate; escalate to TNF-alpha, IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitor per PBS criteria if inadequate response at 3 to 6 months.
key_points: PsA = DIP synovitis + dactylitis + enthesitis + nail changes
RF/anti-CCP negative; pencil-in-cup classic on imaging
Methotrexate first-line; sulfasalazine if MTX intolerant
Avoid hydroxychloroquine and long-term oral steroid (psoriasis flare)
PBS biologic after >=6 months MTX or leflunomide failure
explanation.pearls: Sausage digit + DIP involvement + psoriasis = PsA, even with normal inflammatory markers (eTG).

options.rationale: For peripheral psoriatic arthritis with synovitis, dactylitis and nail involvement and no contraindications, methotrexate is first-line conventional DMARD per eTG/Australasian guidance. It also treats cutaneous psoriasis. Escalate to 20 to 25 mg weekly with folic acid. TNF-alpha inhibitors and IL-17 inhibitors are reserved for csDMARD failure (PBS criteria require this for subsidy).

Sulfasalazine is effective for peripheral joint disease in PsA but does not treat skin psoriasis, dactylitis or enthesitis. With prominent skin disease and dactylitis, methotrexate is preferred first-line. Sulfasalazine is reasonable if methotrexate intolerant (eTG Rheumatology).

TNF-alpha inhibitors are highly effective in PsA but PBS subsidy requires prior failure of at least 6 months of methotrexate or leflunomide (or contraindication). Upfront biologic is not standard first-line for peripheral disease without poor prognostic markers requiring rapid escalation (PBS).
Hydroxychloroquine is relatively contraindicated in psoriasis due to risk of triggering generalised pustular psoriasis or erythroderma. It is not recommended in PsA (eTG; ARA).

Long-term oral steroid is contraindicated in psoriasis as withdrawal can precipitate generalised pustular psoriasis. Short bridging tapers can be used cautiously while a DMARD takes effect, but never as monotherapy (eTG).

explanation.summary: Scleroderma renal crisis is a sudden malignant hypertension with AKI and microangiopathic haemolysis, typically in diffuse cutaneous SSc with anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies, often precipitated by glucocorticoid >15 mg/day prednisolone. Treatment is rapid-titration ACE inhibitor (captopril) even as creatinine rises further. ARBs are inferior. Survival and renal recovery depend on prompt ACEi.
key_points: Risk: diffuse SSc, anti-RNA pol III, recent steroid >15 mg/day
Triad: new malignant HTN + AKI + MAHA with normal ADAMTS13
Treatment: captopril uptitrated 6-8 hourly, accept transient creatinine rise
Avoid: high-dose steroid (precipitant), sublingual nifedipine, PLEX
Many need dialysis; recovery possible up to 18 months
explanation.pearls: Any new hypertension in a scleroderma patient on prednisolone is renal crisis until proven otherwise (eTG).

options.rationale: ACE inhibitors are the disease-modifying treatment for scleroderma renal crisis. Other antihypertensives reduce blood pressure but do not reverse the renin-angiotensin-driven thrombotic microangiopathy. ACEi is the only therapy that improves renal and patient survival in this condition (eTG Rheumatology).

Scleroderma renal crisis is treated with ACE inhibitor (typically captopril for rapid titration), even when AKI worsens transiently. ACEi blocks the renin-driven angiotensin II cascade that is the proximal driver of the malignant hypertension and microangiopathic haemolysis. Captopril is started 12.5 to 25 mg, uptitrated 6 to 8 hourly until BP is controlled; many patients still require dialysis but renal recovery is more likely with ACEi than without (eTG Rheumatology; Scleroderma Australia).

ADAMTS13 activity of 65% rules out TTP (where activity is typically <10%). The microangiopathy in scleroderma renal crisis is secondary to malignant hypertension and renal endothelial injury, not deficient ADAMTS13. Plasma exchange does not reverse it; ACEi does (eTG; KHA-CARI).

High-dose corticosteroid (especially >15 mg/day prednisolone) is a major risk factor for precipitating scleroderma renal crisis, particularly in anti-RNA polymerase III positive diffuse SSc. Escalating steroid worsens the condition. Steroids should be minimised and ACEi started (eTG; ARA).

Sublingual nifedipine causes unpredictable abrupt BP drops with risk of cerebral or coronary hypoperfusion and is contraindicated in hypertensive emergency. It also does not address the underlying renin-driven pathophysiology of scleroderma renal crisis (eTG Cardiovascular).

explanation.summary: Hydroxychloroquine dose should not exceed 5 mg/kg actual body weight to minimise retinal toxicity. RANZCO recommends baseline ophthalmology at initiation, then annual screening from 5 years of cumulative use, earlier if dose >5 mg/kg, CKD eGFR <60, tamoxifen co-exposure or pre-existing macular disease. Modern screening combines OCT, automated 10-2 (or 24-2) visual fields and fundus autofluorescence; Amsler grid is inadequate.
key_points: Dose ceiling: 5 mg/kg actual body weight
Baseline ophthalmology at start; annual from year 5
Earlier annual screening: high dose, CKD, tamoxifen, macular disease
Screening tools: OCT + 10-2 visual fields + FAF, not Amsler
Hydroxychloroquine reduces SLE flares and damage; do not cease in remission
explanation.pearls: Tamoxifen co-exposure dramatically increases HCQ retinopathy risk - flag in clinic letters (RANZCO).

options.rationale: 400 mg in a 58 kg patient is 6.9 mg/kg, exceeding the 5 mg/kg actual body weight ceiling that minimises retinopathy risk per RANZCO and the American Academy of Ophthalmology. Dose reduction is required even if current screening interval is appropriate (RANZCO Position Statement).

Dose ceiling is <=5 mg/kg actual body weight to minimise retinopathy risk; 290 mg for this 58 kg patient, so 300 mg daily or alternate-day dosing achieves the target. RANZCO and AAO recommend a baseline examination at initiation, then annual screening from 5 years of cumulative use. Earlier screening is indicated for tamoxifen co-exposure, CKD (eGFR <60), or daily dose >5 mg/kg. Her prior tamoxifen plus past over-dosing flags this patient for early annual screening.

Clinical remission does not reduce retinopathy risk; cumulative dose does. 400 mg/day in a 58 kg patient is overdose. Screening at 10 years risks missing irreversible bull's-eye maculopathy. RANZCO recommends annual screening from 5 years (RANZCO).

Hydroxychloroquine reduces SLE flares, organ damage and mortality; ceasing in remission predictably leads to flare. Steroid monotherapy increases cumulative steroid toxicity. The correct action is dose adjustment and continued screening, not withdrawal (eTG; ARA).

Amsler grid is insensitive to early hydroxychloroquine retinopathy, which begins as parafoveal photoreceptor disruption detectable only with OCT, automated visual fields (10-2 or 24-2 with central testing) and fundus autofluorescence. Self-testing is not a substitute for formal annual screening (RANZCO).

explanation.summary: Proliferative lupus nephritis (class III/IV) is treated with pulsed glucocorticoid plus mycophenolate mofetil or low-dose IV cyclophosphamide (Euro-Lupus). Hydroxychloroquine is continued lifelong. Maintenance is mycophenolate or azathioprine for at least 3 years. Belimumab and voclosporin are emerging add-ons. ACEi/ARB and BP control to <130/80 are essential adjuncts.
key_points: Class III/IV LN: pulse steroid + MMF or low-dose IV cyclophosphamide
MMF preferred in fertility-sparing context
Hydroxychloroquine always continued
Maintenance: MMF or azathioprine >=3 years
ACEi/ARB and BP <130/80 mandatory adjuncts
explanation.pearls: Euro-Lupus 500 mg IV cyclophosphamide fortnightly x 6 is markedly less toxic than the older NIH regimen with equivalent renal outcomes (KHA-CARI 2022).

sources.label: KHA-CARI Recommendations for the Management of Lupus Nephritis 2022

options.rationale: KHA-CARI 2022 and EULAR/ERA-EDTA endorse pulsed glucocorticoid followed by oral prednisolone 0.5 to 0.8 mg/kg/day (reduced-dose taper) plus either mycophenolate mofetil 2 to 3 g/day or low-dose IV cyclophosphamide (Euro-Lupus 500 mg fortnightly x 6) as induction for proliferative class III/IV lupus nephritis. Hydroxychloroquine is continued. Belimumab or voclosporin add-on is increasingly used. MMF is preferred in women of reproductive age to preserve fertility.
source_refs: KHA-CARI Recommendations for the Management of Lupus Nephritis 2022

options.rationale: Azathioprine is a maintenance agent for lupus nephritis, not induction. Inducting class IV LN with azathioprine accepts ongoing glomerular damage and risks progression to ESKD (KHA-CARI 2022).
source_refs: KHA-CARI Recommendations for the Management of Lupus Nephritis 2022

options.rationale: Rituximab is considered for refractory or relapsing LN, not first-line induction (LUNAR trial did not meet primary endpoint). Ceasing hydroxychloroquine worsens outcomes in lupus and is contrary to all guidelines (KHA-CARI 2022; ARA).
source_refs: KHA-CARI Recommendations for the Management of Lupus Nephritis 2022

options.rationale: Class IV LN with red cell casts and rising creatinine requires urgent immunosuppression. Waiting for creatinine doubling commits the patient to irreversible glomerular sclerosis. ACEi and statin are adjuncts, not substitutes (KHA-CARI).
source_refs: KHA-CARI Recommendations for the Management of Lupus Nephritis 2022

options.rationale: Plasma exchange has no proven benefit in lupus nephritis outside of co-existing TTP or anti-GBM. Used alone it does not address the underlying glomerular immune complex deposition (KHA-CARI 2022).
source_refs: KHA-CARI Recommendations for the Management of Lupus Nephritis 2022

explanation.summary: PMR is a clinical diagnosis in patients >50 with new bilateral shoulder/hip-girdle pain, morning stiffness >45 min, elevated CRP/ESR, and exclusion of mimics (RA, inflammatory myopathy, hypothyroidism, malignancy, late-onset spondyloarthropathy). Treatment is prednisolone 12.5 to 25 mg/day with rapid symptomatic response. Steroid-sparing methotrexate or tocilizumab for relapse or toxicity. Always screen for GCA at every review.
key_points: PMR starting dose: prednisolone 12.5-25 mg/day
Rapid response (within 1 week) is diagnostic and required
Always screen for coexisting GCA at every review
Bone protection from initiation; bisphosphonate if Tx >=3 months
MTX or tocilizumab for relapse or steroid toxicity
explanation.pearls: Failure to respond to 25 mg prednisolone within 1 week means it is not PMR - reconsider RA, inflammatory myopathy or malignancy (eTG).

options.rationale: EULAR/ACR and eTG recommend prednisolone 12.5 to 25 mg daily as the starting dose for PMR. Most patients improve within days; lack of >=75% response by 1 week should prompt diagnostic re-evaluation (GCA, RA, inflammatory myopathy, late-onset spondyloarthropathy). Co-prescribe calcium 1.3 g, vitamin D, and assess fracture risk for bisphosphonate therapy (PBS criteria met when prednisolone >=7.5 mg/day for >=3 months).

PMR without cranial symptoms responds to 12.5 to 25 mg/day; using GCA doses (60 to 80 mg) over-treats and dramatically increases steroid toxicity (osteoporosis, diabetes, infection). High-dose pulse is reserved for ophthalmic or neurological GCA presentations (eTG).

Methotrexate is a steroid-sparing agent considered for relapsing PMR or unacceptable steroid toxicity, not initial monotherapy. PMR is exquisitely steroid-responsive and that response is itself diagnostic (eTG).
NSAIDs are generally ineffective for PMR and risk gastric, renal and cardiovascular harm in this age group. Steroid is the standard first-line therapy (eTG).
Tocilizumab is currently used for steroid-refractory or relapsing PMR (and is the standard add-on for GCA), not as initial therapy. PBS subsidy is for GCA, not PMR alone (PBS).

explanation.summary: Adult IgA vasculitis differs from the childhood form in carrying significant renal risk (~30% CKD/ESKD). Renal biopsy is indicated for: uPCR >100 mg/mmol persisting beyond 4 weeks, creatinine rise, or nephritic features. Histology determines need for immunosuppression: crescentic disease is treated with steroid +/- cyclophosphamide, while milder mesangioproliferative disease is managed with ACEi/ARB and BP control. ASOT is checked to exclude post-streptococcal GN.
key_points: Adult IgA vasculitis: 30% develop CKD
Biopsy if uPCR >100 mg/mmol, AKI, nephritic features
Histology determines immunosuppression intensity
ACEi/ARB and BP control for all with proteinuria
Childhood form usually self-limiting; adult form not
explanation.pearls: An adult with the classic IgA vasculitis tetrad (purpura, arthralgia, abdominal pain, glomerulonephritis) and persistent proteinuria needs prompt renal biopsy (KHA-CARI).

options.rationale: Adult IgA vasculitis carries substantially higher renal risk than the childhood form. KDIGO 2024 and KHA-CARI guidance recommend renal biopsy in adults with uPCR >100 mg/mmol (or proteinuria persisting >4 weeks), creatinine rise, or nephritic features, because crescentic IgA nephritis requires immunosuppression. His uPCR of 105 mg/mmol and creatinine creep meet criteria. Biopsy distinguishes those who need corticosteroids/cyclophosphamide from those manageable with ACEi alone.

Childhood IgA vasculitis is largely self-limiting, but adult disease has a ~30% risk of CKD or ESKD. Significant proteinuria with rising creatinine is not safe to observe for 6 weeks without renal characterisation (KHA-CARI).

Empirical high-dose steroid commits the patient to side effects without confirming histology, and undertreats severe crescentic disease that may require steroid plus cyclophosphamide. Steroid for cutaneous and arthralgic symptoms alone is also non-evidence-based (KDIGO 2024).

ACEi is appropriate adjunct therapy but does not characterise the histological severity. Significant proteinuria with creatinine rise in adult IgA vasculitis is an early-biopsy indication; a 12-week observation can miss crescentic GN window for treatment (KHA-CARI).

Skin biopsy with IgA-dominant immune complex deposition supports IgA vasculitis diagnostically but does not characterise renal involvement or stratify treatment. With significant proteinuria, renal biopsy is the indicated next step (KHA-CARI; KDIGO).

explanation.summary: Obstetric APS is defined by clinical criteria (>=3 unexplained first-trimester losses, or fetal loss >=10 weeks, or severe early pre-eclampsia/placental insufficiency <34 weeks) plus persistent laboratory criteria (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin IgG/IgM, or beta-2-glycoprotein-1 IgG/IgM) confirmed 12 weeks apart. Treatment is low-dose aspirin plus prophylactic LMWH from confirmation of pregnancy until 6 weeks postpartum. Thrombotic APS requires therapeutic anticoagulation; warfarin is the agent outside pregnancy. DOACs are inferior to warfarin for triple-positive APS (TRAPS trial).
key_points: Obstetric APS = clinical criteria + persistent aPL 12 weeks apart
Treatment: aspirin 100 mg + prophylactic LMWH through pregnancy + 6 wks postpartum
Thrombotic APS = warfarin INR 2-3 (outside pregnancy); DOACs inferior
Hydroxychloroquine: adjunct in refractory cases or with SLE
Avoid: steroid/IVIG (not standard), warfarin in pregnancy
explanation.pearls: Triple-positive APS (LA + aCL + b2GP1) has the highest event rate; do not use DOACs (TRAPS).

options.rationale: Aspirin alone is insufficient for women meeting obstetric APS criteria with three or more first-trimester miscarriages. Combined low-dose aspirin plus prophylactic LMWH improves live birth rates over aspirin alone (RANZCOG; ARA). Aspirin monotherapy is reserved for asymptomatic aPL carriers (no obstetric or thrombotic history) requiring primary prevention.

Obstetric APS (>=3 unexplained first-trimester losses, or fetal loss >=10 weeks, or severe pre-eclampsia/placental insufficiency <34 weeks, with persistent aPL on testing 12 weeks apart) is treated with low-dose aspirin plus prophylactic LMWH throughout pregnancy. LMWH is continued for 6 weeks postpartum due to venous thromboembolism risk. RANZCOG and ARA guidance align (Sapporo criteria).

Therapeutic anticoagulation is reserved for thrombotic APS (prior venous or arterial event), not obstetric APS without thrombosis. Warfarin is teratogenic and contraindicated in pregnancy. This regimen over-treats and exposes to warfarin embryopathy (RANZCOG).
Hydroxychloroquine may be an adjunct in refractory obstetric APS or in those with concurrent SLE, but is not first-line monotherapy. Standard care is aspirin + prophylactic LMWH (RANZCOG; ARA).

Glucocorticoids and IVIG were trialled historically with negative results and added maternal morbidity (gestational diabetes, hypertension, PPROM). They are not standard of care for obstetric APS and may be considered only in refractory cases under specialist supervision (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Polyarteritis nodosa is a necrotising medium-vessel vasculitis with multisystem involvement (renal, mesenteric, cutaneous livedo, testicular, neuropathy) and characteristic angiographic microaneurysms. Glomerulonephritis is notably absent. Historically ~30% of cases were HBV-associated; this has fallen with vaccination but remains relevant in patients from HBV-endemic areas. HBV-associated PAN is treated with brief corticosteroid, plasma exchange, and immediate nucleos(t)ide antiviral therapy (entecavir or tenofovir). Idiopathic PAN is treated with corticosteroid plus cyclophosphamide.
key_points: PAN: medium-vessel, microaneurysms, no glomerulonephritis
Always test HBV in newly diagnosed PAN
HBV-PAN: short steroid + PLEX + entecavir/tenofovir
Idiopathic PAN: steroid + cyclophosphamide
Avoid prolonged immunosuppression in HBV-PAN
explanation.pearls: The combination of livedo, mononeuritis multiplex, testicular pain and renal microaneurysms with normal urine sediment is classic for PAN (eTG).

options.rationale: In HBV-associated PAN, prolonged cyclophosphamide and ongoing steroid sustain viral replication and accelerate liver damage. The Guillevin protocol uses a short steroid course followed by plasma exchange and antiviral therapy rather than prolonged cytotoxic immunosuppression (ASHM; eTG Rheumatology).

HBV-associated PAN is treated with a short induction of corticosteroid (to control the vasculitic inflammation), plasma exchange (to clear immune complexes), and prompt nucleos(t)ide antiviral therapy (entecavir or tenofovir) to suppress HBV replication, which is the proximal driver. Prolonged cyclophosphamide is avoided as it perpetuates viraemia and liver injury. This Guillevin-protocol approach is endorsed by ASHM and eTG Rheumatology.

Rituximab is the standard induction for ANCA-associated vasculitis but is not standard for classic medium-vessel PAN, and B-cell depletion increases HBV reactivation risk dramatically. Without confirmed efficacy and with substantial harm risk, this is the wrong choice (ASHM).

Pegylated interferon was used historically for HBV-associated vasculitis but has largely been superseded by nucleos(t)ide analogues (entecavir, tenofovir) which give faster, more reliable viral suppression with fewer adverse effects. Long high-dose prednisolone alongside interferon increases harm without diagnostic benefit (ASHM).

Deferring antiviral therapy in HBV-associated PAN allows ongoing viral replication, immune complex deposition and disease progression; high-dose monotherapy steroid alone permits HBV flare. Antiviral suppression is the disease-modifying intervention and should not wait (ASHM).

explanation.summary: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle includes: measure lactate, obtain cultures, administer antibiotics, commence fluid resuscitation, and initiate vasopressors for persistent hypotension. Among these, early antibiotics have the strongest mortality evidence with each hour of delay increasing mortality by 7-8% in septic shock. All elements should be initiated simultaneously but antibiotic timeliness is the single most important modifiable factor.
key_points: Each hour of antibiotic delay in septic shock increases mortality ~7-8%
Cultures before antibiotics but must not delay antibiotic administration
30 mL/kg traditional target but evidence supports individualised approach
Vasopressors target MAP >=65 during or after fluid resuscitation
All bundle elements initiated within 1 hour of sepsis recognition
explanation.pearls: The mortality benefit of antibiotics within 1 hour is most pronounced in septic shock - in sepsis without shock the relationship is less steep but still favours early administration within 3 hours, informing triage priorities.

options.rationale: Lactate measurement enables better care but the mortality reduction comes from treatments it guides rather than the measurement itself. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

Early antibiotics have the strongest mortality evidence. Each hour of delay is associated with approximately 7-8% increased mortality in septic shock. Appropriate empiric coverage is more important than awaiting cultures. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Fluid resuscitation is critical but recent evidence (CLOVERS, CLASSIC trials) questions universal 30 mL/kg and suggests equivalent outcomes with restrictive approaches. Antibiotic evidence is more consistent. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

Cultures should not delay antibiotics. If obtaining cultures would delay by >30-45 minutes, antibiotics should be given first. Culture collection does not directly reduce mortality. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

Vasopressors address haemodynamics rather than infection source. While timely, the mortality benefit of antibiotics addressing infection is more robustly demonstrated. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

explanation.summary: Lactate-guided resuscitation uses serial measurements every 2-4 hours to assess perfusion adequacy. A declining trend indicates improvement while failure to clear suggests ongoing inadequacy. The target is normalisation or >=10-20% reduction per interval. Persistent elevation despite MAP targets should prompt reassessment.
key_points: Remeasure lactate every 2-4 hours in sepsis with initial elevation
Target normalisation or >=10-20% reduction per interval
Failure to clear despite adequate MAP warrants intensification
Lactate clearance rate independently associated with mortality
Bicarbonate does not treat underlying septic hyperlactataemia
explanation.pearls: Lactate clearance exceeding 10% at 6 hours is associated with approximately 11% absolute mortality reduction compared to non-clearers in septic shock - making 6-hour clearance one of the strongest early prognostic markers at the bedside.

options.rationale: MAP >=65 is only one target. Lactate remaining elevated at 4.8 indicates ongoing hypoperfusion. Poor clearance with low urine output indicates inadequate resuscitation despite adequate MAP. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)
This patient's lactate was elevated before noradrenaline. Type B causes should not be assumed in an under-resuscitated septic patient. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

Only 8% reduction (5.2 to 4.8) in 2 hours indicates poor clearance. Target is >=10-20% reduction per interval or normalisation. Inadequate clearance warrants intensification: further fluid, optimise vasopressor, reassess source control. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021; ANZICS)
Bicarbonate does not treat the cause of septic hyperlactataemia and is not recommended unless pH <7.15 with AKI. Treatment is improving tissue perfusion. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)
Lactate remains valid and guideline-recommended even after vasopressor initiation. It does not replace ScvO2 - both can be used. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

explanation.summary: The distinction between hypertensive emergency and urgency is presence of acute target organ damage, not absolute BP. Emergency requires acute brain (encephalopathy, stroke), heart (ACS, oedema, dissection), kidney (acute rise creatinine), or eye (grade III-IV) damage. Urgency is managed with oral optimisation and gradual reduction to avoid cerebral hypoperfusion in adapted patients.
key_points: Emergency = severe BP + acute target organ damage
Urgency = severe BP without acute damage
Chronic LVH and grade I-II retinopathy indicate longstanding poor control, not acute emergency
Urgency: reduce no more than 25% MAP in first 24-48 hours
Emergency: IV therapy, reduce 20-25% in first 1-2 hours
explanation.pearls: Reducing BP too rapidly in chronic severe hypertension risks cerebral watershed infarction - the autoregulatory curve shifts rightward meaning a 'normal' MAP of 90 may be below the lower autoregulatory limit in adapted patients.

options.rationale: No evidence of acute target organ damage. Headache is the only symptom, CT clear, no papilloedema, stable creatinine, negative troponin, chronic changes only. This is urgency not emergency. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Correctly classified as urgency but 24-48 hours is too rapid for asymptomatic urgency. Target is gradual reduction over days to weeks to avoid cerebral hypoperfusion. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Malignant hypertension requires grade III-IV retinopathy (haemorrhages, cotton wool spots, papilloedema). Grade II is chronic. This is poorly controlled hypertension, not malignant. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Hypertensive urgency (severe BP without acute organ damage). Chronic retinopathy and LVH represent longstanding poor control. Management: optimise oral therapy, reduce no more than 25% MAP in first 24-48 hours, then gradual to goal over weeks. Outpatient follow-up. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular; NHFA/CSANZ)

Headache alone with severe BP does not constitute emergency. Emergency requires acute organ damage. Nitroprusside carries excessive hypotension risk and is reserved for genuine emergencies. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Aortic dissection requires urgent BP and HR control. Aortic wall shear stress depends on both absolute pressure and rate of pressure rise (dP/dt), making HR control equally important. IV labetalol is first-line addressing both targets. Agents causing reflex tachycardia are dangerous as monotherapy. Stanford type B without complications is managed medically.
key_points: Dual target: SBP 100-120 AND HR <60 within 20 minutes
IV labetalol first-line (combined alpha + beta blockade)
Reflex tachycardia agents contraindicated as monotherapy
Target achieved within 20 minutes (unlike urgency which is gradual)
Stanford type B without complications: medical intensive BP control
explanation.pearls: dP/dt (rate of aortic pressure rise) is more important than absolute systolic pressure for dissection propagation - achieving HR <60 is prioritised even before SBP target, explaining why pure vasodilators (increasing dP/dt via reflex tachycardia) worsen dissection despite lowering the BP number.

options.rationale: Nitroprusside causes reflex tachycardia increasing aortic shear stress and propagating dissection. Never use as monotherapy in dissection. Also too aggressive a target. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Hydralazine causes reflex tachycardia which is dangerous in dissection. Increased heart rate and dP/dt propagate the flap. Need agents reducing both BP and HR. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

GTN can cause reflex tachycardia and does not adequately reduce aortic shear stress. Pain resolution alone is not the target - haemodynamic control (SBP and HR) is primary. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Beta-blocker first then vasodilator is conceptually correct but nitroprusside has largely been replaced due to cyanide toxicity. Labetalol achieves both goals with a single agent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

IV labetalol (combined alpha and beta blocker) is first-line for aortic dissection reducing both BP and HR (reducing aortic wall shear stress and dP/dt). Target SBP 100-120 and HR <60 within 20 minutes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular; ESC Guidelines Aortic Diseases)
